#6258. But Our Flag Was Still There

Imagine a time when Americans could be arrested by soldiers and imprisoned without the ordinary opportunity to challenge their detention before a judge. When a former congressman could be tried by a military commission for a political speech, then banished from the country. When newspaper offices could be occupied by troops and publication stopped. Imagine an editor imprisoned in the very fortress his grandfather had immortalized in a song about American freedom.

O say, can you see By the dawn’s early light

I woke up this morning thinking about the question at the beginning of our national anthem.

After an election, we tend to look for answers. This morning, I find myself more interested in what we can still see.

I see a country in which people cast ballots and those ballots have consequences. A country in which officeholders can be challenged and voters can change the direction of government. I see people who care enough to argue, sometimes bitterly, about the future of a place they still believe is worth fighting for.

That is an exhausting way to govern ourselves, but what a remarkable inheritance!

What so proudly we hailed At the twilight’s last gleaming

The president in those opening examples was Abraham Lincoln.

His administration’s restrictions on civil liberties are part of our history, even if they sit uncomfortably alongside the achievements for which we rightly honor him.

Beginning in 1861, Lincoln authorized the suspension of habeas corpus, the means by which a detainee can ask a court to examine the legality of detention. The Constitution permits suspension in cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety requires it. Whether the president could exercise that authority without Congress was fiercely contested. The practical consequence was that people could be held by military authorities without the ordinary judicial protection against unlawful imprisonment.

In September 1862, his proclamation, circulated by the War Department as General Orders No. 141, subjected people discouraging enlistment or engaging in broadly described disloyal practices aiding the rebellion to military trial. It also suspended habeas corpus for those detained by military authority.

These were sweeping powers, with consequences far beyond the battlefield.

Whose broad stripes and bright stars Through the perilous fight

In 1863, a former Ohio congressman was arrested after delivering an antiwar speech, tried by a military commission, and convicted. Lincoln changed his punishment from imprisonment to banishment into Confederate territory.

Another critic, a Baltimore newspaper editor, had been arrested in 1861 and confined at Fort McHenry. His grandfather was Francis Scott Key. Think about that for a moment. The grandson of the man who wrote the words we sing about the land of the free became a political prisoner inside the fort associated with those words.

He was a Southern sympathizer. The former congressman’s politics were deeply objectionable in their defense of a slaveholding order. But we do not need to admire either man’s cause to take seriously the government’s treatment of him. Constitutional protections have little substance if they depend on our approval of the person invoking them.

O’er the ramparts we watched Were so gallantly streaming

General Ambrose Burnside ordered the suppression of the Chicago Times in 1863. Lincoln intervened to have that order revoked. That correction belongs in the account as much as the original abuse.

But in 1864, after the New York World and Journal of Commerce published a forged presidential proclamation, Lincoln himself ordered military action against the papers, including seizure of their printing establishments and the arrest of their editors and publishers.

The forgery was serious. So was the use of military power against newspapers.

All of this happened while the country was fighting a rebellion rooted in slavery, with its survival genuinely in doubt. That context is essential to understanding Lincoln’s decisions. Even so, it does not place those decisions beyond scrutiny and reminds us today there is nothing new under the sun.

I can regard Lincoln as a great president and still recoil at some of the powers exercised under his administration. An honest affection for America must leave room for that.

And the rockets’ red glare The bombs bursting in air

Our anthem was born of an actual bombardment. The danger was physical, and the outcome could not yet be known.

We sometimes speak of our own political moment as though we alone have discovered uncertainty. Every alarming development becomes unprecedented. Every election becomes the final opportunity to save the country.

Some warnings deserve our attention. Rights can erode, and institutions can fail. History offers plenty of evidence for the absolute necessity vigilance.

This country has been torn apart by civil war. It has tolerated profound injustice while congratulating itself on liberty. It has denied the protection of its promises to people who had every right to claim them.

And Americans have challenged those failures…often at great personal cost and against a majority quite comfortable with the way things were.

The work has never been easy, and progress has never been secure. The end of slavery did not prevent the injustices that followed. A constitutional promise could exist for generations before people received anything approaching its protection.

But the promise gave people something to demand. It still does.

Gave proof through the night That our flag was still there

I won’t comment on the outcome itself, but I have great hope after an election like this. The system is working. Imperfectly, unevenly, and with people understandably dissatisfied by its results. Yet democracy remains alive. Voters can register disapproval and impose consequences. Political power remains something that must answer to the public.

One election cannot certify the health of an entire republic. It can, however, demonstrate that the mechanisms of accountability still operate. I think we should allow ourselves to recognize that today, across political lines.

I spend much of my life traveling beyond our borders. That has made me more conscious of how much I value the ability to criticize my government openly and expect another opportunity to vote. Neither should be taken for granted.

We have built something very special here. Its failures are real, and so is its capacity for correction.

Repairing what is broken will require patient work long after the election coverage ends. Some damage will take years to undo. Some losses cannot be restored to the people who suffered them.

Still, Americans before us have undertaken that work under circumstances far more desperate than ours. We can honor them by continuing it.

This morning, I feel grateful that the country remains ours to shape. Grateful that disappointment can find expression at a ballot box. And I’m hopeful that we retain enough humility to recognize our mistakes and enough resolve to address them.

The anthem ends with a question. After all this time, it remains a question worth asking ourselves.

O say, does that star-spangled banner yet wave O’er the land of the free and the home of the brave

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Without a doubt, this is your best writing ever. Well done. History lessons, especially today, are important reminders, especially during the times we came up short, even for the ‘right’ reasons. The best we can do, as citizens, is remember all of our history, not just the convenient parts.

5 years ago, I heard the theory that Trump is a Democratic plant but not from above. Instead, he thought of it himself. He would destroy the GOP himself from within, sort of like a sleeper spy.

He has donated to Democratic candidates. He was a Democrat. The only difference is 1. he is a moderate Democrat, not a far leftist, 2. he likes money himself. So very fitting that he’d destroy the GOP at the last possible moment, the midterms of his last term (or his 3rd term, first 2 being elected in 2016 and 2020, ha ha ha)

I have often heard the complaint in recent years that our nation is more polarized than ever before and that our Congress is too hobbled by factionalism to function. It is always important to remember that there was once a time that members of Congress killed each other over disagreements, and that our nation spent years actively at war with itself because of polarized views on federal power and “states’ rights” to enslave people.

I remember when I was a kid my parents taking me into the voting booth on Election Day and watching them cast their ballots. This year was the first time I got to take my son with me. This seemingly simple action to hold our government to account is what my 7th great grandfather fought for when he joined his neighbors in Concord in insurrection against His Majesty’s government. So long as our politicians are scared of elections, our republic will survive.

Last week an infant died in New York from measles for the first time in 30 years. Head start has been gutted and food benefits for poverty stricken children shaved. Our farmers cannot pay the high costs of the fuel. All but 4 NTSB recommendations after the crash at DCA have been ignored. Can anyone wonder why the election results were brutal?

I don’t have the answer for these problems, thank you Matthew for this thoughtful post. .

United Airlines will expand to northern Mexico next spring despite a cloudy outlook.

The Star Alliance carrier will return to Chihuahua Airport (CUU) in northern Mexico from Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) beginning March 28, 2027.

Edibray Gómez Gallegos, the secretary of tourism of Chihuahua state, said the new route will increase connectivity for the state and "reflects growing interest among North American travelers in discovering the many tourist attractions Chihuahua has to offer."

United last served the IAH-CUU route in 2020, according to schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. It will join American Airlines among U.S. carriers serving the airport.

A spacious Bombardier CRJ-550 will be used on the route. The plane, originally a 70-seat CRJ-700, is fitted with 10 first-class, 20 extra-legroom economy and 20 economy seats.

Other news: United is bringing its nicest plane (with the Polaris Studios) to a city that never sees it

The new CUU route comes as airlines around the globe have been forced to adjust to soaring fuel costs.

United CEO Scott Kirby has previously warned that United has “no hesitation to cut capacity of flights that are losing money” in 2027 if fuel prices stay elevated as expected.

For context, the average global price for a gallon of jet fuel stood at $4.56 during the week ending Oct. 30, up 3.8% from the previous month's average, according to data from trade group IATA.

For now, however, the carrier remains mostly in growth mode. This new route is the latest in a bevy of additions from United in 2027.

The airline will add at least five new routes from San Francisco International Airport (SFO), including to Charleston International Airport (CHS) in South Carolina and Richmond International Airport (RIC) in Virginia, and from O’Hare International Airport (ORD) in Chicago to L.F. Wade International Airport (BDA) in Bermuda.

And then there is United’s blockbuster 10-route summer long-haul expansion that will add destinations including Luxembourg Airport (LUX) and Ljubljana Airport (LJU) in Slovenia to its map.

It is not all growth for United next year, though. The airline will end service to Tulum International Airport (TQO) in Mexico in January.

Overall, these additions and cuts underscore United's efforts to grow its network while keeping an eye on profitability.

#6256. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6255. We've Tested Dozens of Toiletry Bags—These Are Our Top Picks

If there's one travel truth I live by—and hold dear to my heart—it’s that a dream vacation deserves a dream toiletry bag. After all, what’s a perfectly packed carry-on without a designated home for your favorite lipstick, beloved serums, sunscreen, and all those little beauty essentials that somehow multiply before every trip? The best toiletry bags make room for the whole glam squad, without adding any more suitcase chaos to the packing equation.

On all of our worldly journeys, Condé Nast Traveler editors (myself included) have tested dozens of travel toiletry bags to find the ones worth your precious packing space, from streamlined makeup pouches for the less-is-more crowd to roomy, cleverly compartmentalized cases for those who believe in a 10-step skincare routine. It's no easy job finding the best ones: Some tear after just a few months of use, others have awkwardly sized compartments. Many are too big for a standard carry-on, while others have proven too small to fit the simplest of our travel necessities.

With wipe-clean linings and durable construction, plus smart pockets and ultra chic designs, the carefully selected, editor-tested toiletry bags that earned a spot on this list are the crème de la crème. Read on for our recommendations to keep your essentials organized and your travel beauty routine in check.

Tested by: Jessica Sulima, commerce writer

How long have you been using it? About a year now, and despite how much it’s melded to different parts of my suitcase, the leather has stayed nicely intact.

What is it best for? It's best for longer trips, when you need to carry full-size toiletries. That being said, it also works if you don’t have that much to pack, because the leather folds down however you’d like. I like that the products stay upright for the most part, so you don’t have to worry about bottles squeezing open. The shape makes it so that you can rifle through your things comfortably without dumping everything out.

How much does it hold? My entire skincare routine—cleanser, toner, moisturizer, sunscreen—plus my daily makeup. There’s even room for my vitamins too.

Tested by: Madison Flager, commerce director

How long have you been using it? I've been using this Peak Design toiletry bag for five or six years.

What is it best for? If you're in search of a toiletry bag to keep up with an extended itinerary, this is your solution: It's ideal for longer trips of five days and more. Sometimes I pack it on weekend trips too, but it's a bit bulky, so I find it better suited to checked luggage, or trips where I'll need a good amount of product.

How much does it hold? This is one of the toiletry bag's best features—it truly holds so much. Everything in my routine fits like a glove, each with a dedicated space. I usually bring along shampoo, conditioner, body wash, face wash, moisturizer, eye cream, contact solution, a toothbrush, toothpaste, and floss, plus smaller items like tweezers and nail cutters. There's an exterior pocket sized for a toothbrush, and one inside with a magnetic snap where I store a razor. Plus, there’s a hook on the outside, so you can hang it up in the bathroom.

Tested by: Jessica Chapel, commerce writer

How long have you been using it? This gem is a newer addition to my travel rotation. I've traveled with it for around two months now—and knew it had to be mine when I saw it came in a glazed dark cherry colorway. (That's now sold out, but there are loads of other fun colors to choose from in the same style.)

What is it best for? Given its spacious yet puffy, cloud-like design, the Luka bag is ideal for any trip where you have some extra room in your carry-on, or are bringing a checked bag. It's a bit bulky for a weekender or duffel bag, though I'd try to squeeze it in if I was packing light. For any of these trips, you can use the hanging clip for easy access.

How much does it hold? It's a bit deceiving just how much this toiletry bag holds—which is much more than it gives off at first glance! I bring all of my beauty products in here, from foundations to lipsticks and moisturizer galore. And though he packs way lighter than me, it can fit my partner's personal care items, too: a face buzzer, hair gel, a toothbrush, and so on. As well as the main pocket with a zippered enclosure, it has two convenient, grab-and-go side pockets as well as an enclosed compartment on the back.

Tested by: Hannah Chubb, senior commerce editor How long have you been using it? I’ve had Away's large toiletry bag for just over two years now, and have been obsessed with it ever since.

What is it best for? This is my travel companion for holding my go-to skincare products and toiletries, and it comes with me on every trip. I do also keep all my everyday products in there at home, so it's proven to be always at my ready. It's so chic—especially because it has my initials embroidered on the front—and keeps everything contained. I love that it has so many interior compartments, both zippered and clear, to keep small objects like hair ties, jewelry, and Band-Aids separated from my bigger tubes and bottles.

How much does it hold? Full disclosure: I don’t travel light. But this bag truly holds so much. It fits my entire skincare routine, toothbrush case, deodorant, hair products, body wash, razor, and beyond with ease. The two halves make it easy to find a place for everything.

Tested by: Bridget Knowles, associate social media manager

How long have you been using it? Elizabeth Scarlett’s eponymous label is a London-based luxury accessories brand I discovered during a bout of retail therapy in East London eight years ago. I’ve never looked back since—it’s an unspoken “it-girl” possession.

What is it best for? For longer trips, the Wash Bag is really great to keep everything organized. It has a wipe-clean lining fit for all lotions and potions, and you can personalize it with monograms too, which makes for a great gift. For shorter trips and everyday use, I use the Everyday Pouch—which I strongly suggest adding to your cart. (It’s my life companion in many ways.)

How much does it hold? I put everything in the Wash Bag: daytime makeup, going out makeup (you get me), my nighttime routine, and my morning routine. It’s lined with pockets so you can easily organize brushes, and—I mean—my electric toothbrush even fits in it. That’s how good it is.

Tested by: Meaghan Kenny, commerce editor

How long have you been using it? I've been using—and in love with—this toiletry bag for around two years now.

What is it best for? I promise, my adoration of this bag comes from more than just its good looks. I've been reaching for it nonstop to carry my very extensive skincare routine with me wherever I go—and it's made packing easier than ever. I think I've finally cracked the code to keeping my toiletries organized and ready to go whenever I am. The extra roomy toiletry bag is designed to be packed in your checked luggage, where you have more suitcase space and no restrictions on the amount of liquids you can have inside.

How much does it hold? I used to keep all of my reusable toiletry bottles and miscellaneous minis in a small storage bin underneath my bed. And when it was time to pack for a trip, I'd sift through it and decide what I needed for a particular trip. I decided to put all of my go-to toiletries inside The Kit, including cleanser, body wash, moisturizer, shampoo and conditioner, dry shampoo, tooth paste, floss, and even contact lenses. Now when it's time to travel I can easily grab the pre-packed kit and throw it right into my personal item. I don't even open it anymore to see what I need—it's already stocked up and ready to go.

Read a full review of the toiletry bag here.

How long have you been using it? I ordered this Calpak train case in unison with the aforementioned Luka toiletry bag—so around two months now.

What is it best for? With its boxy, clear, and haute look, the train case is best for extended trips where a checked bag is obvious. Otherwise, it's a superb makeup bag at home for those who don't love too many compartments, and like to have their ready products in view: The transparent panels let you quickly locate what you need without digging. (Not to mention, it looks super cute with the Luka, given the matching colorways. I'm obsessed!)

How much does it hold? When this bad boy arrived at my apartment, it was (luckily) bigger than I expected. It's tall, so it can easily hold my toner bottles, makeup brushes, and blending sponges.

At home, not only does it store my everyday beauty products, but a stock of my next-on-the-lists and just-in-cases—it's where my unopened moisturizers, different lip shades, and nail care products go. My favorite part? There's a hidden, dedicated interior organization pocket attached to the top compartment, which holds the products I wish to keep separate.

#6254. United Airlines First Class Steak And Eggs: Great Steak, But Where Were The Eggs?

United Airlines served me excellent cubed steak for breakfast on a recent flight from Chicago to Houston. The problem with its steak and eggs dish? The missing eggs.

For this week’s Meal of the Week, I want to highlight a breakfast that I would happily order again, even though one part of it was very disappointing. On a recent flight from Chicago O’Hare (ORD) to Houston (IAH), I selected the steak and eggs, described on the menu as:

Steak and eggs with home fries and chimichurri sauce

The tray was nicely presented, with sliced steak topped with chimichurri, potatoes, and what I expected would be an egg soufflé.

The steak was excellent for airplane red meat. The chimichurri worked very well with the beef, and this was the highlight of the meal.

Unfortunately, instead of the egg soufflé I expected, I received something much closer to bread pudding…in fact, it was the same bread pudding I had out of Chicago a couple months ago. There may have been egg binding it together, but it had virtually no discernible egg texture or flavor. It was like eating bread.

You can see the bread cubes in the photo. This was not simply a soufflé that turned out a little firmer than expected. Bread dominated the portion that was supposed to provide the eggs in my steak and eggs.

That was disappointing, especially because the steak was so good and because I try to limit my carbs. I hope United can address this with its catering out of Chicago, as I’ve seen other reports of the same problem (this wasn’t a one-off). An actual egg component would make this a much more satisfying breakfast and match the menu…

The accompaniments were better. The chocolate croissant was served warm and was excellent. Between that and the bread pudding, I certainly had enough bread on the tray…

The fruit was ripe, and the Chobani vanilla Greek yogurt was decent. I would prefer a no-sugar-added Greek yogurt, but at least this one provided 10 grams of protein.

The coffee was strong, which was also appreciated. I also requested orange juice, though I must confess that was more to add color to the tray for the photo. I did not drink it.

I would order United’s steak and eggs again. The steak with chimichurri was excellent, and the warm chocolate croissant was great. But United needs to fix the egg issue out of ORD. There is a good breakfast here. It just needs the eggs its name promises.

My Meal of the Week feature examines an airline meal from my travels over the years. This may be a meal from earlier in the week or it may be a meal served over a decade ago.

#6253. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6252. My Favorite Airbnb: A Dreamy Thatched Cottage Tucked Away in the Cotswolds

Choosing the perfect place to hole up for a weekend getaway is not always straightforward. But this spring, the decisions seemed to make themselves. After a relentlessly busy start to the year, I was looking for a place to escape. And the place needed to fit certain criteria: Somewhere my partner and I wouldn't have to speak to anyone but each other; somewhere we could sleep for 12 hours a night and take the days slow and easy without guilt; somewhere within a couple of hours’ drive from our home in northwest London; somewhere rural, where I wouldn’t be woken up by the neighbors’ bathroom light or the sound of the tube; and somewhere we could have the place to ourselves, but still be close to some nice pubs or restaurants, so we wouldn't have to hunt and gather our own dinners, God forbid.

An Airbnb in the Cotswolds was the obvious choice. Luckily, I remembered I’d saved a cozy-looking cottage on Instagram a few months prior to feeling the sudden urge to get away. I revisited my staycation wishlist and found Strawtop Cottages: two 16th-century thatched-roof cottages that sit side by side on a quiet street in the quaint little village of Adderbury. I booked one of them, Strawtop Two, for a long weekend in April.

We checked into Strawtop Two after a speedy drive from London on a Friday night. As we unlocked the front door, we found switched-on lamps casting a cozy glow across the beamed living room; kindling ready to be lit in the wood-burning fire. In the egg-yolk yellow kitchen, a fresh loaf of sourdough was sitting pretty on the chopping board for us; organic eggs and marmalade on the counter; Daylesford butter, bacon, and rosé in the fridge. My partner prepared a simple supper while I nosed around the rest of the cottage, discovering a sweet dining room with floor-to-ceiling windows and an enormous bunch of fresh flowers around the back, as well as a boot room with Barbour jackets, Wellies for stomps across the fields, and umbrellas (likely a requirement, considering we were visiting in April).

I learned that the sister properties are owned by local content creator Josie Irons (@Josieldn on Instagram) and her husband Charlie Irons (who manages the properties), who have been custodians here for just a small part of the cottages’ centuries-long history. Their meticulous renovations have restored the spaces beautifully, preserving all the Grade II-listed original features that make staying here feel like a journey back to a simpler, more peaceful time, while adding plush finishing touches that feel every bit as cosseting as those of the area’s top-of-class hotels.

I originally saved this cottage because of the kitchen, drawn in by sunshiny pictures and clips of its buttery-hued walls, vintage copper pans, and an old-school kettle whistling on the Aga stove. But as I nipped between the two bedrooms—one on the first floor with minty green walls, one folded into the eaves on the top floor with tongue-and-groove woodwork—I found there’s a lot more to love here, like the Bamford pillow mist left next to the beds, and the blackout blinds creating one of the darkest and quietest bedrooms I’ve ever drifted off in. Wrapped up in the bed linens, I snoozed more peacefully than I’d managed to in months.

After homemade coffee sipped while listening to the Roberts Radio on Saturday morning, we headed a few minutes up the road to The Yurt at Nicholsons restaurant. This was one of a handful of recommendations that Charlie had sent us ahead of time. Normally, I’m a stickler for doing my own research (read: a snob and a control freak), but in the name of keeping things as relaxed as possible, I decided to put my faith in his suggestions. I shouldn’t have hesitated: a gooey camembert croissant, cut through with umami bacon, and a full English breakfast with melty pork belly chop and smoky baked beans hit the spot.

Our supper, also recommended (and booked for us) by Charlie, at The Norman Knight was every bit as impressive. I ordered perfectly blushing steak frites and felt smugly like I’d uncovered a hidden gem. Our Sunday lunch at The Duke of Cumberland’s Head, where we shared bowls of cauliflower cheese and crispy potatoes, was one of the tastiest roasts I’ve had in a while. Trust me, having Charlie as a de facto concierge is one of the biggest unsung perks of booking a stay here.

Back at the house, we hibernated on the sofa, reading the paper and watching Netflix in the dinky living room. I took mental notes of my favorite design details: the antique coffee table laden with magazines, the books plopped into recesses in the stone chimney, the deep-green rainfall shower stocked with Bamford products, the Steamery steamer and Dyson hairdryer in the bedroom vanity, and the Soho Home robes. If I could make my London flat one-tenth as comfortable as this little countryside cottage, I’d be thrilled. For now, I’ll bookmark the cottage next door for my next escape.

#6251. Air Serbia Flight To Nowhere: A320 Forced To Return To Belgrade Over Mysterious Security Concern

An Air Serbia flight to Moscow made it as far as Lithuania before turning around and returning to Belgrade over a security concern involving one passenger. Serbian media identified that passenger as the country’s former intelligence chief, who allegedly boarded without completing security screening. He denies wrongdoing.

As flagged by One Mile At A Time, Air Serbia flight JU134 departed Belgrade for Moscow on November 3, 2026, but turned back over southern Lithuania. According to Serbian media, the Airbus A320 left at 6:48 PM and returned shortly before 10:00 PM. Passengers spent more than three hours flying only to end up where they started.

Air Serbia confirmed that airport authorities requested additional security checks concerning one passenger. The airline said it returned in accordance with the instructions it received, but did not publicly identify that passenger.

The passenger in question has since been identified as Aleksandar Vulin, Serbia’s former intelligence chief. It appears that someone helped him board without completing the required screening and that the airport’s corporate security director ordered the return after reviewing surveillance footage.

Vulin insists he completed the required checks, was carrying no prohibited items, and was being targeted for political reasons (his pro-Russian party lost in a snap election last month). He said his trip concerned negotiations over Serbia’s gas arrangement with Russia.

Passengers and their luggage underwent additional screening in Belgrade. The flight eventually continued to Moscow with a replacement crew, arriving about seven hours late.

If the reports are accurate, the obvious question is how someone was allowed to board without completing the required checks. Political prominence should not provide an exemption from an aviation security procedure, though I understand how easy it is to open an employee access door for a VIP).

But Vulin disputes that account, and the airline’s statement establishes only that authorities requested additional screening. That leaves important questions about what happened before departure and what prompted the return. Vulin was allowed to continue on the delayed flight to Moscow.

Belgrade’s Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office has requested an investigation into the circumstances, including whether procedures were followed, who authorized the aircraft’s return, and what security assessment supported that decision.

That inquiry is appropriate. If someone bypassed screening, there should be accountability for how it happened. If the checks were properly completed, authorities need to explain why an aircraft full of passengers was brought back.

This is all may be Serbian domestic politics…

An alleged screening lapse involving a former intelligence chief turned a routine Air Serbia flight into a lengthy journey back to its starting point. The aircraft eventually reached Moscow, but the competing accounts of what happened remain unresolved.

I hope the investigation establishes whether someone received preferential treatment or whether there is another explanation for this extraordinary return. Either way, the passengers arrived very late into Moscow.

#6250. My Favorite Airbnb: A Dreamy Cabin on a Vineyard Just 2 Hours From London

I'm always on the hunt for a new cabin stay in the British countryside. Having visited at least two a year since 2020, I'd now dub myself something of an expert. Living in East London, sometimes all I crave is solitude, and I find that a slightly rustic spot, kitted out with all the necessary amenities, can be more restorative than a jam-packed, buzzy hotel stay.

I don't drive (hey, I'm a Londoner), which can be a rather large obstacle when planning cabin stays. But Liba Vineyard, a luxury glamping site made up of three pod-style homes in Porton, just a 15-minute taxi ride from Salisbury station, presents no such problem. The pods are all bookable on Airbnb, and I scooped up the Hawthorn Pod for a stay this autumn, eager to hunker down and work on writing my upcoming book. Door-to-door from London, I managed to reach it in two hours, armed with enough books and food to last two nights.

Once I'd settled into the Hawthorn Pod, I realized the Wi-Fi was excellent, and I wouldn't need to leave at all during my stay. The pods are dotted along winding wood-chip paths, which branch off towards the three cabins: Hawthorn, Beech, and Elder. All sleep four people and have a wood-fired hot tub, although Hawthorn is slightly more snug than the other two and better suited to solo visitors and couples. Beech is best for anyone traveling with children, while for larger groups, renting all three would be a fun way to celebrate a birthday. It's a spot that can be both solitary and social, depending on what you're after.

Inside, the pods are neutral, bright, and cozy. Draped curtains add a sense of grandeur to the French doors, while the bathroom—the biggest test of any cabin—was a welcome sight. A flushing toilet and strong water pressure are unsung luxuries, and things I'm always relieved to find in a cabin. The kitchen has everything you'd need, but there's also an outdoor barbecue firepit, making cooking here a genuine joy.

Nearby, there are plenty of sightseeing opportunities, pubs, day trips, and activities: UNESCO World Heritage Site Stonehenge is just a 15-minute drive away, while Cranborne Chase National Landscape and the New Forest are both under a half-hour drive. The property itself is full of life as well, with alpacas grazing, chickens clucking, and a muster of peacocks running between hedgerows. On Mondays and Wednesdays, you can join a yoga class in a studio above the winemaking barn.

Each morning, I'd wake to the sound of peacocks, open the drapes to soft golden light trickling in, and breathe in the fresh air before lighting a fire to get breakfast started. Since returning home, I've longed for the calm of those mornings and the methodical mindfulness of cooking over a flame.

The owners have big plans in the works. Soon, wine will be available from the vineyard, which is expected to produce up to 10,000 bottles a year over the next few years. Chris Reynolds, who owns the land with his wife, Louise Marshall, gives every pod guest a tour, something that will become an even bigger selling point once wine is available to taste. Ahead of this, visitors can sponsor a vine through a subscription model in exchange for wine, pod stays, and events such as harvest parties. Liba is already certified organic and is working towards biodynamic certification within the next nine months.

Next summer, the 10-acre farm will be bookable for weddings, while early discussions are underway about an on-site café and additional activities to complement the existing yoga studio.

#6249. American Airlines Dropped Trump’s Name From West Palm Beach Gate Screens Ahead Of Midterm Elections

American Airlines quietly removed the Trump reference from its gate monitors for flights to West Palm Beach. The timing will invite speculation, but the simpler destination label is an improvement regardless of what prompted the change, which does not appear politically-motivated to me.

JonNYC reports that American has changed its destination displays from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL.”

That reverses a change introduced after Palm Beach International Airport was renamed President Donald J. Trump International Airport earlier this year.

so… has anyone noticed that AA has changed the gate monitors from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL” ?

The change is likely not connected to this week’s election and occurred in August as part of a planned transition. The IATA code for the airport is still DJT after the July 9, 2026 change from PBI.

The original change was peculiar because American generally identifies destinations by city, adding airport names when useful to distinguish between airports serving the same destination.

American does not ordinarily add the presidential names associated with airports serving places like Little Rock (Bill Clinton) or Grand Rapids (Gerald Ford). The West Palm Beach label stood out. Then again, as I indicated above, other airports did not change their IATA code.

There is a very practical reason to distinguish New York JFK from New York LaGuardia or Washington Reagan (National) from Washington Dulles. Leading with presidential initials on a flight to West Palm Beach offers less obvious help to passengers.

There was no possibility of similar confusion when flying into West Palm Beach.

Of course people will notice that this reversal surfaced around the midterm elections, but as I mentioned this goes back to August. Even so, it is an irresistible invitation to speculate about corporate America adjusting to a changed political environment, which was becoming clear even over the summer.

But I think it’s safe to say that American’s leadership did not order a “political” retreat, no matter what some MAGA world may be suggesting this morning. This was more likely all part of the transition plan.

I would be equally cautious about declaring that the original wording was personally ordered by executives seeking favor with the administration, though that could well be the choice as well. It was an unusual choice. The reasoning behind it remains a separate question.

Still, American created an unnecessary distraction by departing from a straightforward city label in the first place. Once a company makes a conspicuous change involving a political figure, undoing it will inevitably attract attention too…especially now.

American Airlines has restored the West Palm Beach destination label on its gate monitors, removing the presidential reference it added earlier this year.

The timing will generate political interpretations. Without more information, I would leave those as speculation and it appears wholly unrelated. The practical result is easier to assess: passengers once again see the name of the place they are flying to. That works for me. Now it’s time to move DJT back to PBI…there was certainly no need for that change either, though that ship (plane?) has sailed.

“Why does the screen behind you say, “West Palm Beach, FL”?

#6248. The Same TSA Scanner That Lets Laptops Stay In Your Bag Is Quietly Ruining Other Gear

While some passengers might not directly notice it, airport security checkpoints across the United States are changing. For most travelers, the most visible benefit is simple: laptops, tablets, and approved liquids can increasingly stay inside carry-on bags, removing one of the most familiar airport security rituals of the past two decades. However, this same technology that makes the checkpoint feel more convenient also creates new problems for some travelers.

The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) has been rolling out advanced computed tomography, commonly known as CT, scanners as part of a major security technology upgrade. In March 2022, the agency awarded two orders totaling up to $781.2 million for base and full-size CT X-ray systems for airport checkpoints, while later procurement added even more units to the program. These machines are designed to improve threat detection by creating three-dimensional images of carry-on bags.

TSA officers can rotate and inspect those images in ways that were not possible with older two-dimensional X-ray machines. For the average passenger, this means fewer items need to be removed from bags, while for travelers carrying analog film, overstuffed carry-ons, or other sensitive items, the story is less straightforward.

The new CT scanning equipment represents a major shift from the traditional X-ray equipment passengers have become used to at airport checkpoints. Older systems produced flatter images, making it harder for officers to distinguish between items layered together inside a bag. This is one reason laptops and other large electronics often need to be removed and screened separately.

The introduction of newer CT systems, which use more advanced imaging and algorithms to create 3D views of carry-on content, is increasingly changing this. According to TSA, officers can view and rotate the image on three axes to identify possible threat items more effectively. The agency has described the technology as both a security upgrade and a way to improve the passenger experience. Today, these scanners are already available at some of the largest hubs in the United States, including Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD), and New York JFK Airport (JFK), among many others.

For travelers, the most obvious change is the reduced need to unpack their hand luggage at the conveyor belt. TSA has stated that under current screening procedures for CT lanes, laptops are allowed to remain in bags. In some airport press releases, the agency has also noted that passengers screened through CT units do not need to remove 3-1-1 liquids or laptops. Travelers no longer need to place laptops at the top of a backpack just to remove them quickly, and toiletry bags do not always need to be kept in an outside pocket.

The downside is that CT scanners do not treat every item the same way, and their more powerful imaging is useful for security screening, but it can be a problem for undeveloped photographic materials. This is where the new technology creates a completely different experience for analog photographers than for passengers carrying digital equipment. The new CT scanners can damage or destroy unprocessed film rolls, and the stronger imaging can cause damage in a single screening. CT scanners can fog unprocessed rolls, reduce image quality, and cause permanent damage, forcing analog photographers to change how they move through security.

However, this does not mean that every piece of camera equipment is at risk; digital cameras, lenses, batteries, and memory cards are not affected in the same way. The concern is specifically undeveloped film, including rolls carried separately, film already loaded inside a camera, disposable analog cameras, and instant materials. For most travelers, this may sound like a niche problem, but analog photography has become increasingly popular again among travelers who want a different look from digital smartphone photos. Many unaware passengers might also fail to realize there is a risk until after their trip, when the damage is already done.

Airport security technology has changed greatly over the last 25 years.

As a result of the new scanners, the most important rule for travelers carrying analog materials is simple: do not allow it to go through a CT scanner if it can be avoided. TSA’s own guidance recommends placing undeveloped film and cameras containing undeveloped film in carry-on bags, or taking undeveloped film to the checkpoint and asking for a hand inspection.

That means film should not be buried at the bottom of a suitcase. Instead, it should be packed so it's easy to remove before reaching the scanner. It is also advisable to separate unprocessed rolls from cameras where possible and place them in transparent, quart-sized zipper bags on top of the carry-on. That makes it easier for TSA officers to inspect without delaying the process and the entire line behind.

The hand inspection is not especially complicated, but it does take a bit of time, since TSA officers generally take the film to a separate area, visually inspect each roll, swab it for explosive residue, and then manually clear it. The process typically takes three to 10 minutes, with passengers advised to arrive around 15 to 20 minutes earlier if they know they will need the extra step. It is important to note that travelers should clearly tell the TSA officer that they are carrying undeveloped photographic materials and would like a hand inspection.

TSA PreCheck Touchless ID is available at 65 airports nationwide and supports more than 100 participating airlines

The new CT machines have also changed the carry-on versus checked-bag decision process. Many passengers assume that fragile or valuable items should stay in the cabin, but when flying with film, there is another reason to avoid checked baggage. Checked luggage is also screened using similar powerful equipment, and passengers generally do not have the same opportunity to request a hand inspection once the bag disappears behind the check-in counter.

For that reason, film travelers should keep undeveloped rolls, disposable cameras, and cameras containing film in their hand luggage. This does not mean placing them deep inside a trolley that may need to be gate-checked later. The safest option is to keep film in a personal item or small carry-on that will remain accessible through the checkpoint.

There is also a practical difference between domestic and international travel. TSA guidance applies in the United States, where passengers can request a hand inspection. Procedures abroad may vary, and foreign airport security staff may not always handle film requests in the same way. For travelers connecting internationally, that means planning ahead and expecting the same conversation more than once.

The 100ml rule is finally being scrapped after last year's false start.

Besides the potential risk to analog film, newer CT scanning equipment can also create problems for travelers carrying oversized or overstuffed bags, since the scanners have fixed tunnel openings. This means a bag that does not physically fit through the machine cannot be screened in that lane.

That matters because many passengers have become used to a certain amount of flexibility around carry-on sizes. Most major US airlines use a standard domestic carry-on limit of around 22 x 14 x 9 inches (56 x 36 x 23 cm). However, in practice, the strictness of the enforcement has often depended on the airline policy, gate agent, aircraft type, and how full the flight is. Soft-sided bags and expanded trolleys could sometimes slip through, especially when passengers were not asked to place them in a sizing frame.

However, the CT scanners at security lanes are now changing that dynamic, and if a carry-on is too large for the scanner, the issue arises at the security checkpoint rather than at the gate. In that sense, the new scanning technology has become an indirect baggage-size enforcement tool for airlines, and while passengers might not be trying to break a rule, an expanded carry-on suitcase that once passed through older equipment may now be pulled aside before screening can even continue.

The discovery of two live smoke grenades hidden inside a jar of peanut butter in a passenger's checked luggage highlights the importance of screening.

For passengers, the CT rollout at TSA checkpoints is making security increasingly convenient for the average passenger but less forgiving for travelers carrying certain items. Laptops and liquids staying in the bag is a real improvement, as it avoids the need to unpack half a bag in public, but it does not mean passengers can stop thinking about how their carry-on is packed.

A carry-on now needs to be packed not only to meet the airline’s baggage rules but also to fit within the physical limits of the checkpoint itself. For most travelers, the best strategy is to keep laptops and liquids where they fit naturally, while making sure the bag remains within airline carry-on dimensions and is not expanded beyond its normal size. For passengers traveling with analog cameras and photo rolls, it is important they remain accessible and separated where possible. This ensures it is ready to be handed to an officer for a manual inspection before the bag enters the scanner.

The best approach is therefore not to assume every checkpoint will work the same way. Travelers should still arrive prepared for traditional lanes, especially at airports where older and newer machines operate side by side. At the same time, those carrying analog photographic materials or borderline-sized bags should plan around the newer system.

Welcome offer: Earn up to 80,000 bonus miles: Earn 70,000 bonus miles after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Why we love it: The Explorer offers several useful United benefits, including a free first checked bag for the cardmember and one companion (when the flight is purchased with the card), priority boarding and two United Club one-time passes each cardholder year.

TPG credit cards editor Olivia Mittak has held the Explorer for years and particularly appreciates how easy it is to get value from the card's United-specific benefits.

"The biggest reason I tout the Explorer as often as I do is because of how easy it is to get meaningful value from it without needing to use merchant credits that may not fit your spending habits," she said.

With a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year (then $150), the Explorer could be particularly appealing to travelers who regularly check bags or use United Club access.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Explorer Card.

The Hilton Honors Aspire is a premium hotel card that offers valuable benefits for travelers who regularly stay at Hilton properties.

Welcome offer: Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

Why we love it: The Aspire offers automatic Hilton Honors Diamond status, an annual free night reward and up to $400 in statement credits for eligible Hilton resort purchases each calendar year (up to $200 biannually).

For Carly Helfand, TPG's director of site strategy, the free night reward and resort credits are among her favorite credit card benefits. Both she and her husband hold the Aspire, allowing them to take advantage of two sets of these benefits each year.

The card's perks can help offset the card's $550 annual fee, particularly for travelers who can redeem their free night rewards at high-end Hilton properties.

To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Honors Aspire.

The United Gateway is an entry-level United credit card that lets travelers earn MileagePlus miles without paying an annual fee.

Welcome offer: Earn up to 50,000 bonus miles: Earn 40,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Why we love it: The Gateway offers a straightforward way to earn United miles on everyday purchases while avoiding an annual fee. It's a strong option for occasional United flyers who want to build their MileagePlus balances but don't need the more extensive travel benefits of the airline's higher-tier cards.

TPG credit card writer Becky Pokora appreciates the card's everyday earning opportunities: "I keep my card linked to my toll road and Parkmobile accounts, since it earns extra miles on local transit and commuting charges and defines those categories broadly," she said.

Becky also uses the card for inflight purchases to receive a 25% statement credit on eligible purchases, another perk that adds value without an annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Gateway Card.

These offers can help you boost your transferable points and miles balance or unlock meaningful discounts on your next trip.

As always, be sure to factor in each issuer's unique set of application restrictions and ensure you can meet any spending requirements to earn the bonus.

But with so much value on the table, you won't want to miss out on adding one of these top credit cards (and its bonus) to your wallet.

#6246. 55 Thoughtful Gifts for Men Who Love to Travel

The holiday season will be here before we know it, which means it’s time to start thinking about gifts for the ones you love. When you’re shopping for a special guy in your life this year, skip the things he doesn’t actually need and go straight for the ones that count: thoughtful pieces he’ll put to good use on his next trip, upgrades to his everyday essentials, and a few small luxuries that make being on the road that much better. The best gifts for men, after all, aren’t necessarily the flashiest—they’re the ones that become part of his routine, whether that means packing them in a carry-on or enjoying them on a quiet Sunday morning at home.

I’ve hand-selected over 50 gift ideas for men who love to travel, featuring many talked-about favorites with a few less expected additions too. From a timeless leather weekender that’s perfect for a quick getaway to at-home accessories that will enrich any guy’s space, I've got you covered with plenty of options he’ll love. Read on for all of the best travel gifts for men or jump straight to the section you think will interest him most.

At Condé Nast Traveler, editors spend a lot of time debating, researching, testing, and re-testing all things travel accessories and luggage. If you’re looking for the best suitcase to buy your guy this holiday season, look here. But if you want something a little unique that will absolutely rock his travel routine for years to come, check out some of the gift ideas below. To make his next long-haul flight more comfortable, consider gifting him a comfy neck pillow, sleep mask, or a pair of compression socks. A ludicrously capacious leather weekender or a luxurious Italian notebook are smart upgrades he’ll cherish forever. And in case of emergencies, a good ol' fashioned flask will more than do the trick.

Here’s the thing about men: There’s a part of us that will always relish having a new toy to play with. This category is for those who will appreciate a wild card gift and savor the element of surprise. A perfect pair of travel-sized binoculars made from the best optical-grade crystal in the world? Jackpot! The latest generation of AirPods with top-notch noise-canceling technology? Bingo! A smart watch that can track his steps on the go? Perfect!

Clothes are a tough gift for the holidays. Everybody is different, every body is different, and a lot of guys are just downright picky when it comes to what they get dressed in everyday. That being said, there are a few tricks of the trade to consider here—when gifting clothes, don’t go too big, too outré, or too outlandish. The secret is to select timeless, quintessential pieces that travel well, age well, and can be styled into any wardrobe: a Barbour jacket, a crisp white shirt, or a navy suit that packs nicely into a suitcase. When in doubt, a pair of high-quality sunglasses in a classic silhouette is generally a win too.

Lovers of the great outdoors are a funny bunch to shop for. They typically have all of their most treasured gear ready to go already, so this is a demographic for whom you need to be on your A-game. Gifts for outdoorsy types need to be the newest of the new with smart details, category-leading engineering, and unassailable durability. Think a lightweight Norwegian cooler that keeps drinks cold without any ice (that’s right—no ice), or a comfortable running shoe that can handle endless wear and tear. Outdoorsy folks will say that they can never have too many puffy layer-type things—so go ahead and consider a thick blanket or the iconic Arc’teryx Atom insulated hoodie. And if all else fails you can get them a beautiful Stanley bottle to keep their favorite soups and beverages warm in even the most wintry conditions.

I hate to stereotype the genders—but a lot of self-care products out there are marketed more heavily toward women, leaving the average guy in the lurch. He may not know the benefits of investing in a Dr. Barbara Sturm skincare regimen, or how an Omnilux LED mask can help slow visible signs of aging. There’s a whole world of self-care products out there! Here, I’ve gathered some of the best items to kick-start his journey—sometimes all it takes is Dr. Dennis Gross’ miracle-working peel pads.

Food is one of my favorite ways to experience travel. If you’re not quite ready to gift someone a trip to sample authentic panettone straight from the oven in Italy, the good news is that the marvels of modern packing and shipping have made some of the world’s tastiest foods closer than ever. A sampler of high-quality spices will upgrade his at-home cooking. A $60 bag of beans is the perfectly fun gift for a coffee snob who might not buy it for himself. And a perfectly unassailable upgrade to his go-to sauté pan (if he even has one), or the investment of a proper stand mixer, are foolproof.

No matter what the recipient’s sense of style is, there are certain upgrades that are likely to fit into most any home. Beautiful linen sheets are always welcome, as is a great bathrobe or pair of slippers to remind him of a luxury hotel. When in doubt, the flourish of a Flamingo Estate candle hits just the right notes.

#6245. Cruising to Alaska? Check if Your Next Port, Bus, or Lodge is Indigenous-Owned

The Huna Totem Corporation was featured on Condé Nast Traveler's Bright Ideas in Travel 2026. Read the full list of winners here.

From April to October, cruise ships tower over downtown Juneau’s Marine Way, a coastal path that connects the port zone to downtown. Should a traveler pause for a moment between ship and souvenir store, they’ll notice Kaagwaantaan Kootéeyaa, a tall, intricately carved pole rising against a backdrop of forest and mountains. At its base, a panel explains that the cedar pole depicts five of the Kaagwaantaan Tlingit clan’s crests: a hat, person, orca, eagle and bear. It is an arresting introduction to the long-overlooked human history of this place.

Since 2023, totem poles have adorned this highly trafficked shoreline, part of Kootéeyaa Deiyí (“Totem Pole Trail”)—a city-wide project led by the Sealaska Heritage Institute (SHI) that represents the cultures of the Tlingit people who have inhabited Juneau for at least 10,000 years, as well as the Haida and Tsimshian who arrived a few hundred years ago. Visible evidence of the region’s Indigenous communities was previously limited, says SHI’s Ricardo Worl (Tlingit), who sees the trail as “an opportunity to reestablish our presence on our ancestral lands.” Noting that more than a million cruise ship passengers land in Juneau each year, Worl hopes the trail “is the beginning of their education about our culture.”

Alaska’s cruise industry has long invited travelers to experience the “Last Frontier” while relegating Indigenous peoples to the margins of the tourism economy. Now, a shift is occurring—one that goes beyond simply incorporating Indigenous culture into the cruise experience. Across Alaska, Native corporations are increasingly owning and shaping the tourism infrastructure itself, from cruise docks and terminals to ground transportation, giving them a greater stake in how destinations develop, and how visitors experience them.

I came to Alaska to see how Indigenous ownership is changing the experience on the ground, following a route that took me from whale watching at cruise ports on the coast to bear and moose spotting at a lodge deep in the Interior. At each stop, I saw how Alaska Native corporations are shaping the places that travelers pass through.

Created following passage of the 1971 Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, Alaska Native corporations are for-profit companies run by and for Alaska Native shareholders. For Huna Totem, a Tlingit village corporation representing shareholders with ties to Hoonah and Glacier Bay, tourism is an important part of its economic development strategy. Its best-known development, Icy Strait Point in Hoonah, is Alaska’s first private cruise destination and has become a model for Alaska Native-owned tourism—creating local jobs, keeping economic benefits within the community and making Tlingit culture part of the visitor experience.

When Icy Strait Point opened in 2004, Huna Totem leadership was focused on “providing economic stability for generations, so the culture can be perpetuated,” says Ruth Banaszak, director of marketing and communications. Icy Strait Point has two cruise ship piers located about a half-mile apart and activity areas for 30 different excursions to distribute visitor flow around the site so that it never becomes overwhelming. To get around the vast site, I made use of the forested walking trails and two gondola systems, one of which took me to the summit of Hoonah Mountain, which I quickly and thrillingly descended via the ZipRider, a six-cable zipline. Walking around the museum exhibits housed inside a 1912 salmon cannery that closed when the fishing industry declined, I could connect tourism's present and future with its economic history. The cannery was once a symbol of loss; now it provides new economic opportunities. “We hire around 350 people for the season,” says Banaszak. “So, in a town of 950, anybody who wants to have a job in the community has one.” The model has also allowed local residents to build businesses of their own, including boat tours to Point Adolphus where, in just two hours, I spotted dozens of orcas, a few humpback whales and uncountable numbers of sea lions and sea otters. In each place, instead of being whisked onto an excursion operated by an outside company, I was experiencing a destination that had been shaped by the community whose ancestral home I was visiting.

“We’ve done this for our own community in Hoonah,” says Banaszak, “so now [we’re asking] how can we take what we’ve learned here and help other rural communities do the same thing?”

That thinking has led Huna Totem around Southeast Alaska and beyond. In Whittier, the corporation opened Glacier Gateway cruise terminal in 2024. Huna Totem and Doyon, Limited, another Alaska Native corporation, have also acquired Portage Glacier Cruises and Alaska Coach Tours, creating Native-owned touchpoints that extend from ship to shore and beyond. In Klawock, on Prince of Wales Island, Huna Totem partnered with Doyon and the local Alaska Native village corporation Klawock Heenya to develop a new cruise port in 2024. The destination uses a single-ship model, with development focused on Tlingit culture, local involvement and community values.

Back in downtown Juneau, Huna Totem is developing Áak’w Landing, a cruise dock and waterfront development targeting its first full season in 2028. The project is designed to improve how cruise visitors move through the city—including eliminating the need for tender boats at the site—rather than simply bringing in more ships. Reflecting its approach of being “culturally driven, community-centric, [and] business-focused,” says Banaszak, Huna Totem sees the project as both infrastructure enhancement and an opportunity to incorporate Alaska Native culture into the visitor experience—two poles from SHI’s Kootéeyaa Deiyí will be raised at the site.

The broader ambition is to create a network of Native-owned tourism businesses across Alaska. “So that Alaska Native tourism grows: culturally-led tourism as it should be done, people telling their own story themselves,” Banaszak says.

The cruise industry may seem an odd venture for Doyon, Limited, which is based in Fairbanks and represents the largely Dene people of the Interior, but, says Jordan Sanford, president of Doyon Tourism, “more than 60% of visitors come to Alaska by cruise, so [we realized] if we wanted to grow, we needed to be involved.”

Deep in Denali National Park, Doyon has operated Kantishna Roadhouse, the park’s only Indigenous-owned lodge, for 30 years. Arriving via a small plane from the park entrance—road access, closed for five years due to a landslide, will return in 2027—I spent blissful days backcountry hiking free from cell service. Evenings were spent listening to presentations by staff, such as an introduction to Dene beadwork and regalia; spotting wildlife including grizzly bears, moose, and caribou, then watching the setting sun light up the slopes of mighty Denali. Since 2004, in partnership with Aramark, Doyon has also operated bus tours, transit services, and campgrounds in the park. The partnership with Huna Totem gives Doyon an opportunity to diversify and grow, while responding to a recent shift in cruise passengers’ expectations: “They’re looking for more authentic experiences,” she explains. “We see that as our advantage. We put shareholders to work, and they share their culture,” she says. “There's a lot of businesses here that have been sharing the culture for so long, but from non-Alaska Natives,” she adds.

Next up is the restoration of the 1925 Chatanika Gold Camp near Fairbanks, which is scheduled to open in 2028 as a northern lights experience center, filling a critical infrastructure gap. Aurora viewing in Alaska today typically means pulling off the side of the road and drinking a hot chocolate, says Sanford. With Chatanika, “we're creating a space [with] cultural programming to make it more of an experience.”

It’s another link in an emerging network of Native-owned businesses across the state. The ultimate goal is “an Alaska Native-owned corridor, where [travelers] are visiting Alaska Native-owned businesses along the way,” says Sanford. For cruise passengers, that means more opportunities to encounter Indigenous culture, while knowing that Indigenous people are benefiting from the industry. And it means that your next Alaska cruise itinerary might begin at a Native-owned port, continue aboard a Native-owned bus, lead to a Native-owned excursion, and end at a Native-owned lodge.

#6244. American Resumes Service to Haiti After Two-Year Pause

American Airlines on Sunday restarted service to Haiti after a nearly two-year hiatus brought on by gang violence in and around Port-au-Prince.

The carrier is now operating daily nonstop flights between Miami and Cap-Haitien, using Boeing 737 aircraft.

The inaugural flight on Sunday was staffed by an all-Haitian, Creole-speaking crew, the airline said.

“The connection between the United States and Haiti is incredibly meaningful, which is especially true in South Florida,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “We know the critical role air service plays in linking countries and communities, so we’re beyond proud to reinstate such a consequential connection for so many.”

U.S. airlines suspended service to and from Haiti in 2024 amid a rise in gang violence. Toussaint Louverture International Airport in Port-au-Prince was temporarily closed after bullets struck aircraft taxiing on the tarmac.

So far, American is the only U.S.-based carrier to have resumed service to the country.
