#6233. In Luxor, Ancient Egypt feels newly alive

The water is cold and clear. Half-hidden amid the palm-tufted grounds of the Mortuary Temple of Seti I, this sacred sunken lake on Luxor's west bank was once the domain of ancient Egyptian priests. More than 3,000 years later, women from nearby villages still come, hoping its waters will serve as a fertility aid or a balm for their sick children, says my guide Ahmed Hassan, who was born and raised on this side of the Nile. It's one of the area's many miracles, he adds: No one knows where the water comes from, but it hasn't run dry since those priests of antiquity first bathed here. Hedging my bets, I submerge my hands.

It can be difficult to know what to believe in this transcendent stretch of Upper Egypt, 410 miles south of Cairo, where the Nile exudes a life force of its own; the mountains cradle secret treasures; and the light, particularly at golden hour, plays tricks, almost convincing you that you have traveled back in time. The line between the real and the mystical feels flimsy, whether you are considering the scale of the approximately 1,000-ton, 65-foot-tall colossus of Ramses II, inexplicably carved from a single piece of granite and lying prostrate at the king's statuesque funerary temple, the Ramesseum; or observing the unnerving precision of the hieroglyphs in the tomb of Ramses V and VI, in the Valley of the Kings, that has proved immune to the ravages of time.

Formerly ancient Thebes, Luxor—whose name comes from the Arabic Al-Uqsur (The Palaces)—served as Egypt's capital during the New Kingdom, from circa 1550 BCE to 1070 BCE. On the west bank of the Nile, sugarcane and banana plantations lead to a limestone canyon topped by Al-Qurn, or The Horn, a natural peak shaped like a pyramid. The rulers of the New Kingdom decided that this would be the ideal spot to protect their richly decorated tombs from grave robbers—a failed exercise, since every tomb in the Valley of the Kings was looted in antiquity, bar that of now legendary boy king Tutankhamen.

“There are many sites that have an impressive amount of ‘stuff,’ but what you have in Luxor is truly monumental,” Mennat-Allah El Dorry, from the American University in Cairo's department of sociology, Egyptology, and anthropology, tells me. “You have Karnak and Luxor temples on the east bank, and the mortuary temples on the west, as well as Valley of the Kings. It is such a dense area.”

I take her recommendations, balancing the quiet of the lesser-visited, only partially restored Mortuary Temple of Seti I and the Ramesseum with the many-splendored tombs at the Valley of the Kings, where voyeuristic crowds swell to see the diminutive mummy of Tutankhamen languishing 26 feet below ground. By contrast, the tomb of Ramses V and VI close by is deserted. A toothless, djellaba-wearing guard smiles conspiratorially before letting me behind the barrier. He takes my phone and assumes the practiced ease of a fashion photographer directing his next magazine cover: “Come closer; go there; look over your shoulder.”

Much of Luxor feels like it hasn't changed in centuries. At sunset the sails of felucca boats trace a timeless scene on the Nile's surface. Amid the clip-clop of horse-drawn carriages, the call to prayer tumbles from minarets and the sky settles into strips of apricot and lavender.

Matching the restraint of Arax is the stripped-back Marsam Hotel and discreet yet stately Habu Hotel, the latter just feet away from the Medinet Habu Temple. But Hotel Al Moudira sits at the opposite end of the spectrum. Founded by Italian Lebanese artist Zeina Aboukheir in 2001, and originally designed by famed Egyptian architect Olivier Sednaoui, the hotel revels in its maximalism: a whimsical interplay of domes and arches embellished with terra-cotta plaster, frescoes, and antiques. In 2022, Aboukheir sold the hotel to its new owner, Florian Amereller, but she still guides its creative direction, most recently in the design of six new villas. I stay in one of the five rooms in the salmon pink Villa Casbah, where hand-painted silhouettes of gazelles trip skittishly across the walls.

Chef Gioconda Scott at The Moudira Farm Kitchen

Under its new ownership the now five-star Al Moudira has expanded to include a huge swath of surrounding farmland. It's here, in an open kitchen engulfed in greenery, that I find British Spanish chef Gioconda Scott in the midst of a busy lunch service. In 2025 she launched The Moudira Farm Kitchen, where she transforms the fresh produce grown on-site into an unfussy, seasonal menu inspired by the Mediterranean. “This is simple cooking,” says Scott, who populates her kitchen with young chefs from the local tourism college. “Every element has to be good. If you don't have a good olive oil or a good tomato, there's no hiding.”

The restaurant itself is filled with products made by artisans on the farm. Crockery, rendered in a range of earthy tones, was crafted by potters whom guests can join for classes. I can hear the distant clack of the loom that wove the jaunty turquoise tablecloth, while, in other corners, artisans carve alabaster, blow glass, and upholster furniture.

The same crafts inhabit the decks of Al Moudira's new, 180-foot Nile Canopus, a nostalgia-infused nod to historic travel along this evocative waterway. Open-air decks with safari-tent-style coverings, a cozy library, and rooms fitted with brass beds and bespoke teak and rattan furniture are designed to evoke the age of Amelia Edwards, author of the seminal 1877 travelogue A Thousand Miles Up the Nile.

There has been a proliferation of new dahabeahs on the Nile, which offer more intimate, personalized experiences than do the hulking, 50-cabin motorboats that also ply these waters. Laden with modern conveniences, today's dahabeahs are admittedly no longer sprightly enough to be harried along by wind and sail; instead they are pushed and pulled by dinky-looking tugboats. On the inside they are increasingly elaborate. Karine Hassoun called on Egyptian painters, professors, and artisans for her eight-cabin dahabeah, Nile Divine, a celebration of contemporary Egyptian craft. In the nine-cabin Oro, a dark wood exterior pays tribute to the dahabeahs of old but with a dramatic brass wall in the reception area, a plunge pool extending out over the deck, a full-fledged bar up top, and suites with private terraces and hot tubs. Oberoi Hotels and Resorts will join the fray later this year with two seven-suite dahabeahs featuring interiors by Karim Mekhtigian, founder of Alchemy Design Studio, while Waldorf Astoria Hotels and Resorts' new, 29-suite Nile cruiser will bring to the water all the elements of its land-based hotels, including its Peacock Alley brasserie.

Change is underway on land too. I see the cranes hovering over the east bank, pinpointing where a Four Seasons Hotel, due to open in 2027, is rapidly taking shape. The much-loved Winter Palace—archaeologist Howard Carter's base during his 1922 Tutankhamen tomb discovery and where Agatha Christie was inspired to write parts of Death on the Nile—recently closed for a renovation and will reopen as a Mandarin Oriental in July 2027, exactly 120 years after its official inauguration, hopefully with original features and charm fully intact.

That's only weeks before next year's solar eclipse: On August 2, Luxor will witness the moon masking the sun for its maximum duration, a total of 6 minutes and 22 seconds. Just enough time for that line between the real and the mystical to grow even flimsier.

A few feet from Habu Temple, recommended for its deeply etched hieroglyphs and particularly well-preserved colors, is a property with its own historic pedigree: the unassuming, 17-room Habu Hotel was one of the first hotels to open on Luxor’s West Bank in the 1920s. It has been given a smart revamp, its public areas now filled with antiques, including stately granite busts and wooden statues from the 1800s. Sundowners on the hotel’s charming rooftop terrace bring you close enough to the temple’s chiseled interior that you can admire its exterior engravings from the comfort of your lounge chair.

A day spent tirelessly exploring Luxor’s sites is best ended in the spa at Hilton Luxor Resort and Spa, where treatment rooms look directly over the Nile and the infinity pool is one of the best spots in the city to catch Luxor’s famous sunsets. This is an ultra-convenient base if you want easy access to the historic sites on Luxor’s East Bank—Karnak Temple, in particular, is within walking distance. A private breakfast on a felucca offers a fresh perspective of the Nile, especially if you time it to coincide with hot-air balloons rising majestically over the Valley of the Kings.

For a stripped-back stay that’ll make you feel like an Egyptologist of old, head to Marsam Hotel, which started life as the excavation house for the University of Chicago, before being converted into a hotel in 1939. There’s (very intentionally) no swimming pool or TVs; the 29 pared-back rooms and five suites are designed for guests who are serious about exploring the many sites that surround this historic hotel. Whether or not you spend the night, make time for lunch at Marsam’s farm-to-table restaurant, where the menu changes daily and you’ll be serenaded by the resident donkeys, camels and horses.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6232. Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card Amex Offers Deal: Save $200 On $900+ Flight

The Amex Offers program frequently offers promotions that can save you money on flights, hotel stays, etc. There’s a new Amex Offers deal that seems to be specific to one co-branded Marriott card, and it’s incredibly lucrative.

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) seems to have a new targeted Amex Offers deal whereby you can earn $200 back when you spend $900+ on airfare.

This is really straightforward — targeted members just need to register for the Amex Offers deal, and then spend $900+ across one or more transactions by February 28, 2027.

You can reach that spending threshold through one or more qualifying purchases, and the flights need to be booked directly with airlines (so not through a third party). There are no restrictions as to which airline you can book through, so you can use this both for US and foreign carriers, which is awesome.

Officially Amex Offers deals are all targeted, though this one at least seems to be pretty widely targeted. It seems that it’s specific to this card, and that most people with the card are eligible for the offer.

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card has a steep annual fee. Personally, it’s a card that I have, and one that I find to represent a good value, thanks to the variety of perks it offers. However, an easy $200 in savings beyond the expected value sure helps even more with making the math work!

The card ordinarily earns 3x Bonvoy points per dollar spent on airfare, and I value those points at 0.7 cents each, for a 2.1% return. So if you spent exactly $900 on a ticket, you’d get a $200 statement credit plus 2,700 Bonvoy points, which I value at an extra $19 return, for a total return of around 24%. That’s excellent.

Even if you don’t have an immediate ticket you want to book, most major US airlines let you bank credit if you buy a ticket and then decide that you no longer want to travel. So you could typically buy a $900 (non-basic) ticket, and essentially pick up that much credit with an airline for around $700. That’s a great value, assuming you can use the credit before it expires.

Amex Offers has a new deal that can save you $200+ on the cost of an airfare purchase of $900+. This seems to be specific to the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card, and it’s widely targeted. This is an easy opportunity to save well over 20% on the cost of an airline ticket with few strings attached, so it’s worth taking advantage of, if eligible.

Are you eligible for this Amex Offers deal, and do you plan on taking advantage of it?

#6231. 15 of the Coolest Marathon Courses Around the Globe, From the Arctic Circle to the Great Wall of China

The TCS New York City Marathon is consistently one of the best days of the year in the city—it's emotional, it's inspiring, and it shows off the best of humanity. If you're a runner or a spectator who got the itch for more this past weekend, you're in luck: There are tons of incredible courses around the world, and while they may not traverse NYC's five boroughs, they will take you to world wonders, through safari lands, and across borders.

As someone who regularly travels for halfs, I spend a lot of my time researching and bookmarking races. For me, running through a new place one of the best ways to get to know a destination—you get the lay of the land, see what the community is like, and notice things you might not see from a car or public transportation. And as destination races grow in popularity, the courses offered are getting even more spectacular. The races on this list—halfs, fulls, 10Ks, and more—prove it. Below, I’ve rounded up 15 of the most spectacular races happening in the next year or so, all of which are well worth traveling for.

Date: March 13, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half marathon, 10K, 3.5K

What to know: If you haven't run a Rock ‘n’ Roll marathon yet, you're missing out on a good time. As the name suggests, these music-centric runs make for an extremely lively course—bands and DJs fill the roads and the after party. Locations change each year, and in 2027, the series is going to Taitung on Taiwan's east coast; runners will move between the mountains and the Pacific Ocean on a flat, smooth route. After the race, be sure to check out the area's night markets, hot springs, and endless good eats.

Where to stay: Luxury hotels near the starting line include the Sheraton Taitung Hotel, which has an outdoor swimming pool, and Formosan Naruwan Hotel, with a spa and saltwater pool.

Date: April 25, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, 21-miler, 11-miler, 12K, 5K

What to know: With a cliffside, oceanview course running from Big Sur to Carmel along California’s iconic Highway 1, it doesn’t get much more scenic than this. It’s a Boston qualifier race and has a six-hour time limit, along with several course length options, making it a good one to run with a group, even if your ideal mileage differs.

Where to stay: Room blocks are available at a few different properties in Monterey, closer to the finish line. Of course, there is no shortage of luxury hotels in the area—Alila Ventana Big Sur, Post Ranch Inn, and Carmel Beach Hotel are a few Traveler favorites.

Date: April 4, 2027Registration: The 2027 lottery entry has taken place; check back in May for the 2028 race; charity bibs are still availableDistances included: Half-marathon

What to know: As the name suggests, the course runs past several London landmarks, including Big Ben, the Tower of London, the London Eye, and Somerset House. It’s a lively course—musical performances, DJs, dancers, and themed cheer stations can be expected—and even better, it's a flat one, with 238 feet of total elevation gain.

Where to stay: In 2026, Blue Orchid Hospitality and the Clermont Hotel Group offered discounts for race weekend stays at properties like The Wellington Hotel, The Tower Hotel, and Thistle Trafalgar. We’ll update that list once 2027 partners are announced. For luxury stays near the starting line, consider Raffles London at the OWO or the Corinthia London.

Date: April 04, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half marathon, 10K

What to know: Okay, I'll get the cons over with first (for most, I'd presume): This is a cold and snowy course. Once you've got that fact out of the way, you can weigh the very unique pros. This Finnish Lapland course kicks off in Santa Claus Village square (!) in Rovaniemi, starting exactly on the line of the Arctic Circle. It's put together as part of a five-day running program with log cabin lodging, each with a private sauna, as well as activities like husky sledding, Northern Lights excursions, and an Ice Pool Experience. It all wraps up at a trophy dinner with—wait for it—Santa Claus himself. This is peak whimsy, friends.

Where to stay: Lodging is included in the tour package.

Date: May 15, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half-marathon, 8.5K

What to know: This race lets you run along one of the seven wonders of the world. It’s a strenuous, hilly course, but if the views alone don’t keep you going, the residents in local villages cheering you on along the route just might.

Of note, to register, you must sign up for a tour package; the starting price is $790 and includes race entry plus two nights of accommodations. It’s sponsored by Albatross Adventure Marathons, which also puts on The Big Five Marathon (more details below) and the Iceland Volcano Marathon, among other adventurous runs.

Where to stay: Hotels must be booked along with the packages. For a relaxing post-race stay, check into the Mandarin Oriental Qianmen, Beijing, with its award-winning spa (after a massage, consider the tea meditation too) and standout dining options, from Italian to dim sum.

Date: May 16, 2027Registration: Open now and quite affordable—the most expensive distance is €39 ($44)Distances included: Half-marathon, 10K, 5K (paved course); 17K, 8K (trail)

What to know: Set in Tossa de Mar, a beautiful, historic seaside town on Spain’s Costa Brava, these runs are all about the coastal views. Of course, that does mean a challenging, hilly course for all but the 5K, which boasts a flat route in the town’s center. Of note, the maximum time is on the shorter end: 2 hours 35 minutes for the half, 1 hour 15 for the 10K, and 45 minutes for the 5K.

Where to stay: Zel Costa Brava, about a 10-minute drive from the starting line, was mentioned in our list of the Best Places to Go in Spain and Portugal in 2026. It has a funicular to take guests down to the beach, a huge pool with plenty of lounge chairs to kick back on, and a spa with a thermal circuit, ideal for soothing sore legs.

Date: June 11-12, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half marathon, 5K

What to know: Running around America's first national park, near sites like the Grand Prismatic Spring, is bound to be a highlight for any outdoor-loving runner. While not inside the bounds of the park, the views from the Custer Gallatin National Forest and the Hebgen Lake Ranger District are still impressive. The half marathon starts bright and early at 6 a.m. and has a four-hour course limit. There are five aid stations along the way, and 552 feet of elevation (of note, there are some technical, rocky sections to contend with).

Where to stay: The Lazy Duck Inn is the most convenient choice, given it's location near the start and finish line. To pad out the rest of your trip, check out our guide to where to stay in and near Yellowstone.

Date: June 19, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Full marathon, half-marathon

What to know: The name says it all: You might just see the big five while you run! The course takes runners through the South African Savannah on the Entabeni Game Reserve. It is a smaller race, with a maximum of 300 participants, in a moderate climate (expected to be in the 60s to 70s this year) along a sand and gravel trail. Past participants rave about this one, calling it “The ONLY marathon I have wanted to run twice!” and “the best adventure ever.” Like the Great Wall course, registration requires selecting a tour package, starting at $3,560 for the seven-day package, which includes accommodation, meals, game drives, bush walks, and more.

Where to stay: At the end of any package, you’ll be transferred to Johannesburg International Airport. Give yourself a night to decompress at the Park Hyatt Johannesburg, where peacocks roam the grounds, rooms overlook serene gardens, and Sunday brunch comes with a side of live music.

Date: June 19, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half-marathon, 10K, 5K, kids race

What to know: The Tromsø, Norway, race begins at 8:30 p.m.—but thanks to the midnight sun the event is named after, it’s still light out. One of the northernmost races in the world, with a course surrounded by mountains and fjords, it boasted 9,000 runners from an impressive 88 countries last year. Of note, the maximum time limit is 5 hours and 30 minutes for the marathon and 3 hours and 30 minutes for the half.

Where to stay: Right in Tromsø, St. Elisabeth makes for a lovely stay, especially if you take advantage of the spa’s thermal bath, pool, and saunas. A bit further out (45 minutes or so), the Yggdrasiltunet Farm Hotel offers an even more blissful setting for a post-race escape with its wood-fired barrel sauna, guided ice bathing, hot tub overlooking the sea, and yoga classes.

Date: June 20, 2027Registration: Open now (half marathon is already sold out; sign up for 2028 notifications on the website)Distances included: Half marathon, 10K

What to know: The race website dubs this “the most beautiful run on the planet,” and honestly, that might not be so hyperbolic. Running through Canada's first national park sounds like a dream, especially when the course passes by the Vermilion Lakes, Legacy Trail, and Bow Valley Parkway, with wildlife likely to be spotted along the way. It's not a particularly hilly course, with a total elevation gain of 418 feet, but do note the elevation, which maxes out at 4,620 feet.

Where to stay: The official host partner is Banff Lodging Company, which operates 16 hotels across Banff, Canmore, and Lake Louise, including Hotel Canoe & Suites and Otter Hotel. Guests can receive a 15% discount on these rates. Afterward, consider a wellness-centric stay at the stunning Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise.

Date: July 03, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Full marathon, half-marathon, 10.55k

What to know: Designed for adventure-seekers, this Northern Iceland race explores one of Earth's geological hot spots—you’ll run along the rim of two volcanic craters and over black lava rock, with steaming geysers taking your mind off the miles ahead.

Unless you’re an Icelandic resident, you’ll need to book the six-day tour package, which is around $3,100 and includes accommodation, transportation, meals, a celebratory post-race dinner, and some activities, with add-ons like whale-watching and waterfall chasing available too. Of note, race entrance is not included in that fee ($350 for the half and full, and $223 for the quarter marathon).

Where to stay: Our resident Iceland expert and contributing writer Erika Owen highly recommends one of the tour lodging options, Fosshotel Glacier Lagoon, saying that it “embodies the best of Iceland: seclusion, surrounding nature, and beds topped with Icelandic wool blankets.” On your way out of town, consider a stay at The Retreat at Blue Lagoon; beyond the must-dip-in thermal baths, the tasting menu at Michelin-starred Moss is well worth a splurge.

Date: July 18, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half-marathon, 5K, The Pairing (both!)

What to know: A 13.1-mile route through Napa and Sonoma’s wine country, this course is surrounded by farms, vineyards, and ranches—yes, there are gently rolling hills, but it’s not an overly challenging course. The real prize for the 3,000-ish participants is at the finish line: At the post-race wine festival, top local vineyards reward you with wine tastings, and your goodie bag includes a commemorative wine glass.

Where to stay: Several hotels partner with the race to offer discounted stays, including the Westin Verasa Napa Hotel, notable for its Hyperice Recover & Recharge Kit available at the front desk. (Heads up for other future runs: Hyperice and Normatec products can be found at most Westins across the US! I swear by the Normatecs and Hypervolt for post-race recovery.) Just across the street from the starting line sits Carneros Resort and Spa, a seven-time Readers’ Choice Award winner; down the street is Stanly Ranch, Auberge Collection, a resort with a gorgeous outdoor pool that’s exactly where I’d want to park myself post-race.

Date: October 15–17, 2027Registration: Opens January 1, 2027Distances included: Marathon, marathon relay, half-marathon, 5K, one miler, kids races

What to know: This is one course that’s absolutely on my running bucket list, and one I hope to tackle in 2027 (which happens to be the event's 50th anniversary!). It’s the only US race I’ve found that crosses borders: After starting in downtown Detroit, runners cross over the Ambassador Bridge into Windsor, Ontario, before returning to the US through the Detroit-Windsor Tunnel (yep, an underwater mile!). Uniquely, this means you will have to carry your passport during the marathon and international half.

Where to stay: The AC Hotel Detroit at the Bonstelle is minutes from the start line, and well-situated to other places of interest (Little Caesar’s Arena, Fox Theater, the Detroit Institute of Arts). For a post-race treat, stop by Warda Pâtisserie. JW Marriott Detroit Water Square, opening in February 2027 near the Riverwalk, is sure to be a lovely place to stay too.

Date: November 2027Registration: Not yet openDistances included: Marathon, 10K, 5K

What to know: History buffs will love this course in Greece, which, according to legend, follows the original marathon route Pheidippides ran way back in 490 B.C. when he brought news of victory from the battlefield of Marathon (it’s also the course used in the 2004 Olympics). The marathon course stays open for eight hours and passes by landmarks like the Athens Concert Hall, Eleftherias Park, the Presidential Palace, and the National Garden. There are packages available if you want transportation, accommodations, and tour options baked into your visit; they’re not required for entry, but individual registration tends to sell out first, so plan accordingly.

Where to stay: The race starts in the town of Marathon, northeast of central Athens. For a stay close to the finish line with an excellent spa and both indoor and outdoor swimming pools, consider Hotel Grande Bretagne, a Luxury Collection Hotel. A bit further south, the seaside One&Only Aesthesis offers a touch of coastal glamour, plus a Guerlain spa.

Date: November 2027Registration: Not yet openDistances included: Marathon, marathon relay, half-marathon, 5K, one miler

What to know: The course begins in downtown Tulsa, weaving through neighborhoods and the University of Tulsa campus. Along the way, you'll encounter lots of support from the community, with block parties hosted along the course to cheer runners on. Of note, this is a Boston Qualifier, and race day temperatures tend to sit around the 50s.

Where to stay: Room blocks are available at several partner hotels, including Brut Hotel, a charming boutique hotel a short drive from the start line with an outdoor pool, rooftop bar, and spa. I’m eyeing the Olympian Massage, designed to “relieve tension and restore mobility by utilizing deep tissue and sports massage techniques.”

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6230. Condor Plans To Open First-Ever Lounge At Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3

Germany’s second largest airline, Condor, plans to open its own lounge for the first time ever. However, some more patience will be required, and details are also still quite limited.

Earlier this year, we saw Frankfurt Airport (FRA) open its new Terminal 3, which is the airport’s first new terminal in decades. We’ve already seen all airlines that previously occupied Terminal 2 move to Terminal 3.

The long term plan is that Terminal 1 will be exclusively for Lufthansa and its Star Alliance partners, while Terminal 3 will be for all other airlines. Meanwhile Terminal 2 may eventually be rebuilt, as Lufthansa hopes to take it over as well, but that’s a very long term vision.

As of now, the only airline that hasn’t yet completed the move to Terminal 3 is Condor, which is Germany’s second largest airline. The carrier still operates out of Terminal 1, and uses Lufthansa lounges for its customers, despite Lufthansa’s disdain for the carrier.

The expectation is that Condor will make the move to Frankfurt Terminal 3 in the spring of 2027. As part of that, the airline also plans to open two lounges in the terminal, as reported by aeroTELEGRAPH. The expectation is that one will be a Schengen lounge, while the other will be a non-Schengen lounge.

The catch is that the lounges will only open later in 2027, due to the pace of construction. While the company’s CEO confirmed these plans in a meeting with employees, publicly the airline has only confirmed that “we are currently in discussions with our partners at Terminal 3 of Frankfurt Airport to explore the possibilities for Condor’s own lounge offering.”

No details are yet known about what kind of amenities the lounges will offer… I’m definitely curious to see what they come up with, as it’s always interesting when an airline opens a lounge for the first time!

Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3 is getting quite a nice selection of lounges. As things currently stand:

On top of that, we know that Qatar Airways is opening two lounges in the non-Schengen area of the terminal, which will be for passengers traveling on oneworld airlines.

Condor is expected to move to Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3 in the spring of 2027, as it’s the last (and largest) airline to make the move to the terminal. We now officially know that Condor is planning on opening two lounges in the terminal, though they’ll likely only open in late 2027.

It’s exciting to see the airline open lounges for the first time, and only time will tell how this plays out…

What do you make of Condor opening lounges for the first time?

Earlier this year, JetBlue raised its checked bag fees and kicked off a wave of fee hikes across the industry. United followed. Then Delta, American and Southwest.

Seven months later, JetBlue is leading the fee-hiking charge again.

The carrier on Tuesday raised its bag fees for the second time in 2026.

Going forward, customers will pay at least $50 per bag. That’s a 28% jump from the lowest fee the airline previously charged its customers.

Passengers who don’t pre-pay for their bag will pay $60 for their first piece of checked luggage.

And because JetBlue uses a dynamic baggage-pricing system, flyers will pay even more for their checked baggage on peak travel days.

In a statement about the airline's second bag-fee hike this year, the carrier pointed to rising fuel and operating costs.

“This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one,” a spokesperson said.

Here’s how JetBlue’s bag fees will shake out, going forward.

These fees will apply to flights booked starting Nov. 3.

So if you had already purchased a JetBlue flight prior to Nov. 3 — including trips for the holidays — the previous fees would apply to your trip.

As noted above, JetBlue also raised the fees customers will pay for their second checked bag, too.

Here are the days where JetBlue's "peak" baggage fees will apply, through October 2027.

JetBlue does continue to offer free baggage perks as a benefit of certain cobranded credit cards. Plus, its Mosaic elite status members each get at least one free bag.

Customers flying in JetBlue’s premium Mint cabin are still entitled to their first bag free. The same goes for flyers who book the carrier’s new domestic first-class (BlueFirst) seats, which are set to debut on some flights next month.

As JetBlue raises its baggage fees, the biggest question for consumers is how the rest of the airline industry respond.

If history is any indication, we’re about to see another wave of fee hikes across the industry.

After JetBlue raised its bag fees in late March, it took only weeks for nearly every major U.S. carrier to follow with their own fee hikes.

This would be the latest case of sticker shock for travelers, who are simultaneously battling surging fares.

Even budget airline Frontier last week reported customers had paid 71% more in fares over the prior quarter.

All of this comes as airlines have had to contend with sky-high jet fuel costs in 2026 — which they’ve aggressively passed onto customers.

But while jet fuel costs may eventually fall, it’s unlikely flyers will see any future relief when it comes to baggage fees — typically, once those go up, they don’t come back down.

While JetBlue has raised its baggage fees, it is worth noting that passengers do have freedom to bring a full-size carry-on bag on JetBlue flights, regardless of the fare type. The airline no longer bars its Blue Basic (basic economy) passengers from using the overhead bins.

Of course, the belongings packed in any carry-on bag must meet the Transportation Security Administration's 3-1-1 liquids policy.

#6228. Getting to Know New York Through Its Sandwiches

“By the end of our time together, I will be asking you again: ‘So, what is a sandwich?’”

An expert-led tour that starts by questioning its own object of inquiry is unconventional. But then, so is our guide. Ben Gollan, known to his Instagram followers as A Man and His Sandwich, has spent the last nine years reviewing sandwiches across New York City. Gollan moved here from Australia in 2016, after nearly a decade as a government lawyer. For about as long, he has run an Airbnb Experience that turns a food crawl into a two-hour pilgrimage to the city’s best sandwich slingers.

It was a pastrami sandwich at Harry & Ida’s, a former deli in the East Village, that turned Gollan into a professional sandwich hound. “It was a fourth-generation Jewish deli that broke every rule of pastrami sandwiches: it was thick-cut and fabulous,” he says as we dash across Bowery. We’re scuttling over from a coffee shop in Cooper Square that served as our meeting point and into the East Village—a neighborhood of contrasts that still manages to connect New York's past and present. There are 12 of us in total, mostly locals, a couple of newer transplants, and just one traveler. “It’s usually mostly visitors, so this is different,” he says.

It’s a great introduction to the city. After all, New York runs on sandwiches, and there’s no shortage of great ones, whether it’s a classic Italian deli sub you’re after or a grab-and-go banh mi. They’re economical, versatile, delicious and, as is the point of Gollan’s tour, telegraph the city’s greatest personality trait—its diversity. So is there such a thing as a New York sandwich? “Not really,” he says, "but the chopped cheese, born in East Harlem, might come closest.”

The Bono at Via Della Scrofa, a small family-owned joint that wouldn't look out of place on the streets of Rome

“We start here because it’s closest to what we think of as a traditional sandwich,” says Gollan, before filling us in on the origins of what is the modern-day sandwich. It involves John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, who, in the 18th century, gave his title to the now-ubiquitous food. Gollan loves to talk and think about sandwiches as much as he eats them. “Although I've learned never to trust history, especially when rendered by colonizers,” he muses. “Do we really think it took us till the 1700s to invent the sandwich?”

Named after a Roman street, Via Della Scrofa is the kind of bottega or alimentari you might find in Rome, with a tiny counter selling tiny espressos and focaccia, as well as imported groceries from Italy. “It's small family-owned joints like this that make New York what it is,” says Gollan. While the rest of the group gets to try the Porcodeddena panini (made with porchetta), I’m getting a Bono: grilled eggplants sweetened with sun-dried tomatoes, with arugula and buffalo mozzarella, in a warm roll that’s toasty on the outside and soft and warm on the inside. The bread is perfect—it’s a rosetta (or michetta), a traditional Roman bread roll. I wash it down with a Crodino, a popular non-alcoholic bitter aperitif from Italy.

Around us, the Lower East Side Arts & Culture Open House, an annual event, had taken over the street, adding personality to our time with its bands, pop-up stalls, and lively crowds. Gollan regales us with stories of owner Giovanni Bartocci, describing him as a real character with “a man bun, suspenders, tattoos, and naturally, a Harley," and I look around hoping he'll show up. I ask Gollan why he isn’t eating with us. “I never want to tire of these sandwiches, and if I keep eating them, I will.” The wind picks up and blows over the canvases at an art stall, but the band is undeterred, playing “New York, New York.”

A spicy Pakistani rendition of the chopped cheese at Nishaan

The writer and her chopped cheese sandwich, the chapli kebab replaced with Impossible Meat.

Order: A chopped cheese, but make it desi

An 11-minute walk up 1st Avenue and a few blocks later, we spot our next sandwich spot. A cobalt-blue sign reads Nishaan; bags of rice are piled high along its exterior; and a long line snakes out of what I can only assume is a tiny space inside. Nishaan began as a pop-up at the weekly open-air food festival Smorgasburg and went on to win season 18 of The Great Food Truck Race. While there are other dishes on the menu (elote chaat, mango lassi), it’s Nishaan’s twist on that great New York City bodega staple, the chopped cheese, that many are after: a spice-laden chapli kebab, chopped up on a griddle with peppers and onions, then enhanced with a zingy cilantro sauce and tamarind chutney. When it opened in August 2025, it was one of the most talked-about new restaurants in New York City, which has emerged as a hub for a new generation of Pakistani eateries. “New York belongs to everyone, and so does the sandwich,” proclaims Gollan.

In a city that runs on pastrami, vegetarians like me don’t faze Gollan; he orders me a version with Impossible Meat. We tuck ourselves out of the wind and into an alley and dig in. I can’t stop eating, making a mess as I go along. “Half the fun of a sandwich is the experience of eating it,” Gollan adds.

Regulars love the pho sandwiches at Sunny and Annie’s—sandwiches stuffed to the brim with pho ingredients, minus the broth.

Sunny and Annie’s is a 24/7, 365-day-a-year kind of neighborhood classic with 92 items on its sandwich menu.

“We’re taking a detour,” says Gollan, frantically looking around him. It’s the day of the Tompkins Square Halloween Dog Parade, and the crowds around us are building, as are the dogs in costume—cheese boards, UPS drivers, and, suitably for the occasion, hot dogs. We ditch the idea of cutting through the park and work our way around the revelers.

Our destination? Sunny and Annie’s, a 24/7, 365-days-a-year kind of neighborhood classic that has been open since 1997. There’s no front door here, because there’s always someone around. Inside, past the candy, chips, and dish detergent, we’re greeted by what must be the most extensive sandwich menu I’ve ever encountered, all written out on brightly colored sheets of paper stuck to the glass counter. There are 92 handheld options in total, some named after politicians and celebrities, like the Jackie Chan—bulgogi, cilantro, avocado, lettuce, jalapeños, and onions, served on a roll or hero. There’s also a chicken cutlet sandwich called the Australian. It’s not named after Gollan.

This is not a place to linger, so we keep it moving. Outside, the crowds have thickened, and Gollan instructs us to head to a neighborhood bar called ABC Beer Co., which often features at the end of his tours. As someone who has spent many a night in an East Village bar, I’m disappointed I’ve never been here before. It’s spacious, has a backyard, and is equally welcoming to couples on dates and families with little ones.

The writer's sandwich tour ended at ABC Beer Co, a hybrid beer bar and store with a particular focus on NYC breweries.

Gollan appears with our pho sandwiches, wrapped in spinach tortillas. They smell like pho, taste like pho; only the avocado throws me off.

Some of us get ciders and wine, and the conversation winds back to where we started: So, what really is a sandwich? “I want this to get contentious: bang the tables, let’s have a food fight," Gollan says, egging us on. Hot dogs? Quesadillas? What about a hamburger? A pizza folded in half? Does it have to have a carb? What about a lettuce wrap instead of bread? Gollan briefs us on a famous 2006 Massachusetts lawsuit—White City Shopping Center vs. Panera Bread—which legally answered an age-old culinary debate: Is a burrito a sandwich? The judge ruled that a burrito is, in fact, not a sandwich, clearing the way for the Mexican fast-casual joint to open in the vicinity of Panera Bread. “A sandwich court case is my Roman Empire," he says. “When this question goes to the Supreme Court, I will be there.”

The point of this tour—and the posed question—Gollan says, was never to walk away with an answer, but to open our minds and palates. So, what are Ben Gollan’s own rules for a sandwich, I have to ask. He lists the following:

And then he adds: “Take those rules and throw them in the bin.” And with that, class is dismissed.

The NYC Sandwich Tour can be booked directly on the A Man and His Sandwich website, as well as on Airbnb. Tours run every day of the week, with the exception of Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Ben Gollan, who proudly calls himself the Chief Sandwich Officer, often leads the experiences himself, but he also has co-hosts to help guide fellow sandwich enthusiasts on these two-hour outings. Along the way, guests sample three standout sandwiches—from the classic to the “slightly unhinged”—before finishing up at a bar to settle the debate over what really counts as a sandwich. While my tour focused on the East Village, Gollan also leads sandwich tours around Williamsburg. And word on the street is that he has his eye on opening a sandwich shop of his own one day.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6227. Park Hyatt Phu Quoc, Vietnam, Opening Soon, And I’m Intrigued!

Want to take advantage of Hyatt Privé benefits, including a room upgrade, complimentary breakfast, a hotel credit, and more, when booking a cash stay? Contact Ford ([email protected]) for more details. He may even be able to help if you already have a stay booked.

Back in 2019, plans were announced for an exciting new Park Hyatt resort in Vietnam. The property has been massively behind schedule on its planned 2022 opening. Several months ago, the hotel started accepting reservations for stays as of March 2027. There’s now a positive update, as the timeline has been moved forward to December 2026, so it’s just weeks away.

The Park Hyatt Phu Quoc is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 8, 2026. The delays on this property have been endless, so it’s nice to see the timeline moved forward for once. Here’s to hoping that there are no last minute delays.

For those not familiar with Phu Quoc, it’s Vietnam’s largest island, and half of the island is in a national park and UNESCO site. The Park Hyatt Phu Quoc is expected to feature a total of 168 keys, including 114 rooms and suites, and 54 private pool villas. This is Park Hyatt’s first resort in Vietnam, and second property in the country, after the Park Hyatt Saigon.

The resort is located on the southwestern tip of Phu Quoc Island, and is developed on 160 acres of land, bordered by a mile-long white sand beach on one side, and lush hills on the other side. The Park Hyatt is a 30-minute drive from Phu Quoc International Airport (PQC).

Details about the property are fairly limited, though here are some things we do know:

Below are some renderings of the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc. Given that we’ve had the same renderings for years and the property has been delayed year after year, I can’t help but wonder if the actual property looks anything like the renderings.

With the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc bookable, what are rates like? If you’re looking to redeem World of Hyatt points, this is a Category 7 property, meaning that a free night redemption will cost anywhere from 25,000 to 55,000 points per night, assuming a standard room is available. I value World of Hyatt points at around 1.4 cents each, so that puts the “cost” of a redemption at $350-770 per night.

When it comes to cash rates, they seem to start at just over $700 per night, and that’s before the 13.4% in taxes and service charges, so we’re talking about entry level rates of over $800 per night all-in.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, a hotel credit, and more. Ford and his team are happy to help with these requests, and can be reached at [email protected].

Depending on the award pricing for the nights you’re looking at, redeeming points here could potentially be a very good value.

While I’ve visited major cities in Vietnam several times before, I’ve never gone there for a beach vacation, so I’m intrigued by this property, especially given the value of World of Hyatt points, plus of World of Hyatt Globalist status.

Based on what I’ve heard, currently the top properties on the island are the JW Marriott Phu Quoc, the InterContinental Phu Quoc, and the Regent Phu Quoc. Many people have told me that these properties are among the best of their respective portfolios.

I’m curious, though, for those who have been to Phu Quoc, is it worth a trek from the United States? I’m sure it’s gorgeous and I’ll certainly take Vietnamese food over Caribbean food, but is it otherwise worth traveling that far out of the way?

It’s funny how my preferences in that regard have changed over the years. 15 years ago, I’d almost exclusively take beach vacations in Southeast Asia, given the generally higher standard of everything (service, hotels, etc.), plus the more reasonable prices.

However, as I’ve gotten older, my opinion has changed. For one, the jet lag becomes more challenging the older I get, and can take away from relaxation. Furthermore, flight award options just aren’t as exciting as they were over a decade ago. Like, easily being able to always snag Cathay Pacific first class awards was a great reason to vacation in Asia, as far as I’m concerned. 😉 But that’s no longer so easy.

But I also have another motive here. I’m intrigued by airline startup Sun PhuQuoc Airways, which is just taking delivery of some Airbus A330s. So if I can fly an ex-American A330 directly to here, I’d sure find that to be amusing! For that matter, I really love the Capella hotel brand, and I’ve heard the Capella Hanoi is among the best in the portfolio, so I’d really love to visit that, and pair it with a visit here.

A Park Hyatt property is expected to open in Phu Quoc, Vietnam, and it’s now accepting reservations for stays as of December 2026. This property has been under development for eons, and it’s over four years behind schedule on opening. With the opening being just weeks away, here’s to hoping that the timeline finally actually sticks.

Do you plan on checking out the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc?

#6226. The Key Differences Between Economy, Premium Economy, Business & First Class

Boarding a plane today means stepping into a highly structured, carefully designed world. If you’re a frequent traveler or just interested in aviation, you probably spend your walk down the aisle analyzing exactly how airlines divide up the limited space inside their aluminum — nowadays also composite — tubes with wings. Understanding the real differences between economy class, premium economy, business class, and first class goes beyond just picking a ticket — it’s actually a masterclass in clever cabin design and airline economics that extends far beyond what we as passengers could ever imagine. In this guide, we’ll break down exactly what you get for your money across all four cabin zones.

To understand today's LOPAs (acronym for Layout of Passenger Accommodations), you have to look at how much flying has changed. During the "Golden Age" of the 1950s and 60s, just being on an airplane was a luxury, and even standard "coach" seats offered generous legroom and a sophisticated onboard service. Today, the industry is highly competitive, data-driven, and built on optimizing every single square inch. While we might miss the spaciousness of the past, this high-density approach is exactly what made flying affordable for millions, creating a sliding scale of comfort that fits just about every budget.

Economy class, often called "coach", "standard seating," or "the back of the bus," is the undisputed backbone of the global commercial aviation industry. As someone who spends a lot of time thinking about airplane seats, I look at the economy cabin not only as the cramped space — and barely acceptable experience — that it is, but as an incredible feat of modern engineering and logistics. This is where the vast majority of travelers sit, and it’s the cabin that makes it possible for airlines to transport hundreds of people across the globe at affordable prices. While it often gets a deserved bad reputation for tight legroom and shrinking seat sizes, economy class is actually a masterclass in efficiency, allowing carriers to maximize passenger count while still meeting strict global safety regulations.

The main defining feature of modern economy class is space optimization, which is measured primarily by "seat pitch," the distance from any point on one seat to the exact same point on the seat in front of it. A few decades ago, standard pitch was around 34 inches (about 86cm), but today, most major carriers offer between 30 and 31 inches, with some ultra-low-cost carriers tightening it to 28 inches (about 71 cm). To make up for this lost space, seat manufacturers have developed "slimline" designs, stripping out bulky padding and using lightweight composite materials to carve out a little extra knee room for the passenger. Even with less physical space, today's modern long-haul economy seats often come with a crisp, on-demand entertainment screen, USB power outlets and a very limited recline, which tries to compensate for the uncomfortable and claustrophobic passenger experience that has become standard on almost every airline around the globe.

Despite the obvious physical limitations, economy class delivers exactly what it promises: safe, reliable transport that gets you to your destination at the exact same time as the people paying thousands of dollars at the front of the plane. For the budget-conscious traveler or the weekend adventurer, flying coach is a highly practical decision that leaves more money in your pocket for your actual vacation. Plus, when you consider that a modern twin-engine jet like the Airbus A350 or Boeing 787 is pressurizing the cabin to a more comfortable altitude and pumping in more humidity than older jets, the actual physiological experience of flying in economy today is arguably better than it was twenty years ago — but the truth is that the physical experience isn't.

If you've booked a long-haul flight recently, you've probably noticed that premium economy has become one of the most popular cabin choices available. Introduced back in the early 1990s by airlines like EVA Air and Virgin Atlanticpremium economy was designed to sit — literally — right in the middle of standard economy and business class, filling a massive gap in the market. As business class tickets got more expensive and economy seats got tighter, a whole new demographic of travelers emerged: people who wanted just a bit more comfort and space, but couldn't justify the sky-high prices of a lie-flat bed. Premium economy essentially brings back the standard of comfort from the older days of flying, repackaging it as an upgraded experience for the modern era.

The physical differences when you upgrade to premium economy have a surprisingly big impact on a long flight. You usually get a wider seat — often 19 or 19.5 inches compared to the standard 17 to 18 inches in economy — and the seat pitch is bumped up to a very comfortable 38 inches, giving you plenty of room to stretch your legs and have a decent amount of recline. The seats also feature wider armrests that you don't have to fight your neighbor for, and usually a fold-out footrest or leg rest to help you sleep better. On top of the physical seat, airlines elevate the "soft product" as well, meaning you might get priority boarding, an upgraded amenity kit, and meals served on real ceramic dishware with metal cutlery instead of plastic trays.

From an airline business perspective, premium economy is an absolute home run. Industry data shows that this cabin often generates the highest profit margins per square foot of any zone on the aircraft, because it only takes up slightly more floor space than standard economy but sells for significantly more money — close to two times the price of an economy ticket. It’s the perfect product for small business owners, corporate employees whose travel policies won't pay for business class, or leisure travelers who want to start their vacation feeling rested.

The seat is the foundation of premium economy comfort. Airlines can add better amenities, but none of those compensate for an uncomfortable seat.

The constant push for innovation in business class seating has been amazing to watch in the last 10 years. We went from "angle-flat" seats that tended to slide you downward while you slept, to 180-degree fully lie-flat beds, and now to direct-aisle-access layouts where nobody has to climb over their neighbor to go to the restroom or the galley. Carriers like Qatar Airways with its famous Qsuites, or Japan Airlines with its brand new A350-1000 suites, have added sliding doors to the seats, turning them into private mini-rooms. Inside these suites, you’re treated to massive 4K entertainment screens, multiple storage compartments, designer bedding, and Michelin Star restaurant-quality dining that you can order on demand.

The reason business class has become so luxurious is simply that airlines have realized what premium passengers value most: uninterrupted sleep. Business travelers are paying a premium to avoid a day of lost productivity due to jet lag and back pain. By providing a true bed and a quiet, private environment, airlines are selling time and well-being rather than just transportation, making it the most important competitive product in their entire lineup.

While business class is focused on comfort and productivity, first class is all about pure, undeniable exclusivity and personalized service. It’s the highest tier of commercial air travel — and almost better than flying on a private jet in every aspect — as it is a space usually reserved for ultra-wealthy individuals, celebrities, or very dedicated travel hackers who have saved up millions of credit card points. First Class goes beyond just giving you a bed; it tries to replicate the experience of a five-star luxury hotel, making you forget that you are actually flying on an airplane at 35,000 feet.

The biggest difference between first and business class today comes down to real estate and the passenger-to-crew ratio. A Business Class cabin might have 40 to 60 seats, but a true first class cabin on a plane like the B777 or A380 usually only has six to eight massive suites and in smaller aircraft like the A350, between three and six. The space you get in first class is just incredible, sometimes featuring a separate leather armchair alongside an actual, standalone bed, rather than a seat that mechanically folds down. This is where airlines pull out all the stops: Emirates has its famous onboard shower spas exclusively dedicated to first class customers, Singapore Airlines offers double beds if you're traveling with a partner, and Etihad Airwaysgoes even one step further with their "Residence" — which features an incredible wide sofa for up to two passengers together with a private bathroom that even has a shower, and to round up the experience a queen-sized bed onboard their A380s. The food for first class passengers on most premium airlines is almost always prepared by a dedicated onboard chef, featuring caviar and high-end vintage champagnes, and every single luxury you could expect for a seating experience that almost never goes below the staggering price of 5,000 US dollars on a one-way ticket, and that can sometimes reach 30,000 or 35,000 US dollars for an ultra-long-haul return ticket.

However, despite how amazing it looks, international first class is actually becoming pretty rare. Because business class has gotten so good with lie-flat beds and sliding doors, most passengers and companies simply aren't willing to pay three or four times the price for first class. As a result, many airlines have completely removed first class from their fleets, using that valuable floor space to install more business and premium economy seats instead. Today, first class is mostly kept around as a "halo product" — something that looks great on billboards and social media to build brand prestige, even if very few people can actually afford to fly in it. For this reason, the only airlines still offering a true first class product are the following:

One of the most common questions I hear from friends and readers is, "Should I pay for the upgrade?" The answer is actually very complicated and depends heavily on how airlines price their tickets and how you value your own comfort. Deciding whether to upgrade from economy to a premium cabin is a personal choice that involves considering your budget, the length of the flight, and the condition you need to be in when you land. Here is a chart with all the key differences between the different classes:

Upgraded menu, real china and metal cutlery

On-demand fine dining, caviar, exclusive wines

Exclusive lounges, tarmac transfers, escorts

If you want to look at it logically, try breaking down the upgrade cost by the hour. For example, if you're taking a six-hour daytime flight from New York to London, sitting in Economy is completely fine for most people; paying an extra $2,500 to upgrade means you're spending over $400 an hour just to have a wider seat while you watch movies. On the other hand, if you're flying 15 hours on a red-eye from Los Angeles to Sydney, the math changes completely. On ultra-long-haul flights, upgrading to a lie-flat bed isn't just a luxury; it's an investment in your physical well-being, meaning you won't lose the first two days of your trip to exhaustion and jet lag — but only if you can afford it.

It’s also helpful to know how airlines handle these upgrades today. In the past, you might have gotten lucky by dressing nicely and asking the gate agent, but today, upgrades are controlled by complex algorithms. Airlines use yield management software to try to sell empty premium seats for cash right up until departure. Many carriers now use digital bidding systems that let you offer a specific amount of money for an upgrade a few days before the flight. It turns the whole process into a silent auction, allowing the airline to squeeze a bit more revenue out of the seat while giving you a chance to fly better for less than the standard fare.

When you really think about it, walking through the different cabins of an airplane shows us how many different ways there are to experience the exact same journey. Whether you are drinking champagne in a massive First Class suite or settling into a window seat in the very last row of Economy, the core product is identical: you are flying through the air at 600 miles per hour, crossing oceans and continents in a matter of hours, from point A to point B. The segmentation of the cabin simply reflects the different priorities of travelers, allowing the people who pay the most expensive tickets at the front to essentially subsidize the more affordable tickets in the back, making global travel possible for everyone.

Looking at the industry today, it's incredible to see how far we've come in terms of safety, technology, and cabin design. We take it for granted that we can watch live TV and browse the internet while miles above the ocean. But as a seat designer, I'm always thinking about what comes next. Airlines will always look for ways to optimize space and increase revenue, but there is a growing demand from passengers for better ergonomics, smarter storage, and more creative uses of the cabin space that doesn't solely rely on standard horizontal rows.

As we look toward the next generation of aircraft and the future of commercial aviation, the big challenge will be balancing airline economics with the passenger experience. With new aircraft materials and potential shifts in fuselage shapes on the horizon, will we continue to just tweak the traditional rows of seats, or is it finally time to completely rethink the three-dimensional space of the cabin to give every passenger — regardless of their ticket class — a better way to fly?

#6225. Denver Air Connection Plans First Florida Service

Denver Air Connection will launch its first-ever service to Florida, and it will be outside the scope of any Essential Air Service (EAS) contract. The only other place in the carrier’s network that isn’t directly part of an EAS contract is its service to Telluride, Colorado, from both Denver and Phoenix.

Beginning January 9, 2027, DAC will begin nonstop flights from Muskegon, Michigan, to Orlando Sanford, with service operating on Saturdays using the 50-seat Embraer E145XR.

While Muskegon itself only has one other destination, Chicago O’Hare, which is also operated by DAC under the EAS contract, DAC will compete indirectly with Allegiant, as it has a sizable operation and a base in Grand Rapids, Michigan, which is located only about 45 minutes east of Muskegon.

The 1,030-mile route from Muskegon to Orlando Sanford on the E145 will become the longest at-risk flight operated by any EAS carrier, and one of the longest commercial airline flights operated by an Embraer E145 in the country, overtaking the current record holder, United’s 830-mile route from Washington Dulles to Mobile, Alabama, by almost 200 miles.

That record for the E145 is a little bit of a technicality, as JSX does operate a handful of flights over 1,000 miles with its Embraer E145s, but the carrier is not considered a commercial airline, and is instead classified as a “public charter operation.”

Muskegon Airport director Ken Efting did have something to say about this new service: “This is a historic milestone for MKG and the communities we serve…This is exactly the kind of opportunity we’ve been working toward, and it’s a testament to our growing community support and strong partnership with Denver Air Connection.”

This isn’t the first time an EAS carrier has operated at-risk service to the state of Florida from an EAS community. These smaller carriers sometimes begin flights to leisure destinations like Florida and other leisure-heavy destinations to entice higher passenger numbers that boost the communities they serve.

Muskegon will join the small but growing list of Essential Air Service communities that are now connected with nonstop flights to the state of Florida, but they will be the only EAS community in Michigan to have Florida flights.

#6224. What Is A Lifestyle Hotel? The “Cool” Hotel Trend That Means Nothing

It goes without saying that the hospitality industry has a lot of trends. At times there might not actually be much substance to these trends, but the idea is that executives in the industry think certain things are “hot,” and they perceive it to reflect consumer demand.

Along those lines, if you look at trends among the major hotel groups, the concept of “lifestyle hotels” has become incredibly popular. There are an endless number of brands like these that have emerged. I think one logical question is what the term actually means. What makes a property a lifestyle hotel, rather than an… umm, not lifestyle hotel?

I know I’m generally pretty verbose and use a fairly limited vocabulary when it comes to describing things, but that’s intentional. In part, my issue is that many of the descriptors used in marketing, particularly in the travel industry, are so beyond meaningless:

My point is, we’re completely desensitized to useless descriptions of every aspect of the travel experience… unless you’re currently enjoying a seasonal fruit plate served by a private Michelin star chef on a plane, in which case I can’t save you. 😉

Anyway, that brings us to lifestyle hotels, one of the hottest trends in the hotel industry. It’s easy to name brands that claim to be lifestyle hotels — we’re talking Hilton’s Canopy and Curio Collection, Hyatt’s Andaz and Thompson, IHG’s Kimpton and voco, Marriott’s W Hotels and Autograph Collection, etc.

I guess the best way to define a lifestyle hotel would be to step back for a moment, and separate out the two words. Generally a lifestyle brand is a company that sells products by associating them with a specific way of living, set of values, or identities, that customers want to adopt.

A lifestyle hotel is generally defined as a property offering the personalization of an independent boutique hotel, with the attributes of a chain hotel (meaning loyalty, distribution power, etc.). Generally (but not always) these properties have a strong food & beverage or social concept as a core pillar, since that’s a large attribute that can make a hotel popular with a certain guest profile.

The issue with the concept of lifestyle hotels is that hotels can choose how they want to market themselves, and I think some hotels take a “fake it till you make it” approach. If you ask me, the concept of a lifestyle hotel should come down to two factors:

We can of course create all kinds of more specific distinctions, but I think it’s unnecessary. I’ve already written in the past about the concept of “boutique” hotels, another term that means so little. As far as I’m concerned, a lifestyle hotel could be small or big, as the big question is how bustling it is relative to its size.

But this also gets at the issue of how hotel groups choose to label their brands. For example, Marriott labels AC Hotels, Aloft, Autograph Collection, Element, Moxy, Tribute Portfolio, and W Hotels, all as lifestyle brands. From my perspective:

I mean, I live pretty close to a Moxy, and I’ve never thought to myself “hey family, maybe we should go to the Moxy for dinner tonight” (as much as my older son would probably love going somewhere and being able to microwave his own dinner).

So to me, these are the hotels that very much fit into the “fake it until you make it” camp. Like, the major hotel groups want to convince investors and customers that these are somehow something they aren’t. I mean, I’ve also had pleasant stays at AC Hotels properties, and that’s described as “a lifestyle brand that celebrates a new modern aesthetic complemented by a European soul and Spanish roots.” I mean… really?

Hotel groups love to grow and market their lifestyle hotel brands, but I feel like they take a lot of liberties with how they define these. On the most basic level, the idea is supposed to be that lifestyle hotels offer a boutique hotel-style experience, while being associated with one of the major brands.

However, I’d say more accurately, it’s about how much of a “destination” a property is, as that also determines the vibe of the place. I’d love if someone could help me understand just how hotel groups can in good conscience categorize some brands as being lifestyle hotels. Like, how does Marriott include AC Hotels, Autograph Collection, EDITION, and Moxy, all under that same umbrella?

How do you define the lifestyle hotel concept?

A lot of these stylish, boutique hotels enter the points world through curated hotel collections that participate in loyalty programs, giving hotels a wider reach of potential guests without having to adhere to strict brand standards that change the spirit of the property.

One of the pioneers in this space is Design Hotels, a collection of hundreds of independently-owned hotels and resorts dotting the globe, each with its own identity, personality and approach to hospitality.

"Every hotel is picked for its originality [and] the vision that's behind it," Stijn Oyen, managing director at Design Hotels, told TPG, adding that each property has "a strong point of view and cultural connection."

And it's not necessarily easy to make the cut for this collection: According to Oyen, only about 5% of the hotels that apply to join Design Hotels are accepted in an effort to "stay true to the original roots and values of what makes a design hotel."

Then there's the loyalty twist: Marriott actually owns Design Hotels, and many (but not all) of the collection's properties participate in Marriott Bonvoy.

Here's a quick guide to everything you need to know about Design Hotels, plus a few standout properties where you can earn and burn Marriott Bonvoy points.

Related: 12 new boutique hotels worth redeeming your points for

Founded in the early 1990s, Design Hotels was created to bring together independently owned, design-forward hotels that shared a commitment to originality, creativity and local culture.

Today, that collection is more than 300 members strong, with new properties regularly joining. What differentiates the collection is the individuality of each property — each one has its own unique point of view, rather than a prescribed set of standards travelers will see at more traditional hotel brands.

"We're set up around design," Oyen explained. "It's about the vision. It's about being independent with a voice."

Design Hotels became part of Marriott's portfolio following the hotel giant's acquisition of Starwood Hotels & Resorts in 2016, giving Marriott a majority stake in the company. By 2021, Marriott had acquired full ownership of Design Hotels, though the collection continues to operate as a separate entity, with member hotels retaining their individual identities and independence.

The company describes its properties as "design-driven hotels that function as social hubs and spaces for purposeful experiences."

But what does that actually mean? To start, getting into the collection isn't easy, and Design Hotels is looking for one distinguishing factor before choosing a new member: "the originality in its concept."

According to Oyen, only about 5% of applicants pass the test. Hotels are also evaluated on everything from design and sustainability to cultural programming and the property's connection to its local community.

"It's a strong, strong sense of place," Oyen explained, adding that beyond their physical design, the hotels should have vibrant public spaces that attract locals and feel like an extension of the neighborhoods they call home.

It's also about the people. According to Oyen, about 60% of Design Hotels owners are first-time hoteliers, bringing fresh perspectives and new approaches to hospitality. The company calls the creative minds behind its properties "Originals," describing them as "the engines behind pioneering design and revolutionary hospitality," according to the brand's website.

Without rigid brand standards dictating every detail, these hoteliers have the freedom to pursue projects that seasoned hospitality pros might consider too risky. That might be as simple as removing TVs from guest rooms or as dramatic as building a hotel accessible only by cable car, like Vigilius Mountain Resort in Italy's Dolomites.

For Marriott Bonvoy members, Design Hotels offers a truly independent, boutique-like stay while still allowing them to earn and burn points. Something that, frankly, a lot of people don't realize is available to them in the loyalty world.

Just don't forget: Not all Design Hotels participate in Marriott Bonvoy. To see a full list of the 120-plus participating hotels, visit Marriott's dedicated Design Hotels landing page.

For Design Hotels, according to Oyen, the relationship with Marriott is a win-win situation: Hotels gain access to nearly 300 million loyalty members while maintaining their "complete independence."

But because these properties operate differently from traditional Marriott hotels, Bonvoy elite members shouldn't expect all their usual perks to apply.

Here's what members can expect based on their status.

The following Marriott Bonvoy benefits are excluded at Design Hotels:

Set near the beach in Casablanca, Villa Sahrai pays respect to "Casablanca’s Art Deco tradition" across its 56 rooms and public spaces. Be sure to take advantage of the spa and its Moroccan hammam before settling down for food at one of two restaurants or a nightcap at the bar.

How to book: Cash rates from around $160 per night or 34,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

To get to Vigilius Mountain Resort, guests must ascend a private cable car that travels between the mountain hotel and the village it soars above. But once up at the top, guests are treated to beautiful Dolomite views, architecture that incorporates nature and wellness experiences around every stylish corner.

How to book: Cash rates from about $341 per night or 47,000 Marriott Bonvoy points.

At The Austin Proper Hotel, patterns, textures and colors combine in unexpected and beautiful ways from the moment guests step inside until their head hits the pillow. The hotel is as cool as Austin itself, but also full of surprises: You can grab classic Tex-Mex to eat or opt for a French Japanese tasting menu or soak up the sun at the rooftop pool before a lymphatic drain at the Verbena Spa.

How to book: Cash rates from $350 or 54,000 Marriott Bonvoy points.

Kyoto is no stranger to incredible hotels, but Genji Kyoto offers an intimate experience with just 20 rooms that feel distinctly Japanese and totally sleek and fresh. As serene as they come, spend a day getting lost in Kyoto's ancient history before heading to the rooftop bar and garden to unwind.

How to book: Cash rates from about $227 per night or 47,000 Marriott Bonvoy points.

Condesa is one of Mexico City's trendiest neighborhoods, so it only makes sense to stay in a hotel that also fits the description. At this hotel, enjoy rooftop sushi or French-Mexican fusion food; relax in the hydrotherapy pool or kick back on the patio and watch the city's cosmopolitan set roam the area.

How to book: Cash rates from $339 per night or 42,000 Marriott Bonvoy points.

As major hotel companies continue to expand their portfolios beyond traditional hotels, from independent boutique properties to outdoor-focused experiences, collections like Design Hotels are helping diversify what travelers can experience with points and miles.

For Marriott Bonvoy members, that means more opportunities to stay somewhere truly unique without giving up the ability to earn and redeem points. And while the elite benefits might look a little different, the chance to experience a hotel with its own distinct personality might just be worth the trade-off.
