#6210. How to Sing Karaoke Every Night, in Every Borough of New York City

In 1968, Daisuke Inoue decided he was going to be in two places at once. A musician who played in a backup band working Kobe’s nightlife circuit, Inoue soundtracked the evenings of soulful salarymen whom he befriended. With drums as his instrument of choice because “all you have to do is hit them,” he turned those relationships into business, arranging entertainment for their other engagements. As the legend goes, he couldn’t make it out to a gig he had booked at an insurance company’s trade show, so he invented the next best thing. Combining a standard eight-track tape player used in car stereos, a microphone, an amplifier, and a 100-yen coin slot, he placed his ghost in the machine, which he fashioned into the Juke 8. Inoue’s device—the progenitor to the modern-day karaoke machine—was a success.

A more rigorous history might question whether Inoue really invented the first such machine or whether that credit belongs to electronics manufacturer Shigeichi Negishi’s Sparko Box a decade earlier. But the meteoric takeoff of karaoke has soared far past its humble—and slightly murky—origins. A portmanteau of the Japanese words kara, meaning empty, and oke, meaning orchestra, karaoke evokes both loneliness and collective belonging. Nearly 60 years on, we still root for the little machine that could—and all the brave singers who bare their heart through age-revealing ballads and club classics.

An impassioned rendition of Celine Dion’s “It's All Coming Back to Me Now” transpires at Beats Karaoke Cafe in Williamsburg

Perhaps nowhere is karaoke’s full breadth more on display than in New York City, where, on one side, you’ve got lounges complete with floor-to-ceiling video walls and speakers with built-in auto-tune capabilities and, on the other, decades-old dives whose performers are as much an institution as the establishment.

A karaoke spot is the one place where post-prom dates, wedding parties, and career performers alike gather to spend their time and money on gloriously subpar entertainment, entirely without irony. When you’re the one behind the mic, it becomes something mythic—a reprieve from the passive consumption dominating much of the city’s nightlife. Tally up the past year’s most recent headlines, and you’d get the impression that we’re becoming less fun—we’re having less sex, drinking less alcohol, going to fewer parties, and hosting fewer of our own. The karaoke bar might be one of the last, thriving places in New York where we wait half an hour to openly embarrass ourselves, and for that it’s well worth our nights out.

With the hundreds of sing-along nights and 30-plus specialized bars in New York City listed on trackers like Karaoke Crowd, there was no way we’d be able to cover them all. So we visited one place a day for a week, crisscrossing the boroughs for a taste of the city’s diversity. We commenced our week in Koreatown, where some-dozen private rooms are conveniently concentrated on a single street, and continued our spree at an Irish pub on the Upper East Side, where shouting for sport and song are one in the same. We hit up a Staten Island dive of devoted locals and a year-old Astoria restaurant where, once the Tagalog ballads have begun, you must push the plate away and join in. These watering holes, old and new, are living proof of the many shapes karaoke takes and the unifying joy of belting it out together, even when so much else threatens to divide us.

A singer takes the stage at Iggy’s on the Upper East Side to perform Billy Joel and Elton John’s “Piano Man”

We began the week where many end it, on the dense corridor of West 32nd Street between Sixth and Seventh Avenues. Along this stretch of Koreatown, karaoke bars, podiatrists, escape rooms, and coworking spaces stack atop one another. Our crawl started at Gagopa, whose BYOB policy is a favorite among the large-group partiers and Midtown corporate crowd for fast-tracking camaraderie. The bar eluded us at first, not for a lack of signage but for its location on the fourth story of its building, and the search more or less provided a template for our crawl: a ride up an elevator the size of an airplane lavatory and head-scratching decor. At Gagopa’s sister bar, 32 Karaoke, this last item consists of Polaroids of visiting groups on the walls—the very karaoke canon that, once you’ve stepped through its doors, you become part of.

Anticipatory staircases aside, no amount of symbolic literacy can prepare you for a K-town elevator panel. Despite its abundance of labeled buttons, deciphering them only makes things more confusing. To reach Space Karaoke Bar and Lounge, for instance, you have to avoid accidentally ending up at Space Ping Pong, one of two Space sports bars, or the Space golf simulator. Take it as a sign to stop trying to make sense of things and just embrace the ride.

Across the street, Chorus Karaoke Lounge has a clubbier feel, with a purple-and-blue-lit bar. To the left is a hallway of private rooms, lined with porthole window portraits of Madonna, Morrissey, Elvis, and all the other greats. On the evening we visited, only one karaoke room at the end of the white hallway was occupied—by a lone singer crooning to himself. It may well have been a strict weekly ritual, the first step in a vocal warm-up regimen. “I sing, therefore I am,” read a sign near its entrance as we left, a reminder that although thinking may be proof of existence, song is proof of life. —Skyli Alvarez & Kat Chen

Pianist Mark Benjamin, left, accompanies performers at Sid Gold's Request Room on 26th Street, which has additional locations in Detroit, Nashville, and Washington, DC

In the liminal space between Chelsea and Flatiron, Sid Gold’s Request Room is a bit of an outlier. Sandwiched between an empty office space and halal buffet, its old-timey façade simply reads “piano” and “karaoke.” Both await you in the spacious piano lounge, tucked behind a pair of velvet curtains at the back of the cocktail bar.

We arrived around 9 p.m. and slid into one of the alcoved booths closest to the stage, a small black platform beside the bar centerpiece: a Baldwin baby grand. As we settled in, a singer, backdropped by pianist Mark Benjamin’s harmonies, wrapped up his performance to a crowd of now four; he then came to take our order. Fortunately, others trickled in: tourists and their New Yorker friends; Tuesday-night regulars; a dog named Henry. Many, as we learn, were here for Benjamin's performance—and succor.

As we came to find out later on in the week, karaoke works better in numbers, but Sid Gold’s makes the case for a small yet mighty group. A particularly moody evocation of Chris Isaak’s “Wicked Game,” prefaced by the singer’s memories of angst-ridden high school years, drew out lower-than-low notes. In what could only be described as a shouty but otherwise cheery cover of “Back to Black,” each verse’s forceful delivery was more unpredictable than the last. At some point Benjamin called upon someone named Eric, who kicked off his flip-flops to sing “Part of Your World,” a method for getting into character (one can only assume) that would be frowned upon everywhere else but here.

If you think you can evade the stage, Benjamin will make sure you get on up there. He’ll harmonize and improvise riffs even if he’s never heard the song (or wants you to think this); pause to match your pace; and convince you that it was made for you to sing. —S.A.

I was immediately given the cousin treatment when I passed the threshold of Barkada Social Club. In case there was any ambiguity about the cultural identity of this Astoria restaurant and bar, let it be known I walked into Bruno Mars’s “Risk It All,” with plates of lumpia and kwek kwek covering the tables. It was a good night to come—Barkada NYC, a separate but similarly named LGBTQ+ Filipinx community group, hosts its monthly Kikay Konek karaoke event here. Joey, a queer-affirming physical therapist by day and programming coordinator with Barkada NYC, was my gregarious host for the night. When I asked them about encountering struggles with finding kindred souls, they gave me a considerate look before breaking out into a smile and saying, “I honestly can’t relate.” This came as no surprise as I watched them record the “Toxic” floor routine for BNYC’s Instagram before rushing off to plan next month’s programming, discuss bringing BYNC to the Bronx, finalize plans for a hike three weekends away, and introduce me to their boyfriend. It takes a social whirlwind like that to bring together a collective of members from across all five boroughs, plus exotic reaches like Tenafly, New Jersey. The crowd is in constant flux, peeling off and joining in depending on what the song queue has in store. The one exception to the rule is when someone requests Jesse Zaragoza’s “Bakit Pa,” a sweeping Tagalog ballad from the ’90s about unrequited love that brings everybody rushing to the fore. “It’s like our national anthem,” Joey says. —K.C.

Tim sings at Steiny's Pub in Staten Island

At Sid Gold's, patrons are more than ready to be called up for a harmonized performance

At the site of the former Mayfair Bar and Grill, a favorite among St. George’s queer patrons in the 1950s and ’60s, Steiny’s Pub was once a low-key gay bar turned sports joint that now exists somewhere between the two. It’s fitting for a borough that’s often the butt of the joke, cloaked in its perceived suburban isolation, though an eight-minute walk from the Staten Island Ferry makes it surprisingly less difficult to reach from Manhattan than one might assume. We passed a small group of local 30-somethings smoking near the entrance and, once inside the dive, encountered a lively emcee who goes by the DJ name Nazz Raidience. We’re quickly singled out for not being regulars and handed a Sharpie and clipboard to add to a queue that Nazz only loosely followed.

As co-owner John Michael works behind the bar, a few seated patrons watch tennis and baseball while others belt it out to their backs. The L-shaped booth seating next to the DJ setup operates as the stage. Most who perform adhere to genre: bar patron Dia’s heavy metal numbers by Kittie are complete with death growls, Connor does Eminem with breakdancing and triple-threat delivery, and others insist on 1980s ballads. Nazz shepherds the queue at an auctioneer’s pace, sometimes joining in and always poking fun, calling upon you to spin the prize wheel that could lead to a free drink or 10 push-ups. Although they host karaoke nights across the city, Steiny’s is their favorite for the many different worlds it attracts, and they'll convince you to stay for the ferry sailors who, post-shift, are said to come singing around 2 a.m. When it became clear to us this would not be the night, we left without sea chanteys in our hearts but with a better understanding of the appeal of the city’s least-populated borough. —S.A.

Performing karaoke cosplaying as Shadow the Hedgehog, hands full with impulse purchases from Comic Con’s artist alley, is my penance. I had postponed this visit for too long, leaving me with no option but to come as I was. Bronx Beer Hall is nestled within a larger food hall in the historic Italian neighborhood of Arthur Avenue (please, try the veal). By the time Friday karaoke night is in full swing, all of the surrounding businesses are fully closed. From the outside the telltale sign that anything is happening is the ambient trail of music. Channel an ’80s B-movie slasher victim, and follow the noise into the darkness. Upon emerging into the light, you’ll see a hallway lined with T-shirts printed with lines like “Call it gravy, not sauce!” or “I’m not a gynecologist, but I’ll take a look.” As for the music selection, it’s what you’d expect from a generationally eclectic crowd. There’s tender performances of Bon Jovi and Air Supply following the crowd-rousing momentum of “NUEVAYoL” by a man wearing a snapback with what was certainly a record-breaking number Yankees logos embroidered on the design. Every three songs the DJ would queue up 50 Cent’s “In Da Club” to announce yet another birthday, and BBH turned out to be just the kind of place where an unrelated 24-year-old and 40-year-old blow out their candles together. Being Shadow the Hedgehog did not go unnoticed either. Our millennial bartender who grew up playing the original Sonic games requested “Live and Learn,” the main theme song of Sonic Adventure 2. As I took in the lyrics for the first time on the TV screen, I lived and I learned. —K.C.

The karaoke room at Iggy’s becomes rowdier as the night progresses

This Irish karaoke bar was our first reporting excursion, and it established a curious precedent. Between its Upper East Side location, Gaelic rafters, and portraits of 27 Club musicians, the place seemed tailor-made for Xennial dads. We assumed butt rock was inevitable and hedged our bets on at least one rendition of Hinder’s “Lips of an Angel.”

My hunch came from Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, specifically her theories of homosociality: the nonsexual bonds between people of the same sex. Spend enough time at karaoke, and you’ll notice that “Lips of an Angel” is almost always performed as a duet between two men. For the uninitiated, the song imagines a phone call between a singer and an ex he still quietly yearns for, wishing she were there instead of the “girl” in the next room. Sure enough, two friends took up the mantle. Maybe it was simply a fun song to sing; maybe karaoke offered a safe conduit for expressing something else. We encountered the song at every subsequent karaoke night, always sung by two people of the same sex.

While some bars use online queues for song requests, attendees go analog at Iggy’s

As a week of karaoke draws to a close, you will come to find specific crowds come in waves. First come those who learned to love performance in youth-theater productions, usually in duos or trios, and take their sing-alongs seriously. Then there are the harder-to-place groups: coworkers, reunited friends, or couples using karaoke as a social buffer. Next come the balladeers and lone yearners, eager to broadcast exactly how they’re feeling, followed by the humble soloists who know they’re good and have nothing to prove. Finally, the rowdy late-night crowd of after-partiers spills in, at worst hogging the mic and at best uniting an entire room.

In our five hours at Iggy’s, the former theater kids delivered truly spectacular covers of “Defying Gravity,” the Irishmen shouted Irish pub songs, and the soloists flirted by way of song choice. Three dollars grant you one song that you select from an impressively up-to-date binder and scrawl onto a piece of paper, then the waiting game begins. “We just met in the photo booth” is how one performer introduced a B-side from The Cure, an effort to woo over a stranger who he knew shared at least one common interest. Karaoke gives singers permission to say what they otherwise cannot or will not admit, though the message is rarely subtle. —S.A. & K.C.

Though Seventh Heaven's evenings often begin with film screenings, watch parties, and other community events, they always end in karaoke

During a week when we spent every other waking hour thinking about karaoke-ing, we sometimes looked past dives and private rooms for other ambitious reinventions, like on a boat; in a taxicab en route to the airport; or in an East Williamsburg apartment turned karaoke rental. Still, it’s ultimately the most obvious spots that draw the crowds. Take Williamsburg’s Beats Karaoke Cafe, an eight-minute walk from the Bedford Avenue station, with a rustic bar on the first floor, leading to a hall of private rooms that continue downstairs. We eventually wound our way into film production coordinator Natalie’s group of eight, who told us this was their go-to whenever they “want to add a little divorced dad rock to the night,” and we had caught them testing out new material. Still, they made their way through classics like The Cranberries’ “Zombie” and “Time of My Life,” while also executing many Dirty Dancing lifts.

Farther along the L train, it was only appropriate that we ended up at a bar named Seventh Heaven. We were among the youngest crowd by far, at least in taste. Karaoke-goers swarmed the stage and fluently rattled off the romaji lyrics of “A Cruel Angel’s Thesis,” the theme song to ’90s anime Neon Genesis Evangelion. This bar gets its crowd, with a cocktail menu filled with allusions to the fandom, like the Apothecary’s Negroni fashioned after popular light novel series The Apothecary Diaries, or my own drink, the Boy’s Love G&T, which is named after the popular fiction genre that focuses on the romance between male characters. Turns out, there are plenty of effusive ex–theater kids who understand the assignment.

The DJ cued up our request, “Viva la Vida.” From the vantage point of the stage, the outstretched hands of the crowd looked not unlike the Eugène Delacroix painting of the Revolution of 1848, which Coldplay used as cover art their 2008 album Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends. A notably resigned wedding party lingered at the back of the audience, while city newcomers hailing from nearby venue House of Yes gleefully accepted our mic to unleash a few verses. The karaoke-goers had in the very least not given up on tonight. —S.A. & K.C.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

That makes this the ideal time to apply. Not only that, but this is a card that many people will want, given that it’s my favorite American card for earning AAdvantage elite status, since you can basically double dip Loyalty Points.

Also keep in mind that credit card spending will qualify for Loyalty Points (helping you earn elite status, including Gold, Platinum, Platinum Pro, or Executive Platinum), though the welcome bonus as such won’t. If you’re interested in applying for the Citi AAdvantage Business Card, the typical Citi credit card application restrictions apply, including that you can be approved for at most one Citi card every eight days, and at most two Citi cards every 65 days.

On top of that, the bonus isn’t available to those who have received a new account bonus on this exact card in the past 48 months. Eligibility is unrelated to having any other American Airlines credit cards.

If you’re concerned about Chase’s 5/24 rule, note that applying for a Citi business card generally won’t count toward that limit. I should also mention that at least anecdotally, this card seems to be quite easy to get approved for.

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card has an annual fee that’s waived for the first year, so you can “try” the card before you have to pay a fee. While the fee after that is technically still $99, it’s increasing to $150 as of January 24, 2027, so that’s what you’d pay on account renewal.

So this is a way to essentially get two-for-one elite status qualification, which is awesome.

#6208. 15 Best Arch Support Shoes for Long Travel Days

I grew up believing that sore and throbbing feet were a necessary evil of long travel days, until a physical therapist said three magic words: arch-support shoes. She’d noticed the inside forefoot and outside heels of my shoes’ soles were completely worn through—a sign of overpronation because I have no natural arch. With that kind of misalignment, it was no surprise that even a simple day of set-jetting through The Sound of Music sites in Austria or strolling through the compact center of Prague was wreaking havoc on my feet.

As it turns out, as much as 37% of the population is believed to have some degree of flat foot, according to a National Library of Medicine study. But how it affects everyday life can vary by person. Initially, I only noticed the pain on high step-count days, but when I started long-distance running 10 years ago, I knew it was time to invest in supportive shoes capable of going the distance.

So I visited my local Fleet Feet in Hoboken, New Jersey, where nowadays its complimentary Fit ID 3-D scan can get granular, most recently showing me that my two feet have different lengths, as well as varying ball and heel widths. Most blaringly, both my arch heights are on the lowest possible end of the scale.

What I’ve learned more than anything is that there is no one-size-fits-all supportive shoe that works for everyone, which is why individual fittings are so crucial. (In extreme cases, like when I got posterior tibial tendinitis after running a half marathon, be sure to consult a healthcare professional.) But for a dose of stability, here are 15 arch-support shoes that are primed for long days on your feet.

For the last decade, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS has been my go-to shoe—that’s what GTS stands for, after all. The shoe’s GuideRails technology works its magic not by trying to correct your stride, but by guiding it in the direction that feels natural. Not only did it get me through my first few races with New York Road Runners, and eventually NYC Marathon training, but it’s always the shoe I go back to when I crave stability with just a sprinkle of cushioning. Whenever I slip these on, I feel locked in. The new version, which launched on November 1, retains its trusted features, while refining the heel tab and tongue to be sleeker and more functional.

During the most wrenching times of my foot pain, when every step I took hurt, an orthopedic doctor encouraged me to get a pair of Hokas and start running again. The brand may have led the way with oversized cushioned soles, but one of its bestsellers is this stability shoe, with an H-frame to prevent arch-less feet from turning inward. The newest version features a tighter mesh upper on the inside portion of the shoe, adding support to its arch side while retaining that soft cushiony feel. It even bears an American Podiatric Medical Association (AMPA) seal certifying that it’s beneficial to foot health.

Oofos may be known for its slides and recovery footwear (I wore a pair for a week after the 2024 Boston Marathon), but the same lightweight support strategies are applied to this casual sneaker. Its trademark high-impact absorbing Oofoam soaks up 37% of impact compared to regular shoes. Best of all, it’s machine washable with a closed-cell foam that prevents odors.

Let’s face it: Hiking shoes can be a pain to pack—which is what makes this Columbia hiking boot that's disguised as a sneaker so brilliant. Without any breaking in, they were immediately comfortable yet firm, and have kept my feet dry through sudden downpours and even river crossings on a hike in Thailand. This fall, they doubled as a sporty shoe, as I ran and biked the 32-mile Moose Loop Trail around Anchorage over three days, including a drizzly four-mile run on the final day.

Most impressively, during my Intrepid Travel Kenya Safari Adventure earlier this month, rain started falling while we were planting trees in the Mt. Kenya region’s Intrepid-adopted forest until we were trudging through mud. But the Konos’s sophisticated underfoot system provided support with maximum cushioning and traction so that I never doubted my stability any step of the way.

During the worst of my foot issues, I thought I'd be confined to a life of bulky orthotics. That’s when Vionic saved me. Every shoe in its collection—from sandals to dress shoes—is powered by its podiatrist-approved Vio Motion technology with a deep heel cup for stability, shock-absorbing cushioning, flexible movement, and most noticeably, strong arch-support that realigns the body while improving balance. This casual sneaker merges all that into a lace-up design that’s as supportive as it is cute. Not only was there zero break-in period for instant comfort, but it also meets the One Planet sustainability standard.

As I learned during my most recent Fleet Feet fitting, arch support and heel stability are inherently linked—and Kuru’s own patented sole hones in precisely those two traits. Together, they turn these lightweight court shoes into a secret weapon, able to endure the miles without an inkling of fatigue. Plus the versatile style can be dressed up or down.

The 90-year-old brand from the Italian Dolomites is best known for its mountaineering gear—and it’s that kind of technical expertise that was used to develop its Pedrock hiking shoe. The visible 3F System ties together flexibility, fit, and support. The adjustable laces ensure that the shoe fits like a glove while an EVA plate provides stability, along with reinforced heel and toe caps. All together, the urban-to-mountain shoe transitions perfectly through every step of your travels.

When it comes to technical gear, there are so many bells and whistles to consider that it’s easy to overlook the basics—namely, support. Teva never goes wrong in that realm and uses its own Lite-Comf midsole for a cushiony step, along with a patented universal heel lock system and Vibram grip for traction on the outer, so there’s no reason to teeter, even on multiple-day hikes over varied terrain. Those looking for less bulkiness with the same support can also opt for the lightweight road-to-trail Aventrail R2T shoe, which launched earlier this year.

The dependability that comes with Merrell’s high-performing outdoor wear is merged with Gore-Tex’s gold standard of waterproofness in this simple yet powerful hiking boot. It's easy to see why it's become my go-to for the last few years. At 16.36-oz. per shoe, it’s a hearty design, which equals stability throughout. The Kinetic Fit–blend contoured footbed strengthens the heel and a molded nylon shank adds arch support, while Vibram traction on the soles prevents slipping on slick surfaces, eliminating any flat-footed hiker’s worries—and taking me on adventures I thought were out of my range.

Cold weather footwear has long been a struggle for me—until I met this travel-friendly ankle boot from my trusted Vionic. Its classic design is easy to pair with anything from dresses to jeans, and the full-length zipper makes it easy to slip on and off. But don’t underestimate its durability, equipped with a completely waterproof leather upper and sealed seams to ensure not a drop seeps in. Plus, it conquers my fear of slippery sidewalks with articulated pods that provide traction for steady steps while still feeling cushiony.

The Kizik brand may seem like a novelty, focused on the ability to step in and out of shoes hands-free—yes, even these boots with laces (that don’t actually need to be tied). But the Juno 2 goes beyond just speeding you through TSA checkpoints. It’s chock full of support, boasting a molded EVA foam midsole for comfort and an Arch Form insole that molds to your foot shape.

Here’s what Vionic does best—take the patented footbed it's known for with orthotic-grade arch support and apply it to styles that don’t disclose your foot problems. This everyday loafer, made with post-consumer recycled materials, combines that solid support with extreme flexibility and a grippy sole. But the best part for travelers is how packable these loafers are—the upper (which comes in either super soft leather or suede) squishes easily, yet retains its shape and support. I’ve worn these to conferences and events, and often get asked who makes them, as it’s rare to find business casual shoes that are so supportive. I stocked up with three pairs waiting in my closet for when my first ones wear out—though after more than a year, they’ve shown no signs of aging.

A ballet flat with actual arch support? Only Birkenstock can make that possible with its trademark cork-latex footbed known for its firm arch support, along with a natural leather insole and suede lining. All that support may sound stiff, but it’s evened out with EVA cushioning. All together, it’s that free-flowing feeling from its famous Big Buckle sandals wrapped in a cozy exterior.

This leather slip-on may look like an everyday flat, but its comfort features are where it shines, starting with sturdy arch-support designed for all-day wear. Unlike most shoes of this genre, it has a removable footbed to slide in custom orthotics (I’m used to having to tear them out of flats!), plus a lightweight rubber outsole to keep you on your feet. Available in regular and wide, the Larisa also proudly wears an APMA acceptance seal.

The first time I slipped on the Aetrex Collette loafers, I immediately stood up straighter. There’s something about its sloping arch-support that directed not just my feet but my entire posture into a more confident stance. It turns out the footbed is designed to follow the natural curvature of each person’s foot, alleviating issues from plantar facilities to heel pain. The brand puts an emphasis on personalized fit, with the strap across the shoe cleverly doubling as an adjustable Velcro and, making them feel more like snug sneakers than loafers.

While it may seem like only people with flat feet or low arches require arch support, that’s not the case. “Anyone with tired feet or discomfort may benefit from a more supportive shoe,” Jenny Simpson, three-time Olympian and Fleet Feet’s chief running officer, tells Traveler. She adds that the specifics of your foot will dictate the support that works best. Generally, those with low or flexible arches can benefit from stability shoes, while those with high and rigid arches might do better with more cushioned shoes.

What to look for in an arch-support shoe?

Simpson cautions not to choose a shoe based on arch height alone: “Support should feel like it is meeting your arch, while the heel should feel secure,” says Simpson. Only you can tell what feels right once it’s on your foot, as “how you move and what feels comfortable to you” are the ultimate factors.

No singular shoe will address soreness for everyone. “The right choice depends on what is causing the discomfort, how your foot moves, and whether you need more cushioning, more stability, or a combination of both,” says Simpson. Since no product photo or descriptions can replicate how shoes will feel on your feet, in-person fittings are the most valuable.

Are arch-support shoes good for heel pain?

Simpson says that insoles can definitely be “an excellent tool for anyone looking for more tailored solutions for their footwear.” In particular, for those dealing with plantar fasciitis-induced heel pain, the extra support can reduce strain. Alternatively, cushioned shoes—like Hoka is known for—can make standing and walking more comfortable.

What brands design the most supportive shoes?

Running and walking shoes are built to endure the long days that travel requires, as Simpson calls out Brooks, Hoka, Asics, New Balance, and Saucony as strong options. She suggests trying different models since two styles from the same brand can have totally different fits. Other lifestyle shoes aren’t necessarily designed for the same level of wear. “My strongest advice is not to shop by label alone,” Simpson says. “Many shoes are labeled ‘supportive,’ ‘stability,’ or ‘orthopedic.’ They can be useful descriptions, but your foot gets the final vote. The best shoe is the one that fits your anatomy, supports your activity and allows you to move comfortably.”

#6207. Air Tahiti Nui Will Offer Free Starlink Wi-Fi On Its Boeing 787s As Of 2027

Air Tahiti Nui has just announced a massive upgrade to its inflight connectivity, as the airline will be rolling out free Starlink Wi-Fi across its (small) fleet in 2027.

Air Tahiti Nui has revealed that it plans to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its entire fleet, which consists of four Boeing 787-9s. The airline plans to offer this service for free to passengers in all travel classes.

Starlink will be introduced in 2027, though no timeline beyond that is known yet, so it could be early or late in the year. Presumably once installation starts, it’ll be completed very quickly — four planes could easily be fitted with Starlink in a single week.

Air Tahiti Nui operates some very long flights — including from Papeete (PPT) to Paris (CDG) via Los Angeles (LAX) so having fast and free connectivity is super valuable. While so many airlines market their Wi-Fi as being high speed, Starlink is the only product currently in service where you can consistently stream videos, etc.

Currently, Air Tahiti Nui’s Dreamliners are equipped with Panasonic Wi-Fi, which actually has relatively decent speeds. The catch is that Air Tahiti Nui chooses to have insanely high pricing based primarily on data usage, rather than just offering a full flight pass for a fixed amount.

Below is Air Tahiti Nui’s current pricing chart for Wi-Fi… could they make this any more complicated? $28 for 100 MB of data is absurd, and $98 for unlimited data is even more ridiculous.

This kind of pricing just strikes me as being so stupid. All you end up doing is frustrating passengers, and I also have to imagine this isn’t actually the system that maximizes usage. It’s weird to have a provider with speeds that are actually semi-usable (Panasonic is better than OnAir), and to then do this with it.

So anyway, Starlink will simply be a massive upgrade for Air Tahiti Nui in every way. Speaking of which, I’d sure love to return to French Polynesia at some point (and fly that all-business class Air Tahiti turboprop, while I’m at it).

In 2027, Air Tahiti Nui intends to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its fleet of four Dreamliners. It remains to be seen exactly when in 2027 it’ll happen, but this represents a huge upgrade to the passenger experience. The airline currently offers Panasonic Wi-Fi with awful data-based pricing (or an unlimited package that will run you close to $100).

What do you make of Air Tahiti Nui introducing Starlink?

#6206. Delta CEO Calls Heathrow Move ‘Short-Sighted’

Delta CEO Ed Bastian is pushing back against a planned terminal move at London Heathrow, calling the airport’s decision “short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers.”

In comments posted Monday on LinkedIn and published by Delta, Bastian objected to Heathrow’s decision to relocate the airline from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4. The move, planned for 2028, would separate Delta from joint venture partner Virgin Atlantic, which would remain in Terminal 3.

Bastian said the airlines’ shared operation has served millions of passengers for more than a decade, providing connections, premium amenities and access to their combined networks. He argued that splitting the carriers would undermine years of investment and the benefits of operating from the same terminal.

Delta will “pursue all available remedies to correct this decision,” he said, urging Heathrow to reconsider. Bastian did not outline specific legal or regulatory steps.

Virgin Atlantic has also challenged the plan. CEO Corneel Koster said separating the two airlines would complicate journeys, weaken competition and reduce passenger choice. The carrier is considering its options to contest the relocation, Sky News reported.

Heathrow says the changes will help ease congestion and make better use of its terminals. The airport began notifying airlines of the outcome of its terminal occupancy review on Oct. 27.

A Heathrow spokesperson told Sky News that the plan followed consultation with airline customers and would improve the passenger experience, strengthen operational resilience and provide room for growth.

Delta is one of five airlines slated to change terminals. Finnair and Japan Airlines would also move from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4, while LATAM would relocate from Terminal 3 to Terminal 2. China Southern would move from Terminal 4 to Terminal 5.

Delta consolidated its Heathrow operation in Terminal 3 in September 2016 to operate alongside Virgin Atlantic. In announcing that move, Delta cited easier connections and last-minute flight changes, along with access to Virgin Atlantic’s premium facilities for eligible passengers.

For anyone looking for a fun weekend getaway, Nashville almost always makes the short list of options. And for good reason, it’s a city packed with character, history, live music and excellent food.

I was lucky enough to grow up in the Nashville area, so the world of the Ryman Auditorium, the Grand Ole Opry and even excellent airport musicians will always feel like home. I recently went back for a short trip, and while I was there, I made sure to hit some of my favorite food spots — and check out some new ones while I was at it.

If you have Nashville on your list, don’t miss these favorite eateries. And for any food-focused trip, a card that earns on dining is worth having, like the Navy Federal Flagship Premier Visa Signature®. It earns 3 points per dollar on dining purchases and 4 points per dollar on travel purchases, a strong combination for a trip like this, and all for just a $95 annual fee.

If you need a great travel and dining card, now is the perfect time to add the Flagship Premier card to your wallet. For a limited time, new cardholders can earn 50,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 in the first 90 days from account opening. Offer ends Jan. 3, 2027.

Here’s how to use the card to make your food-focused weekend trip to Nashville even better.

I live on the West Coast now, so my go-to flight is usually a nonstop on Alaska Airlines, but I sometimes opt for another airline. With the Flagship Premier card earning on a wide range of travel purchases, I can compare prices and book whichever flight makes the most sense — no loyalty to one airline or travel portal required.

The Flagship Premier card can also help you save on your flight to Nashville with its $100 annual airline credit, which offsets the cost and gives you more flexibility when booking.

And when you’re at the airport, you’ll be thankful for Flagship Premier’s statement credit of up to $120 for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck® to help you zip through security.

When it was time to choose my hotel, I knew I wanted to stay at The Thompson Nashville. It’s in the Gulch, making it within walking distance of many of my favorite dining and shopping spots.

Regardless of which hotel you choose, you’ll earn 4 points per dollar when you book on your Flagship Premier card. That means you’re free to pick whichever hotel you want, without worrying about staying within a single brand or portal to earn bonus points.

Flagship Premier tip: Earn 4 points per dollar on a wide range of travel spending — not just hotels and airfare. Ground transportation counts too, whether you’re in a rental car, on public transport or using rideshare services.

Nashville has quite the dining scene, and the list of standout spots seems to grow every day. To make sure I fit in as much as possible, I turned one day into my own food crawl, with a combination of old favorites and a few newer ones.

For a food-focused trip like this, the Flagship Premier card earns where it matters most. It earns 3 points per dollar on dining purchases, so you’ll earn bonus points wherever your taste buds take you.

Since moving away from Nashville, I’ve come to realize that few places make a better chicken biscuit than Biscuit Love. Biscuit Love is an iconic Nashville staple, but it was new to me, so I knew it would make the list when I saw it around the corner from my hotel.

It absolutely lived up to the hype. From the fun southern and country-music themed decor to the food worth writing home about, Biscuit Love has landed a permanent spot on my list of favorite Nashville eateries.

The menu spans southern staples like biscuits and gravy and shrimp and grits, as well as lighter options like oatmeal and omelets. I knew I wanted to try their Princess biscuit, a buttermilk biscuit topped with fried Nashville “Hot Chicken” and homemade pickles. I also added the summer special Sunshine latte to my order — an iced latte with tangerine, cinnamon and vanilla and topped with housemade salted honey cold foam. And, of course, a side of bacon.

The entire meal was excellent. The chicken was perfectly fried, the biscuit light and fluffy and the pickles delightfully tangy. And the sunshine latte, I discovered, is a favorite for a reason. It was the perfect morning treat to start the day.

After such a big breakfast, I had to wait a while before I could even think about lunch. But when the time finally came, I knew I was headed to Ladybird Taco for my favorite tacos in Nashville.

A location a few blocks from my hotel made it an easy walk. Wanting to pace myself a bit this time, I opted for just one brisket taco and a side of chips and queso.

While I haven’t been to all the taco joints Nashville has to offer, the Austin-inspired menu at Ladybird has been my favorite for years, and I was thrilled to be back for a taste. If you happen to be there for breakfast, be sure to check out their breakfast tacos and Crema coffee — I’m always surprised at how well their coffee and queso go together.

After lunch, I was ready for an afternoon pick-me-up. Living on the West Coast has raised my coffee standards pretty high, but Barista Parlor never disappoints.

I popped in for an iced whiskey-caramel latte as a post-lunch treat to keep me going through the rest of my day in Nashville.

While Jeni’s isn’t Nashville-exclusive, it's only available in select cities and is a spot I make sure to visit every time I’m in town for its creative, seasonal flavors. I originally went in for my favorite — Brambleberry Crisp — but was tempted by the new fall lineup on the menu, which included Pumpkin with Brown Sugar Blondies.

I took a risk and ordered a half scoop of each and was delighted to discover that they pair beautifully. (Just learn from my mistakes and be sure to eat your ice cream quickly if you happen to be there during a heat wave.)

To close out my food crawl day, I headed to The Optimist, a seafood restaurant from chef and restaurateur Ford Fry that was new to me. I love every restaurant of his I’ve been to, and so many of my friends had raved about this one that I wanted to see if it lived up to the hype.

One of my good friends joined me, and we set out to try some of the hottest dishes.

While we surveyed the menu, our server brought rolls for us to enjoy. They were soft and fluffy — and the perfect thing to snack on while deciding.

Per our server’s recommendations, we landed on the Alabama Blue Crab dip and a half dozen oysters, which were both an excellent start to the meal (and complement to our Champagne).

We then moved to the spicy kale salad, which was aptly named. While delicious, it was too spicy for either of us to enjoy more than a few bites.

For our main dish, we ordered the Crumbed Halibut (with brown butter, parsley and charred lemon) and a side of “Proper ‘Chips’” (with malt vinegar aioli). The Halibut was crispy on the outside and tender on the inside, and the brown butter made it sing. The fries were equally well-executed, and the aioli took them to the next level.

The verdict: The Optimist lives up to the hype. I’ll definitely prioritize going back the next time I’m in town.

Flagship Premier Tip: Earn 3 points per dollar on all dining, making this a great card to have handy when exploring local cuisines — from a nearby coffee stop to the splashiest seafood dinner in town.

A card that earns on both travel and dining makes a trip like this Nashville weekend a breeze, and that’s exactly what the Flagship Premier card does.

With the card, you’ll earn 4 points per dollar on your travel purchases — from hotels and flights to transportation while you’re there, without having to deal with booking through a travel portal.

The $100 annual airline credit and up to $120 Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit (once every four years) take the edge off both the cost of flying and the airport experience.

No one likes to juggle multiple cards while traveling, and the Flagship Premier card keeps things simple. With 4 points per dollar on travel and 3 points per dollar on dining purchases, one card covers the two categories that matter most on a trip like this.

Plus, there are no limits on the rewards you can earn (other than your stomach at the end of your food crawl).

If you haven’t been to Nashville lately, be sure to add it to your list — along with these excellent food spots while you’re there.

And wherever your next trip takes you, the Navy Federal Flagship Premier card is worth bringing along, especially for trips centered on food and travel. Between the travel credits and elevated earning rates, it’s the perfect card for any trip.

#6203. Flying Blue Delays SAF & Donation XP Changes Until December 2026

One unique aspect of the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has long been how environmental contributions have contributed toward elite status, whether through the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), or through mileage donations to environmental causes.

A couple of days ago I covered how seemingly overnight, the Flying Blue program drastically decreased status qualification through these methods, requiring 50% larger contributions to earn the same number of XPs (experience points, the method by which one earns status). There’s now an update, and I’m pleased to see the way this is being handled.

Flying Blue has announced that it’s delaying the changes it’s making to the ability to earn XPs through SAF and mileage donations, and this will now be implemented as of December 1, 2026. Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, shared the following with me:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite program. We want to ensure we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; even at the new rate, no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I am happy to see how Flying Blue leadership is handling this situation. Let me share my take on this situation, broadly.

I don’t necessarily think Flying Blue had to make some big, public announcement about the change in advance. After all, this isn’t an official part of the program, and there has really never been any member communication about these opportunities.

I think what was frustrating is that the change was implemented before the website was even updated. So you had the higher pricing already showing, while the page about SAF and mileage donations still reflected the old cost, leaving many people wondering if the change was a glitch or intentional.

At a minimum, I think it’s appropriate to update the webpage before the changes go live, and ideally even give a little notice on the page dedicated to this, just so members aren’t caught off guard.

When it comes to the change as such, Flying Blue does indeed have the most generous opportunities to qualify for elite status through these types of contributions. Selfishly I love this option, but it’s not like members are “entitled” to a certain rate of qualification through this method, since there’s not actually any objectively “fair” way to reward elite qualification for contributions.

So for Flying Blue, it’s presumably about balancing environmental goals with elite ranks. I know with the 50% price hike, I’ll be much less likely to buy SAF, and that’s fine.

As of December 1, 2026, the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program will be decreasing the number of XPs that members earn for contributing toward sustainable aviation fuel and environmental causes. This was initially supposed to be implemented a couple of days ago, but members were caught off guard, so I appreciate that the implementation of this has been delayed.

British Airways is one of ten scheduled users of the Airbus A380. Mainly due to airframes being taken out of service to be retrofitted with just 421 seats, Cirium Diio shows that the carrier now only has the sixth-highest number of double-decker flights. Last November, it was second.

Ch-aviation shows that the oneworld member has 12 double-decker quadjets, the last of which was delivered in June 2016. While they currently have 469 seats, they're being retrofitted with new seats, with a higher premium offering. 88 economy seats are being removed, enabling 13 more business suites and 29 more premium economy seats. The equipment is, of course, used in high-volume and high-yielding markets.

The UK flag carrier's first commercial flight on the superjumbo took place in August 2013. The equipment was initially deployed to Frankfurt for crew training and familiarization. Many airlines have deployed their superjumbos on very short routes for this purpose. For example, Air France did so to London Heathrow Airport (LHR), while Singapore Airlines flew it to Kuala Lumpur. BA used the A380 to Frankfurt and Madrid in 2021 for the same reason, which was ahead of the type's reentry into service due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Comparing BA's schedule between August 2013 and October 2026 with what's planned from November 2026 through 2027 shows that the following eight routes no longer see the huge equipment. Singapore would also have featured, but BA reintroduced superjumbo service to Lion City two months ago: more on that later.

Notice Dubai. Ordinarily, BA would fly the 469-seater to the United Arab Emirates' massively popular destination during the winter, when the temperature is hot but not extraordinarily so. This is, therefore, the main tourist season. However, due to the ongoing war in Iran, the equipment is no longer deployed there. While no flights are currently scheduled through next October, the type may return next winter. BA only just returned to Dubai at the start of November 2026, with the Boeing 787-10 operating daily.

On September 6, BA11 left the UK's busiest airport for Singapore Changi Airport (SIN), having last been deployed to Lion City in early 2025. It is unclear if the return to SIN was influenced by the unease of passengers in connecting at Gulf hubs, although this seems to be dissipating. Whether coincidentally or not, other A380 operators have removed the type from SIN recently. Qatar Airways did so in March 2026, followed by Etihad three months later.

The return of BA's A380s to SIN is notable in various ways. First, it became the airline's sole remaining superjumbo destination in Asia, with only Hong Kong, Doha, and Dubai previously served. Second, LHR-SIN has three double-decker operators for the first time in 16 months, with BA joining Qantas and Singapore Airlines. It is now the only airport pair with three A380 operators.

Third, and just as significantly, if Emirates (the granddaddy of A380 operators) is excluded, LHR-SIN now has more superjumbo flights than any other airport pair, with four flights each day. SIN-Sydney comes close, but has three daily flights at times.

Five ended earlier this year, while one will do so later this month. Find out more here!

Like other Northern Hemisphere airlines, BA switched to winter schedules on Sunday, October 25, 2026, based on IATA slot seasons. It'll maintain winter operations through Saturday, March 27, 2027. In this period, and primarily reflecting aircraft undergoing reconfiguration, BA will only fly the double-decker on four routes from LHR: to Johannesburg (two daily), Miami (daily), San Francisco (daily), and SIN (daily).

Compared to last winter, superjumbo services have been reduced by 27%, which is why BA has temporarily fallen from being the second-largest operator by flights to sixth. At the time, six routes existed: LHR to Dubai (daily), Johannesburg (daily), Los Angeles (daily), Miami (two daily), San Francisco (daily), and Washington Dulles (daily through early November 2025). The equipment will return to Los Angeles in 2027, but it is unclear if Dubai will see it again.

#6200. Transfer Citi ThankYou Points To Turkish Miles&Smiles With 40% Bonus: Worth It?

At the moment, it’s possible to earn up to a 40% bonus when you transfer Citi ThankYou points to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, the bonus isn’t being offered on Citi’s end, but instead, is being offered on Turkish Airlines’ end.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from the Citi ThankYou program in the United States to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, there are some important terms to be aware of:

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,400 Miles&Smiles miles for every 1,000 Citi ThankYou points transferred, though only after the fact.

There are several great cards earning Citi ThankYou points, including the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) and Citi Strata Elite℠ Card (learn more), and it’s easy to combine points between the cards.

Back in the day, the Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles program offered incredible redemption values across the board, but that’s no longer really the case. At this point, I’d say the sweet spot with the Miles&Smiles program is if you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines specifically to or from Istanbul.

That’s because the Miles&Smiles program now charges per segment for awards on Turkish Airlines metal. You can find the cost of one-way saver awards below, just to give you a sense of pricing.

So as an example, a one-way business class award between the United States and Istanbul will cost you 65,000 miles. In other words, with a 40% transfer bonus, you’d be paying around 47,000 Citi ThankYou points for a business class award, which is a pretty great deal.

If you know what you’re doing and have specific redemption plans in mind, this could be a great deal. Just be sure you understand the complexities of the program, and read my guide to the Turkish Miles&Smiles program. Also keep in mind the Miles&Smiles expiration policy, which is that miles expire at the end of the third year after which they’re earned, regardless of activity.

The other big restriction is that the bonus miles will only post after the campaign is done, so you couldn’t transfer points and then immediately redeem all of them (including the bonus). The cap on 50,000 bonus miles is also limiting. But hey, if you value Turkish miles, this could definitely offer some value.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from Citi ThankYou to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. The catch is that the bonus miles only post after the end of the campaign, and you can only earn 50,000 bonus miles with this offer.

If you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines to or from Istanbul, there are some good deals to be had by taking advantage of this.

Many of us here at TPG love to leverage our favorite credit cards to enhance our travels. From trying out the newest lie-flat product to relaxing in an airport lounge, these products can go a long way in unlocking memorable experiences.

But for many Americans, credit cards represent a tangible way to support their household’s bottom lines — especially in the face of rising costs and the unexpected hurdles that life can throw in their way.

Recently, TPG founder Brian Kelly sat down with three everyday families to help them maximize their wallets — and the conversations demonstrated the true power of making rewards work for you.

Here are some real-world stories that show just what credit cards can unlock for you.

One of the most under-the-radar benefits of credit cards is how they can build financial literacy and set your children up for success in the real world. No, this isn’t about giving teens or young adults unfettered access to a big credit limit. Instead, it’s the power of adding them as an authorized user to an existing credit card.

That’s exactly what we recommended to Seungah Jeong for her 14-year-old daughter, Emi. She just started high school and is starting to spend her own money. By becoming an authorized user on her mom’s card, she can start building up a credit history for when she’s ready to go off on her own.

Even better? Some cards allow you to set individual spending limits for your authorized users, so your kids can learn about budgeting in a controlled environment.

Everyone has different needs when it comes to credit cards, and making the most of your everyday spending requires two important items. Put simply, you need to know:

If you never eat out, a credit card with a bonus on dining purchases won’t do you any good. If you’re a frequent international traveler, you don’t want to swipe a card and incur foreign transaction fees. And if you focus on earning rewards with a single travel provider, you may be missing out on more flexible rewards.

We saw this play out with all the families we met.

Take the Goralczenkos. Parents Andrew and Tracy have quadruplets who are heading off to college, and both were laid off two years ago when the company they worked for suddenly went out of business. They had been collecting rewards on their favorite theme park credit card for years, but in their current situation, that’s not doing much for them.

Instead, they can shift their focus to cash-back rewards, picking up a new card that awards them 3% back on some of their biggest purchases — like gas and groceries.

It was a similar story with Seungah, whose 18-year-old son Oliver was heading off to Greece for college. Our recommendation was to get a new travel rewards card, specifically one that offers flexible rewards and waives foreign transaction fees. That means Oliver won’t be hit with up to 3% in fees every time he swipes the card in Europe.

Finally, there was Renee Lewis-Mance. She and her husband, Chris, are retired, but she’s very into the points game, focusing primarily on a single airline and a single hotel loyalty program. While these programs can be valuable, Renee is missing out on one of the biggest benefits of being retired: flexibility.

That’s why we recommended adding a new transferable rewards card to her wallet. Earning points or miles in one of these programs provides an array of redemption options when she’s planning a trip. She’s not locked into a single airline or hotel chain, which could limit her options.

Beyond earning with your everyday spending, most popular cards offer one-time bonuses for new applicants (subject to minimum spending requirements). This allows you to take home a big haul of points, miles or cash-back rewards up front while picking up a new card that better fits your spending habits.

This was particularly appealing for the Goralczenkos. The card we recommended came with a $100 welcome bonus, plus 3% back on some major everyday spending categories. That won’t get them a flight to Europe, but in their current situation, cash back is much more appealing.

Chris Mance found himself in a similar boat. He was able to grab a one-time, $200 cash-back bonus on a new card that was also a better fit for where he spends his money each month.

But even more importantly, this new card will help him address the final strategy ...

Here at TPG, we like to joke that there’s no “point” to using cash for your everyday purchases — but there’s certainly risk. Carrying around a bunch of cash leaves you vulnerable to theft, and even if you opt to swipe a debit card, you’re generally earning no rewards on those purchases.

That’s the exact situation that Chris Mance found himself in. While his wife (Renee) loves playing the points game, Chris usually pays cash or uses a debit card for his regular trips to Home Depot and the grocery store. However, by shifting those purchases to a cash-back credit card, he can unlock some significant rewards.

Based on our estimates, his grocery purchases alone could turn into $250 in cash back every year.

In addition, since Chris was spending a good chunk of money on home improvement purchases — tools, gardening supplies, plants — we recommended a card that will allow him to customize his rewards by picking a category to earn 6% back in the first year. That alone should net him around $300 in rewards.

The best part? This card had no annual fee.

In both cases, Chris isn’t spending more money than he already planned to spend. He’s just switching to a payment method that rewards him for his existing spending habits.

The world of credit cards features an array of products to meet the needs of virtually every American. Sure, there are options geared toward luxury travelers with a variety of benefits to help elevate their next trip. But many others can be a great fit for everyday pursuits, like shopping at the grocery store or building your child's credit history.

Ordinary families can easily take advantage of cash-back rewards to support their household bottom lines, and can boost their earnings by carefully analyzing their spending habits to select the best card(s) for their wallets.

And as long as you’re responsibly managing your credit and spending within your means, the only way to lose is by not participating at all.

#6198. The Best Hot Dogs in Chicago, According to Someone Who Has Tried 'Em All

If you’re looking for the best hot dog in Chicago, you’ve come to the right place. While I can’t tell you how many hot dogs I’ve eaten in my life, I am sure that number is in the many thousands. After high school, I worked at Nick’s Nest, a hot dog stand in my Massachusetts hometown, where I would have one for lunch every day. They’re a favorite food to eat while traveling, and I regularly grab them in my daily life as well, because I live in Chicago, where the hot dog is a local staple.

Served in a steamed poppyseed bun, the Chicago dog has specific toppings: mustard, chopped onions, neon green relish, tomatoes (slices or wedges), pickles (usually spears, sometimes chips), spicy sport peppers, and celery salt. The all-beef dog has a natural casing, which gives a perfect snap when you bite into it. While most Chicago dogs are pretty good, the best ones are constructed so you taste everything in every bite. And you probably know this, but just to be sure: that bite will not include ketchup, as the tangy condiment doesn’t mesh with the other toppings (this is a real if-you-know-you-know thing in Chicago—and you want to be in the know). When you’re in the city, whether you’re siddling up to a hot dog stand or popping into a casual restaurant, order yours as a “Chicago dog” or ask for it “dragged through the garden”—a signal that you know what’s up, and that you want everything on it.

These are the best places to get a hot dog in Chicago, according to a dog-loving resident.

Read our complete Chicago travel guide here, which includes:

It feels very Chicago that you can get an excellent hot dog inside Home Depot. Fixin’ Franks is a family-owned spot with outposts in stores around the city. You’ll find the stands tucked near the exit, where it’s a treat for finishing all your home-repair shopping. There’s a tight, locally sourced menu of hot dogs, Polish and Maxwell Street sausages, Italian beef, and elotes. Get a classic Chicago dog—and if you want to push the envelope, add J.P. Graziano hot giardiniera on top.

1017 W. Irving Park Rd., Lakeview; 1701 W. Lawrence Ave., Ravenswood

While most restaurants follow the dragged-through-the-garden approach, Byron’s, which served their hot dogs at the White House during the Obama administration, takes a different approach. The standard dressing at the 51-year-old stand consists of mustard, relish, onions, tomato, pickle spears, and celery salt, and adds lettuce, green peppers, and cucumber slices (hot peppers are available on request). While this is, admittedly, a lot to maneuver while eating, the salad approach adds a lot of freshness and almost makes it seem like a healthy choice.

1250 S. Union Ave., University Village; 2775 N. Elston Ave., Avondale

Must order: Polish sausage sandwich, pork chop sandwich

Chicago’s hot dog stand culture includes more than just dogs. Jim’s is the best place for two other local beloveds: The Maxwell Street Polish and the pork chop sandwich. The Polish, a garlicky smoked beef and pork link, is generally credited to the stand’s namesake, Macedonian immigrant Jimmy Stefanovic, who took over his aunt and uncle’s stand in 1939. It’s served with mustard, tons of grilled onions, and sport peppers. The pork chop sandwich, served bone-in (bite carefully!) comes with the same garnishes, as does the all-beef hot dog. There’s no seating at the University Village location, which is open from 6 a.m. to 1 a.m., but you can eat at the metal counter or sit on the curb—Jim’s always feels like a party.

Must order: Hot dog, chocolate cake shake

When visitors come to town and want to try Chicago classics, I send them to Portillo’s. The local chain, which Dick Portillo founded in 1963, offers solid versions of local favorites, including hot dogs, Italian beef, and a Maxwell Street Polish. The steamed dog is expertly done and a go-to. Also a go-to is the chocolate cake shake, which is made with—you guessed it—a slice of chocolate cake blitzed into a milkshake. It’s decadently rich, and a true Chicago experience.

3057 N. Ashland Ave., Lakeview; 2449 W. Armitage Ave., Logan Square; 500 W. 35th St., Bridgeport; 4811 Dempster St., Skokie

Must-order: Hot dog and fries, RHR double cheeseburger

With four locations of this locally beloved stand (the O.G. Bridgeport location goes by 35th Street Red Hots), you are never far from one of the city’s best dogs. The links are served Depression-style, which means they have stripped-down toppings: just mustard, onion, relish, and sport peppers, with a pile of fries on top, for a full meal that tops out at just $5.20. Many locals, myself included, feel that Red Hot Ranch’s double smashburger is the best in the city, so get one of those to split as well.

6363 N. Milwaukee Ave., Norwood Park East; 333 S. Milwaukee Ave., Wheeling

In 1948, Maurie and Flaurie Berman opened their drive-in with two signatures. First, the couple appears as 12-foot hot dog statues on the building’s roof—you can’t miss this duo. And second, they serve a hot dog with a point of view: It’s a custom all-beef dog a bit larger than your standard link, and topped with mustard,

a pickle, sport peppers, and chopped onions, plus piccalilli and a pickled green tomato. It comes tucked with crinkle-cut fries in a custom cardboard box, which you can even peep in an episode of The Bear.

Must-order: Chicago-style Duck Inn Dog, fried cheese curds

What happens when you take a Chicago classic and put it in the hands of one of the city’s best chefs? You get Kevin Hickey’s Duck Inn Dog. Every element is made to Hickey’s specs: The juicy beef, pork, and duck fat sausage is grilled, tucked in a brioche poppyseed bun, and dressed with a “supercondiment” of mustard and relish mixed with tomato and onion. It’s finished with a dill pickle, pickled serranos, and celery salt (and perfect with fried cheese curds alongside). This is the glow-up the humble dog deserves.

Much of the love for 43-year-old The Wiener’s Circle is for its heckling servers, led by local institution Poochie Rollins. That experience is one reason to visit the Lincoln Park stand, which is famously open until 4 a.m. on weekends (and 2 a.m. the rest of the week). The other? The excellent food, like the char dog. Most stands steam their dogs, but the charring approach here adds a smoky flavor and crisper texture. Do not miss the fantastic cheese fries, with a generous dollop of tangy cheddar sauce.

Most hot dog stands in Chicago use locally made Vienna Beef links, and it’s worth venturing straight to the source to try one at this cafe, which is located across the street from the factory. Snag a red stool and order the textbook Chicago-style dog and a side of crispy fries. After lunch, peruse the goodies in the shop, which range from cases of hot dogs to hot dog stuffies.

Artur Wnorowski’s casual Polish joint serves some of my favorite sausages in town. All are made in-house: The kielbasa, which he learned to make from his grandfather, is smoked over pecan wood and dressed with caramelized onions, sport peppers, and hazy IPA mustard, while the all-beef dog is available Chicago-style or Polish-inspired. With sauerkraut, onions, sour cream, and a potato and cheese pierogi on top, it’s a nod to the sense of fun Chicago’s hot dog stands deliver.

#6197. Former China Eastern Chairman Jailed In $10+ Million Bribery Scandal

The former chairman of China Eastern Airlines has been sentenced to 14 years in jail, as he accepted more than $10 million in bribes in his official role. Yowzers!

A court in China’s Liaoning Province has sentenced former China Eastern chairman Liu Shaoyong to prison. The court ruled that he accepted over $10 million in bribes in his official capacity as chairman of one of China’s largest airlines.

The court found that between 2002 and 2023, Liu abused his position at the airline to provide assistance to companies and individuals in business operations, project contracts, and flight route management. Liu has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, and has been ordered to pay a fine of $600K, plus his illicit gains and related proceeds have to be recovered.

While the court ruled that his conduct constituted bribery “in an exceedingly large amount,” the sentence he got was actually lighter than it could’ve been, due to mitigating circumstances. These include his confession, voluntary disclosure of previously unknown offenses, and expression of remorse and cooperation in recovering illicit gains.

Make of this what you will, but it’s interesting to note that this is all part of China’s “anti-corruption campaign,” targeting officials at various levels, including executives of state-owned enterprises.

In June 2025, Liu had been placed under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) and the National Commission of Supervision, for violations of party discipline and state laws. In January 2026, he was expelled from the Communist Party of China (CPC), after investigators found that he had abused his authority for personal gain, and he was formally charged in May 2026.

China Eastern’s former chairman has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, after he admitted to taking over $10 million in bribes in his official role. This came as part of a larger crackdown by the government, which also saw the executive expelled from the Communist Party of China.

Over the years we’ve seen a decent number of airline executives charged with corruption — after all, they control a lot of spending, and in some cases, might get influenced for the wrong reasons.

What do you make of this punishment for China Eastern’s former chairman?

#6196. This Train Offers a Front-Row Seat to One of Colorado’s Greatest Natural Wonders

“Locomotives all have their own attitudes and personalities,” says Adam Clawson, the 24-year-old engineer at the helm of Royal Gorge Route Railroad, as our train winds along the Arkansas River. “They are their own living, breathing machines, and you have to learn their personalities.”

It’s a warm Saturday afternoon in October, and Clawson is at the controls of a locomotive he knows well: “Black Betty,” a jet-black, 3,000-horsepower diesel-electric unit that runs along a 12-mile stretch of tracks in Southern Colorado. Clawson is a third-generation railroader, following in the footsteps of his grandfather and great-grandfather, who both worked along this same route.

The Royal Gorge Route Railroad winds along the Arkansas River in Colorado.

As he eases the rumbling locomotive through the gorge, he offers a running commentary on the geology and history unfolding outside the window. Millions of years ago, he says, as the Rockies rose above the plains, the Arkansas River began carving its ancient path through the emerging peaks. Over time, the water wore away the hard granite, cutting a narrow, V-shaped gorge that plunges as deep as 1,250 feet in places.

The result is the Royal Gorge, a geological wonder nicknamed the “Grand Canyon of the Arkansas River.” Visitors can experience the dramatic 10-mile-long chasm from several perspectives: From above, while gazing down from the Royal Gorge Bridge, the tallest suspension bridge in the nation (or for more adventurous travelers, while rock climbing a 5-hour via ferrata); and from below, while paddling the Arkansas’s roaring rapids on a whitewater raft. But for travelers looking to sit back and savor the scenery passing by, there's no better viewpoint than the Royal Gorge Route Railroad's open-air car, standing face-to-face with the staggering canyon walls.

The writer's view aboard the Royal Gorge Route Railroad

This train line is as historic as it is scenic. Though the tourist train didn't launch until 1998, the route itself has been here for nearly 150 years—but it was close to never being built in the first place. In the late 1870s, a pair of competing railroad companies—the Denver & Rio Grande and the Santa Fe—duked it out for the chance to build tracks through this narrow canyon. Their two-year battle, which involved everything from court injunctions to sabotage to gun-slinging hired guards, became known as the “Royal Gorge War.” Eventually, the two companies signed a treaty and the Denver & Rio Grande prevailed, building tracks that eventually reached the lucrative mining hub of Leadville.

Decades later, the train still threads through the same Old West landscape, but the ride is decidedly more comfortable. Today passengers can choose from three classes: Vista Dome, which offers nearly unobstructed views of the gorge from glass-enclosed dome cars; Deluxe Class in the vintage dining car, where four-top tables with cushioned booth-style seats and a bar are nestled against the large windows; and Coach Class, with four-person table seating and the option to order food and drink from the casual grill menu and bar. On select dates, there are also First Class dining tickets available for lunch and dinner, with elevated menus and wine pairings. Regardless of where you sit, all ticket holders have access to the open-air car, which is standing-room only. With Clawson or one of his fellow engineers at the controls, all travelers have to do is sit back and let the scenery unfold.

The journey begins roughly an hour south of Colorado Springs in Cañon City at a historic depot originally completed in 1914. A few miles later, a dilapidated pipeline comes into view, running along the canyon wall just above the river. Completed in 1910, this eight-mile-long, mostly wooden structure provided water to Cañon City until 1973. As the train passes under the Royal Gorge Bridge, Clawson encourages me to open the cab window, lean back, and look up. The wind whips my hair as I stare at the bridge some 1,000 feet overhead. It’s 18 feet wide, according to Clawson, but from this vantage point, it looks like a thin wire that’s been strung across a gaping expanse.

As the train works its way through the river gorge, water rushes past and red rock walls tower on both sides.

Next, the train squeezes through the gorge’s narrowest and deepest section, the towering red granite walls growing taller and more imposing as they tighten around the tracks. Then we chug over the famous “Hanging Bridge,” which was an engineering marvel when it was completed in 1879—and remains one even today. At this point, the chasm narrows to just 30 feet wide, creating a bottleneck that required a little ingenuity to get a train through. Engineer C. Shallor Smith came up with a brilliant solution: He designed a 175-foot-long bridge that’s suspended above the rushing water by A-shaped supports anchored to the canyon wall.

Soon after, Clawson spots a pair of plastic kayaks hauled out on a small beach on the other side of the waterway. “We might get mooned,” he warns, referencing how paddlers traditionally greet the train when it passes. But when we spot the kayakers standing on the bank a few minutes later, they simply smile and wave. Clawson blares the train’s horn in response.

Eventually, the train reaches its western terminus, the town of Parkdale. Clawson hits the brakes and we jump down onto the tracks. Standing in front of the train up close, I’m struck by just how imposing she is. Thinking back to Clawson’s personality comment, I imagine her as fiercely independent—a self-assured, no-nonsense type of gal who’s not easily pushed around.

We clamber back into the cab and the train heads in reverse, retracing the route toward Cañon City. I relax back into my seat, letting the engine’s vibrations and the rhythmic drone of the wheels lull me into a pleasant daze. Outside, the rocky surfaces of the gorge’s walls alternate between light and shadow while the river glints in the midday sun. High overhead, I spot a turkey vulture circling on a thermal, its wings arching in a shallow V as it glides without flapping.

Clawson follows my gaze. “You can’t make this up,” he says. “Somebody might type into AI, ‘Take this picture of me and make it look like I’m in paradise.’ [But] all I gotta do is step outside."
