#6195. Air Serbia Flight To Moscow Diverts After Politician Reportedly Skips Security

An Air Serbia flight that was supposed to fly from Serbia to Russia ended up turning around over Lithuania, in order for additional security checks to be carried out on passengers. The circumstances surrounding this sure are unusual, given who was onboard.

This incident happened on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and involves Air Serbia flight JU134, scheduled to fly from Belgrade (BEG) to Moscow (SVO). The 1,074-mile flight was operated by an Airbus A320 with the registration code YU-APH. The flight was scheduled to depart at 6:25PM and land at 11:40PM, with a two hour time change, so it was blocked at 3hr15min.

The plane took off at 6:48PM, basically on schedule, and it started flying north, over Hungary, Slovakia, Poland, and then Lithuania. However, around 90 minutes after takeoff, while more than halfway, the plane u-turned, and flew back toward Belgrade.

The plane ended up landing in Belgrade at 9:57PM local time, a little over three hours after it first departed. The plane ended up once again taking off in the early morning hours of November 4, departing at 1:56AM, and landing at 6:43AM, over seven hours behind schedule.

Diversions happen, though it’s definitely unusual for a flight to turn around to the origin when it’s already more than halfway to its destination, especially when maintenance wasn’t to blame. Officially, the airline has shared that the decision to divert was made “in accordance with the instructions received and all applicable security rules.” That’s obviously really vague, though… so what really happened?

Here’s where the story gets really interesting. Onboard this Air Serbia flight were a few associates of former Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic, who just recently lost an election. One of the people onboard was Aleksandar Vulin, who served as deputy prime minister until 2025, and is viewed as being very pro-Russia. The US had even imposed sanctions on him due to his close ties with Russia.

Media reports in Serbia suggest that the reason for the diversion was that security camera footage at Belgrade Nikola Tesla Airport had been reviewed, and it was determined that someone had helped him avoid security checks. Now, I understand the need to carry out security checks, though I’m also not sure the point of diverting when you’re already more than halfway to your destination.

Vulin denies that he was the reason that the plane diverted, claiming that it was instead a political showdown. After the diversion, he went on national TV in Serbia, to say the following:

“It’s all a lie, an act of violence and an attempt to prove to these new authorities how ready they are here at the airport, how much they are on the defensive of their ideology. So, of course it’s all a lie, of course it’s all utter nonsense. I’m really sorry and uncomfortable, so many people have returned, their lives are being ruined, their obligations are being ruined because of the attempt to politically deal with me.”

“I am completely calm, I know that I am in the right. And you know, I did not go to Moscow as a tourist, I went on business. I am going there to fight for the extension of the gas agreement. Not for me and you, but for all citizens of Serbia.”

He also said he was asleep at the time of the diversion, and had no clue what was going on until the plane landed back in Belgrade:

“We just woke up, to be honest, I fell asleep. I was sleeping on the plane, I wake up, they say: You are in Belgrade. How are you in Belgrade? When we went outside, I see the police, the special forces gathered. I say: ‘Colleagues, have you come for me?’ They laugh. They say: ‘We are not, Minister.’ I go down with all the other passengers. I go through the procedure with all the other passengers again. I go through another procedure by myself. And now, I am standing and waiting for them to let us get on the plane again.”

An Air Serbia flight from Belgrade to Moscow turned around while over halfway to its destination. The decision to divert was made in accordance with “applicable security rules,” and all passengers were screened when the plane landed back in Serbia.

While it’s believed that a pro-Russia Serbian politician who was onboard may have avoided security checks at the airport, the politician denies that, and claims this was a political move.

What do you make of this unusual Air Serbia diversion?

#6194. 10 Magical Christmas Traditions Around the World

Living far away from family is hard at the best of times, but it becomes particularly difficult around the holidays. If there's one thing that makes it a little easier for me, it's being able to mix and match festive traditions from different countries to create something that's uniquely ours. As an Italian living in France with a British husband, I love bringing together the best of each culture for a rather extravagant Christmas. On Christmas Eve, we have oysters and Champagne, as per French tradition, followed by an Italian feast and plenty of Christmas crackers—although I draw the line at Christmas pudding, preferring a simple pandoro over anything else.

Whether, like me, you spend Christmas far from your family, are planning to chase the sun this December or are driving home for the holidays, one of the great joys of Christmas is making memories and indulging in nostalgic traditions. All over the globe, different countries and cultures celebrate the season in different ways, marking the holiday with long-established rites and rituals or merging heritage to create beautiful new traditions. Below, we run through some of our favourite Christmas traditions around the world, and ask the Traveller editors about their own personal festive rituals. From seafood feasts on Christmas Day in Australia to surfing Santa’s taking to the waves in SoCal, these are the most wholesome traditions for some festive joy this season.

Christmas is not recognized as a national holiday in Japan, but the festive season is still celebrated—albeit slightly differently from how you’d expect. As part of a marketing campaign launched in 1974, a few years after KFC first opened in Japan, the brand came up with the slogan ‘Kentucky for Christmas’, and it stuck. On Christmas Day, many Japanese families tuck into a full feast of fried chicken—a tradition so popular that you often have to order weeks in advance to make sure you’ve got your bucket guaranteed for the big day. The original Christmas meal even came with a bottle of wine. Christmas cake is just as surprising in Japan, too—strawberry shortcake, made with layers of sponge, whipped cream and fresh strawberries, is a festive favourite.

As you might imagine, food is at the heart of Christmas celebrations in Italy. Every region has its own traditions and dishes, enjoyed on Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and throughout the festive season. While northern Italians might tuck into tortellini in broth and other comforting dishes, in the south we go all out. In my family, we have twelve different dishes—mostly fish-based—served for Christmas Eve dinner, before indulging in traditional desserts and an unholy amount of nuts while playing tombola. If there is one tradition that the whole country shares, it's the rather quirky tradition of La Befana – a witch-like old woman who flies through the skies on a broomstick on the night of January 5, leaving gifts for children to discover on the morning of 6 January, known as Epiphany (Epifania in Italian). Well-behaved children receive sweets and presents, while naughty ones get coal – although these days it's usually sweet, sugary charcoal, which is actually delicious.

The real difference between the Scottish festive season and that of much of the rest of the world is Hogmanay. Once Christmas Day is done and dusted, the focus is on New Year’s—or, as the Scots call it, Hogmanay. Street parties in cities such as Edinburgh roll on until the early hours, Robert Burns’ Auld Lang Syne is sung at midnight, and the ‘first-footing’ custom takes place—the first visitor to a home after midnight is believed to bring good luck for the year ahead (along with traditional gifts such as whisky, shortbread or a lump of coal, of course). Traditionally, a tall, dark-haired man is considered the luckiest first-footer.

While much of the Northern Hemisphere is wrapping up against the cold, Christmas in Australia falls in the middle of summer, meaning festive celebrations often revolve around the beach, sunshine and outdoor gatherings. "The traditional Christmas lunch in Australia is usually seafood, a roast ham served cold, lots of salads and then a pavlova for dessert," explains Lauren Burvill, CNT’s senior commerce writer and resident Aussie. "After lunch the classic traditions are to play cricket in the backyard, or if you're lucky, on the beach. It's not unusual to see Santa on the beaches as well, often riding on an inflatable rescue boat from the local surf club. On Boxing Day the country's favourite pastime is to watch the cricket or the Sydney to Hobart yacht race."

Forget snowy landscapes and cosy fireplaces—in Southern California, you might spot Santa Claus swapping his sleigh for a surfboard during the festive season. "I grew up in greater Los Angeles, and though December isn't typically beach weather, something uncanny almost always happens on Christmas," explains Megan Spurrell, Conde Nast Traveler US’s associate articles director. "The temperatures spike to the mid-70s Fahrenheit with shining sun and many families, including my own, end up at the beach. But we also go to look out for a very SoCal figure, known as Surfing Santa. We keep our eyes out at Manhattan and Hermosa Beach, especially near the piers, though I've heard of surfing santas in Malibu and Santa Monica, too. Most are just local dudes with a Santa suit who reliably hit the waves on Christmas morning to entertain their neighbours (and get a surf session in)."

While many Western traditions see Santa leaving lumps of coal in stockings for badly behaved children, in Austria it's the terrifying Krampus who comes to punish them. As the folklore goes, the Krampus is a fearsome horned figure with a long, snake-like tongue, who accompanies Saint Nicholas on 5 December, otherwise known as Krampusnacht, the eve of Saint Nicholas Day. While Saint Nicholas rewards well-behaved children with sweets and small gifts, Krampus is said to frighten or punish those who have been naughty. Today, the tradition is celebrated with Krampuslauf parades, during which people dressed in elaborate horned masks and furry costumes take to the streets, particularly in Alpine towns and villages. The folklore even inspired a Christmas comedy horror film in 2015, starring Adam Scott and Toni Collette.

In Peru, Christmas Eve, known as Nochebuena, is the main event, with families gathering for a festive dinner and celebrations that often continue well past midnight. "We alternate years of spending Christmas in Southern California with my mom and sisters, and going to Lima, Peru, with my husband's family" says Megan. "Though Peru has plenty of traditions tied to Christmas, perhaps my favourite is the sheer fact (shared in many Catholic and Latin American countries) that the whole affair begins at midnight on the 24th. It can be torture waiting until midnight proper to dig into the feast of turkey and arroz arabe that sits out waiting, but the entire city explodes in fireworks when the clock strikes 12. And then the party doesn't stop until the wee hours of the morning, sometimes at a family member's house or at the city's bars and clubs. It almost feels like a preview of New Year's Eve, just a few days earlier."

Dumplings are a major part of Polish cuisine day to day, and Christmas is no exception. The traditional Christmas Eve supper, known as Wigilia, begins when the first star appears in the sky, with families gathering around the Christmas table for a feast that traditionally includes 12 meatless dishes. "My favourite part of seasonal eating has never been the Great British Christmas Roast, but instead 'Polish Christmas', celebrated by my family on Christmas Eve, a haphazard tribute to the Polish side of my family tree," says Olivia Squire, Traveller's features editor. "When I was a child, my grandmother used to make pierogi (Polish dumplings filled with mashed potato and cottage cheese) from scratch, which in more recent years has been taken over by my mum and I and usually involves a lot of swearing and tears. It's all worth it when we sit down to eat them alongside a vegetarian version of bigos (hunter's stew—an insult to my meat-loving ancestors), breaded fish and holy wafers, soundtracked by Carol's at King's, my English dad's addition."

Forget spending a fortune on Christmas presents—in Germany, the tradition of Schrottwichteln puts a rather amusing twist on exchanging gifts, with friends and family swapping unwanted, bizarre, or downright useless objects instead.

"For gifts, we follow the German tradition of Schrottwichteln (literally 'junk Secret Santa'), where everyone brings something completely useless, unwanted or gloriously ridiculous, often something they were given once and never knew what to do with. The more pointless, tacky or absurd, the better," Karin Mueller, Traveller's visuals director, tells us. "Our children have grown up with this ritual, and what began as a cosy dinner has become the highlight of the year. They never miss it. Now that they’re young adults, they bring their partners along, and it’s turned into this wonderfully chaotic, joyful, very-London celebration that I’m pretty sure they’ll keep going long after we stop hosting."

Across England, Christmas is celebrated with familiar traditions, from exchanging gifts to tucking into mince pies and singing Christmas carols. But each county and neighbourhood has its own customs, too. In some seaside towns, brave locals take part in a Boxing Day dip—sprinting into the freezing sea to shake off the Christmas excesses, often while raising money for charity. There's also the age-old custom of burning a Yule log, traditionally associated with good fortune and protection from misfortune. In Cornwall, some communities gather in local pubs for a traditional Cornish ‘shout’, joining together to sing folk songs and sea shanties.

"In the hazy betwixmas period, the days of lounging on the sofa and gorging on Terry’s chocolate orange are punctuated by one magical evening at a local pub for a Cornish 'shout'", explains Lucy Bruton, CNT's social media manager. "A shout refers to the community coming together to sing sea shanties and folk songs in the pub, and the Lerryn (where my family live in Cornwall) shout is a particularly special one to me. The tiny pub feels packed to the eaves with people of all ages belting out some of my favourite Cornish songs – from "Trelawney" to "Lamorna" and, of course, “Cornwall My Home”. It’s dark, cosy and a real slice of the magic of Cornwall."

#6193. Last-minute strategies for earning Delta Medallion elite status

With just two months left in 2026, time is running out to qualify (or requalify) for Delta Medallion elite status.

If you have not done so already, check your elite qualification metrics, tally up your travel for the rest of the year and see where that puts you in terms of elite status for next year. If you're short of your goal, you still have time to close the gap. There are plenty of ways to earn Delta status — and they don't all involve flying.

Here are some ideas to help you earn what you need by the end of the year and reap the benefits of Medallion status in 2027.

Related: Reciprocal earning coming soon from new Delta-Hyatt partnership

Remember that as of Jan. 1, 2024, Delta consolidated all Medallion status earning activities into Medallion Qualification Dollars, axing Medallion Qualification Miles and Medallion Qualification Segments.

Now, flyers earn MQDs not just on eligible travel purchases with Delta and its partners, but also on other activities, such as spending on Delta-issued credit cards and vacation packages. You'll need to reach the following MQD thresholds for each Medallion status tier:

Of course, the most obvious route to status is by booking paid flights through Delta: You'll earn 1 MQD per dollar on the ticket price of any Delta-marketed flight operated by Delta or its partner airlines (except in basic economy, which doesn't earn miles or MQDs). However, Delta's new "basic" premium fares still earn MQDs.

However, there are plenty of other ways to earn MQDs without setting foot on an airplane. Here are some last-minute strategies to help put you over the top for Delta elite status in 2026.

One of the best changes to the SkyMiles program in recent years is that Delta award tickets booked in Main Cabin or higher now earn MQDs. This can make earning status much cheaper.

If you have a stash of SkyMiles in your account, consider redeeming them to close the gap to your desired status tier. The number of MQDs you'll earn is calculated by dividing the number of miles redeemed by 100. (And remember, holders of select Delta American Express cards automatically save 15% on Delta-operated award tickets.)

There is one major exception to keep in mind: Only Delta-ticketed award flights earn MQDs. Your award ticket must be booked with Delta SkyMiles through a direct Delta channel in order to qualify (though it does not need to be operated by Delta). For example, using Air France-KLM Flying Blue miles to book an award flight operated by Delta won't earn MQDs, even if you add your SkyMiles number to the itinerary.

Related: Your complete guide to the Delta SkyMiles program

Since achieving Delta Medallion status now requires hitting spending thresholds, mileage runs are not the useful tool they once were if you're flying on Delta metal. On the bright side, you can still leverage partner fares to earn MQDs quickly. This is because these flights earn MQDs based on a percentage of the flight distance rather than the ticket price.

If you go this route, know that earning rates vary depending on which carrier and fare class you fly. For example, an Air France flight in full economy will earn MQDs based on 20% of the miles flown, while a full economy WestJet ticket will earn 15% of the miles flown. Remember, MQDs are not to be confused with SkyMiles.

You can also earn 1 MQD per dollar spent on Delta Vacations, the airline's platform for booking all-in-one vacation packages. However, Delta Car Rentals and Delta Stays bookings no longer earn MQDs.

Some Delta cobranded credit cards allow cardholders to earn MQDs. The following cards give you an automatic 2,500 MQDs each year (known as MQD Headstart), plus additional MQDs when you spend on the card:

It may be worth applying for one of these cards to close the gap for next year's Medallion status. If you already have one and your everyday purchases won't get you close enough to your desired status level, you might consider ways to increase your spending temporarily — such as paying your rent or mortgage with your cobranded card or making purchases for a friend and having them pay you back.

Just be aware that purchases on these cards must post to your account in 2026 to help you qualify for elite status in the 2027 status year. Purchases made in late December may go toward the following year instead, depending on the transaction date submitted to American Express by the merchant (which may differ from the date when you made the purchase). For example, if you make a purchase on Dec. 31 and the merchant lists the transaction date as Jan. 1, the MQDs you earn will count toward next year instead of this year.

Related: Delta SkyMiles Reserve Amex card review

Delta SkyMiles has historically been one of the most generous programs when it comes to status challenges. After temporary unavailability during recent program changes, the SkyMiles Medallion Status Match Challenge has returned. This means travelers who hold elite status with another airline can request a match through Delta Medallion. If approved, you'll receive the equivalent Delta status for three months, along with a status challenge to extend your shiny new Medallion status.

In 2025, Delta also offered a new program called Elevate Your Status that allowed members to make a one-time MQD purchase to reach the next Medallion status tier, as long as they already had the required number of MQDs to qualify. This limited-time promotion has ended, but keep an eye out in case Delta brings it back for 2026.

Delta's Choice Benefits for Platinum and Diamond members include MQD Accelerators to help you get closer to next year's status. In 2026, Platinum members can select this Choice Benefit to boost their MQDs by 1,000, while Diamond members can earn an extra 2,000 MQDs this way. These MQDs typically take six to eight weeks to deposit into your account — so, if you plan to use this route to achieve next year's status, now is the time to make your Choice Benefit selection.

Another Choice Benefit option allows you to gift Medallion status to other members. Platinum Medallions can choose to gift Silver Medallion status to four people, and Diamonds can gift Gold status to four people. So be nice to friends or family who might be able to give you a hand up into the club.

Note that Platinum status members can select one Choice Benefit, and Diamond status members can select three benefits. You can select your Choice Benefit as soon as you earn status, and you have until Jan. 31, 2027, to select your 2026 benefits.

Related: The ultimate guide to Delta Choice Benefits

This option is probably not feasible for most travelers, but it's worth mentioning.

Thanks to Delta's partnership with Wheels Up, a private jet subscription service, Wheels Up members can receive one Diamond Medallion status for every $100,000 spent in a Wheels Up Fund during a calendar year. If you don't have a subscription, you can still get one Diamond Medallion status after making at least $125,000 in flight spend. However, travelers who earn status either way will not get access to Choice Benefits.

This is obviously not the cheapest option for earning Delta elite status. However, if you or your business use the service anyway, it may be a good way to bypass the other requirements and go straight to the top.

Even though 2026 is coming to a close, there's still time to level up your Delta Medallion elite status so you can travel in comfort next year.

The most important thing is to know where you stand after accounting for the rest of your planned travel for this year. Once you determine how many extra MQDs you need, you can use these strategies to ensure you earn your desired elite tier for next year — and all the perks that come with it.

#6192. Is World Of Hyatt Points + Cash Worth It? The Value Varies Wildly

While the most popular way to redeem World of Hyatt points is for free night redemptions, the program also has a Points + Cash option, whereby you can redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a hotel stay.

The reality is that the value of Hyatt Points + Cash has fluctuated significantly over the years. Going back a decade, it was the primary way that I redeemed my points. Then it was devalued significantly, and then some value was brought back. So I’d like to take a look at the current state of things… is Hyatt Points + Cash worth considering nowadays?

As the name suggests, with Hyatt Points + Cash, you can redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a Hyatt stay. More specifically, you’ll redeem 50% of the points required for a stay, and will receive a 30-50% discount off the standard rate for the room type chosen.

Now, there are some important things to be aware of:

Just as a reminder, below is the standard room World of Hyatt award chart, which shows the award pricing for a free night hotel stay based on which of the five pricing tiers applies for a particular night (lowest, low, moderate, upper, or top).

When booking Points + Cash, you’d pay half of the points, plus 50-70% of the flexible revenue rate, so below is that chart.

With the basics of Hyatt Points + Cash out of the way, let’s do some number crunching. Let me state upfront that based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each, though I usually get quite a bit more value out of them in comparison to what a hotel stay would cost with cash.

For the purposes of the below examples, I’ll simply be comparing the cost for a free night redemption to the cost of a Points + Cash redemption. This doesn’t consider the outright cost of a stay if paying cash, so for more on that, see my post about when you should redeem points for a hotel stay.

I picked six hotels at random, belonging to different brands and in different regions. I picked totally random dates, so let’s take a look at what I found.

For the night I picked, the Grand Hyatt Tampa Bay is charging 15,000 points per night, or 7,500 points plus $103 ($116 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 7,500 extra points to save $116, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.55 cents each.

The Park Hyatt Los Cabos is charging 55,000 points per night, or 27,500 points plus $500.50 ($680.68 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 27,500 extra points to save $680.68, which is like buying Hyatt points for 2.48 cents each.

The Hyatt Studios Mobile is charging 3,000 points per night, or 1,500 points plus $61 ($71.98 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 1,500 extra points to save $71.98, which is like buying Hyatt points for 4.8 cents each.

The Thompson Rome is charging 35,000 points per night, or 17,500 points plus $281.20 (that includes taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 17,500 extra points to save $281.20, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.61 cents each.

The Hyatt Centric Dubai Jumeirah is charging 20,000 points per night, or 10,000 points plus $115 ($145.14 including taxes & fees). You’re spending $145.14 to save 10,000 points, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.45 cents each.

The Grand Hyatt Seoul is charging 20,000 points per night, or 10,000 points plus $221 (that includes taxes & fees). You’re spending $221 to save 10,000 points, which is like buying Hyatt points for 2.21 cents each.

As you can see, the value of Hyatt Points + Cash varies significantly. In the above six examples I randomly pulled up, you’re essentially “buying” Hyatt points for anywhere from 1.45 cents to 4.8 cents each (these aren’t actually points in your account, but rather you’re spending some amount of cash in lieu of points).

So the idea is that if the “purchase” price on points were relatively low, it could be worth booking Points + Cash, rather than just redeeming outright. On the low end of the spectrum, some people might find this to be worthwhile, though I think on the high end of the spectrum, we can all agree this represents an awful deal.

Before you make a final decision, just keep in mind:

Lastly, let me just mention that in many cases Points + Cash is a better value compared to redeeming points outright in situations where the cash rate is lower than usual, and a hotel is in low season. In those situations it might not make sense to redeem points at all. This comes down to how reimbursement for these awards works between World of Hyatt and individual hotels.

For example, the single best Points + Cash deal above is at the Hyatt Centric Dubai, but if you look at the cash rate, you’ll see that redeeming points isn’t a great deal in the first place. There’s no reason to redeem 20,000 points (or 10,000 points plus $115) when the cash rate in the first place is well under $200.

Hyatt Points + Cash lets you redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a hotel stay. While it’s nice to have the flexibility of this redemption opportunity, more often than not it doesn’t represent a good deal, in my opinion.

The value you’re getting per point through Points + Cash does vary wildly, but one thing that’s fairly consistent is that you won’t get outsized value. In a majority of situations where Points + Cash represents a good deal compared to the outright points cost, it’s a hotel where a points redemption isn’t a good deal in the first place.

Personally, I avoid Points + Cash redemptions, though it’s always worth checking and crunching the numbers.

What’s your take on Hyatt’s Points + Cash option? Do you ever use it?

#6191. Delta Plans Another Austin Route

Delta is expanding its Austin, Texas, network with a new daily route set to launch next spring.

The carrier will begin flights between Austin and Northwest Arkansas National Airport, which serves Fayetteville and the surrounding region, on March 7, 2027. SkyWest will operate the route under the Delta Connection brand using an Embraer E175.

Service from Northwest Arkansas to Austin begins March 8. Tickets are now on sale.

Flights will depart Austin at 8:59 p.m. and arrive in Northwest Arkansas at 10:49 p.m. The return flight will leave at 6 a.m. and arrive in Austin at 7:50 a.m. All times are local.

“Connecting Central Texas and Northwest Arkansas with new nonstop service brings two dynamic, growing regions closer together while giving our customers even more choice and convenience,” Luis Guitart, Delta’s Austin-based regional sales manager, said in a statement.

Guitart described the addition as another example of the airline’s investment in Austin.

Delta has been building its Austin operation, with plans to offer more than 70 peak-day departures to approximately 30 destinations by summer 2027. That expansion includes new service to Paris and San Diego, a second daily flight to San Jose, California, and year-round service to Cancun, Mexico.

#6189. The Best Airbnbs in Colorado, Including a Ski-In Chalet and a Cliffside Cabin

I’ve always found Colorado a little hard to resist. After a handful of trips, I’ve explored everything from Aspen’s glitzy streets to Denver’s spirited food and cocktail scene to the many smaller towns in between—and somehow, there’s still more to discover. With four national parks; miles of hiking and biking trails; world-class ski resorts; and cities brimming with independent shops, restaurants, and bars, Colorado is a year-round playground with plenty to keep you busy (and plenty of reasons to come back).

Finding the right Colorado Airbnb is part of the fun. Think tucked-away mountain cabins with front-row seats to the snow, sprawling homes made for group getaways, and character-filled apartments that put you right in the middle of the action. While there are plenty of gorgeous Colorado hotels, there's something pretty wonderful about having your own Airbnb to return to after a day of chasing fresh powder, hiking, or exploring a new town. Whether you're plotting a winter ski escape, a summer adventure, or a fall foliage getaway, these are the 13 best Airbnbs in Colorado to add to your wish list.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

It's close to the light rail, making it easy to get around when you so choose. With succulent-filled rooms, large paintings, five cozy bedrooms, and two-story windows, there’s lots to love about this space.

Any kids you're traveling with will favor the foosball and ping-pong tables in the basement, while adults will enjoy lounging in the sunken family room. #6188. Is the Venture X Business worth the $395 annual fee?

The Capital One Venture X Business is a great option for small-business owners who want to earn miles on their spending. It features a solid welcome bonus and many of our favorite features found on its consumer counterpart, the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card.

One such similarity is the $395 annual fee. This is a bargain compared to some other premium business cards, such as The Business Platinum Card® from American Express with its $895 fee (see rates and fees).

Still, a $395 annual fee is a meaningful expense. Does the Venture X Business offer enough benefits and earning potential to justify that premium fee? Here's what you need to know if you're on the fence.

Currently, new Venture X Business applicants can earn up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 travel credit:

*To use within 16 months from account opening

This bonus is worth up to $6,550 when you factor in TPG's November valuations of Capital One miles at 1.85 cents and the travel credit.

If you can meet the steep minimum spending requirements, the bonus alone is valuable enough to justify paying the card's $395 annual fee more than 16 times over.

Related: How to maximize your Capital One miles

Beyond the Venture X Business welcome bonus, you'll earn:

And when it comes to redeeming your miles, you have options. If you want to keep it simple, you can redeem your miles for a statement credit to cover travel expenses (charged to the card within the previous 90 days). This option offers a value of 1 cent per mile.

To get more value out of your miles, you can also transfer your miles to any of Capital One's 15-plus hotel and airline partners, including valuable options like Air Canada Aeroplan, Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer and Wyndham Rewards.

TPG values Capital One miles at 1.85 cents each when used with transfer partners, though the value you receive depends on your redemption.

This makes the Venture X Business an especially attractive option for big-spending business owners who don't want to worry about bonus categories.

With this card, you can feel confident knowing you're earning valuable rewards no matter what you're buying.

Related: Should you transfer Capital One miles to partners or redeem them directly?

Venture X Business cardholders receive $300 in credits each year for travel booked through Capital One Business Travel. This credit is automatic, making it relatively easy to use.

However, since the credit is limited to travel booked through Capital One Business Travel, you'll likely give up any hotel or rental car elite status perks. The drawbacks of booking through a portal can put a damper on the value of this annual credit.

Still, fully taking advantage of this perk will bring your effective annual fee down to just $95.

Related: How to decide whether to book travel directly or through a portal

The travel credit isn't the only annual perk you'll get as a Venture X Business cardholder. Every year, on your account anniversary, you'll also receive 10,000 bonus miles, worth $185 according to our valuations.

Even if you redeem these anniversary miles directly for travel at a rate of 1 cent per mile, this annual bonus is worth $100. This perk and the travel credit combined more than justify the card's $395 annual fee each year.

As a Venture X Business primary cardholder, you get unlimited access to Capital One Lounges, currently open at:

Capital One also operates dining-focused "Landing" facilities at LaGuardia Airport (LGA) and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

This card also includes access to Priority Pass lounges.

Without an eligible credit card, you can pay $90 for a lounge day pass. Five visits alone would cost $450 out of pocket, so you'll make up the annual fee's value quickly if you can take advantage of your Capital One Lounge access.

Related: Capital One Venture X vs. Venture X Business

On top of these benefits, the Venture X Business includes additional travel perks:

These benefits are more difficult to quantify, but they'll provide added comfort and peace of mind during your travels.

Related: A comparison of luxury hotel programs from credit card issuers: Amex, Capital One, Chase and Citi

If you can take advantage of key Venture X Business benefits, such as the annual travel credit and anniversary bonus miles, you can offset the card's annual fee year after year.

However, if you can't maximize the annual travel credit or airport lounge access, you may want to go with another of our favorite business credit cards. You may also want to consider a different card if you anticipate struggling to meet this card's lofty welcome bonus spending requirements.

For more details, read our full review of the Venture X Business.

#6187. Frontier Shakes Up Leadership Team

Frontier is reshuffling its leadership team, hiring a new chief operating officer, and announcing the departures of two senior executives.

Michael Delehant will join the carrier as executive vice president and chief operating officer on Nov. 30. He will oversee all airline operations and report to CEO Jimmy Dempsey, Frontier said Monday.

Delehant most recently served as group managing director at Wizz Air, overseeing operational and commercial activities. He previously held senior positions at Vueling, including chief strategy and network officer, and worked in several leadership roles at Southwest.

Dempsey said Delehant’s experience would be “instrumental as we continue growing our airline and executing against our strategic priorities.”

The appointment comes as Trevor Stedke, senior vice president of operations, and Alex Clerc, senior vice president of customers, prepare to leave Frontier on Nov. 13. The airline did not give a reason for their departures in its announcement.

“I want to express my sincere gratitude to Trevor and Alex for their dedication and contributions to Frontier,” Dempsey said.

Frontier also promoted James Fenner to senior vice president and chief revenue officer. His responsibilities include pricing and revenue management, loyalty, and network planning.

Fenner has spent more than a decade at the airline, most recently serving as vice president of revenue and loyalty.

Bobby Schroeter will move into the role of senior vice president and chief marketing officer, overseeing the airline’s brand and customer experience. Both Fenner and Schroeter will report directly to Dempsey.

The changes follow Frontier’s third-quarter results, which showed a $104 million net loss, compared with a $77 million loss a year earlier. Excluding special items, the carrier reported a $40 million profit on record revenue of $1.36 billion.

#6186. Citi AAdvantage Business Card Loyalty Points Double Dip Explained

The single best way to earn American AAdvantage Loyalty Points with credit card spending often flies under the radar, so I’d like to talk a little more about that in this post, especially since this tends to cause some confusion. Furthermore, this was recently made an “official” card perk, rather than something that just unofficially applied to most cardmembers.

Link: Double dip your Loyalty Points earning with the Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard®

With the American AAdvantage Loyalty Points program, you can typically earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on a co-branded American credit card. However, there’s one card that’s an exception, and by far the best.

The Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® (learn more) is the co-branded Citi and American Airlines business card. There’s a quirk to the card, though, when it comes to authorized user rewards. On the surface, the authorized user ordinarily earns the Loyalty Points for their spending, and not the primary cardmember, which is an unusual policy for a small business card.

However, through December 31, 2028 (and it’s possible this will be extended again, as it has been in the past), both the primary cardmember and the authorized user earn Loyalty Points for authorized user spending. It basically means you earn two Loyalty Points per dollar spent, just in different accounts. Just to be abundantly clear here:

So the key is for the spending to be on the authorized user’s card, so that this spending unlocks double Loyalty Points (spread across two accounts).

Either way, the Citi AAdvantage Business Card offers several valuable perks, and also has an excellent welcome bonus, making it a good time to apply. So if you are eligible, I’d consider applying even if the double Loyalty Points opportunity doesn’t work out (though hopefully it does).

Personally, the Citi AAdvantage Business Card Loyalty Points double dip is how I qualified for AAdvantage elite status last year. I had a hard time justifying putting spending onto co-branded American cards compared to some other cards out there, when I was only earning one Loyalty Point per dollar.

But if I can qualify for elite status for two people at once, and earn the corresponding Loyalty Point Rewards perks, the math on that spending starts to look much better:

For example, earning 250,000 Loyalty Points per account could potentially earn you a combined total of 12 systemwide upgrades or 170,000 bonus miles. That’s a pretty substantial reward, beyond just the miles you earn for spending and the status!

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card offers an easy opportunity to double dip Loyalty Points earning through authorized user spending. This opportunity is available to all cardmembers, and is currently valid through December 31, 2028 (though has the potential to be extended beyond that). This is a great opportunity, so if you’re pursuing AAdvantage elite status, I’d highly recommend this method.

#6185. The 50 Best Restaurants For 2026 Have Been Announced—With a Remote European Spot in First Place

The 50 Best Restaurants have just been announced for 2026 as part of a prestigious awards ceremony in Lima on Wednesday, 5 November 2026.

The Best Restaurant in the World for 2026 is hidden away in sleepy Basque village, Axpe

Climbing up from its number two spot in last year's list, this year’s winner is Asador Etxebarri in Spain's Atxondo.

Basque wood-fired cooking is at the heart of this rustic fine-dining restaurant. Chef-owner Víctor Arguinzoniz (also known as Bittor Arginzoniz) is considered a pioneer of grilling and live-fire cooking. At Asador Etxebarri, every course of Bittor Arginzoniz's €300 (about $337) tasting menu touches the wood and charcoal grills—from Palamós red prawns to smoked milk ice cream.

Hidden away in the sleepy mountain village of Axpe, about 45 minutes by car from Bilbao, foodies have been making the pilgrimage to try Arguinzoniz's signature grilled dishes since the restaurant opened in 1990. It's been an 18-year journey to the top, as Asador Etxebarri has been a mainstay on The World's 50 Best Restaurants list since 2008, starting at number 44.

Once a restaurant gets the coveted number one trophy, it is ineligible for nomination in forthcoming years—with the intention of allowing other restaurants a chance to earn top billing. Top-placing restaurants are then inducted into a new list, called the Best of the Best. This list includes such legendary eateries as Chef Thomas Keller's The French Laundry in Yountville, California, and Disfrutar in Barcelona, Spain. Last year’s winner, Maido in Lima, Peru, is the most recent inductee to this prestigious list.

It’s tempting to imagine the enviable job held by a panel of judges that sample every restaurant in the world. But that’s not quite how the 50 Best works. Rather, the 50 is an international media company that taps the expertise of over a thousand hospitality experts from around the world to weigh in on the industry that they know best. Chefs, restaurateurs, food journalists and well-traveled gourmets all anonymously nominate restaurants that they have dined at within the last 18 months. Members can’t vote for a restaurant they have a financial interest in. Professional services consultancy Deloitte has access to the voting data to ensure the validity and fairness of the process.

Because of the voting-style nature of the awards, a restaurant might fall off the list one year only to return later. This year, previous entries to the list such as The Ledbury—a fine-dining beauty in London, United Kingdom where chef Brett Graham marries British produce, Japanese flavours, and French culinary techniques—returns to the list in the number 83 spot. Similarly, Luxe Mosu in Seoul, South Korea—home to chef Sung Anh's elevated interpretations of traditional Korean fare—returns to the list at number 78.

“Every year The 50 Best Restaurants list gives us a snapshot of where more than 1,100 individuals who live and breathe this industry have had their most memorable restaurant experiences over the previous 18 months," explains Rikki Tidball, managing director of awards and rankings for The 50. “And I think that’s what makes it so special. Each Academy member votes independently, so nobody at The 50 or any of our partners has a say in who makes the list and restaurants can’t nominate themselves. This means every restaurant on the list has genuinely earned it.”

Gaggan in Bangkok climbed up to no. 2 after last year's no. 6 spot

As always, the highest-ranking restaurants on each continent have been given a special mention during tonight's awards—and there are a few repeats from last year. Gaggan in Bangkok (this year's number 2) won the best restaurant in Asia again. Mexico City's Quintonil (no. 4) was the best restaurant in Latin America again, while New York City's Atomix (no. 11) was the best restaurant in North America. Dubai's Trèsind Studio (no. 28) was named the best restaurant in the Middle East for another year. The best restaurant in Africa was Cape Town's La Colombe (no. 35). Sydney's Saint Peter (no. 50) was the best restaurant in Oceania, while top spot Asador Etxebarri took the best restaurant in Europe award.

Every year, the panel awards special prizes to chefs, front-of-house staff, and activists who are leading the charge in hospitality. In 2026, the Best Female Chef Award went to Jessica Rosval, head chef of Al Gatto Verde. Bangkok’s Dej Kewkacha won Best Pastry Chef Award, Lesley Liu of Odette in Singapore won the Best Sommelier Award while the Estrella Damm Chefs' Choice Award went to Junghyun ‘JP’ Park from Atomix in New York City. Doris Lam won The 50 Best Restaurants Scholarship. Spanish chef Ferran Adrià of El Bulli won the SevenRooms Icon Award.

Restaurants given a special mention during the 2026 ceremony included Tuju in São Paulo, which earned the Highest New Entry Award. Copenhagen's Kadeau won the Highest Climber Award after soaring 33 places this year and Naar in Kasauli, India, won the Sustainable Restaurant Award.

This year, only one US restaurant made the top 50: Atomix, in New York. It came in 11th place, rising one place from 2025, where it came in 12th.

#6184. How to get United Club lounge access: From credit cards to paid memberships

Airport lounges can serve as oases from a busy, crowded or outdated terminal. Some lounges participate in membership networks like Priority Pass, while others, like the United Club lounge, are operated by individual airlines.

If you're a loyal United Airlines flyer or frequent one of the carrier's largest hubs, visiting a United Club lounge is probably already on your radar. However, the airline made some major access changes in 2025.

Here's what you need to know about accessing United's lounges.

The Chicago-based airline operates a network of standard lounges known as United Clubs, as well as more exclusive Polaris lounges for eligible premium-cabin travelers on select long-haul international, transcontinental and Hawaii routes. Both offer complimentary food, drinks and Wi-Fi, while Polaris lounges feature additional amenities, such as sit-down dining, relaxation areas and shower suites.

So, how can travelers gain access to United's network of lounges?

You'll need a same-day boarding pass to access United lounges. This can be a same-day boarding pass for a United-operated flight or a flight operated by a Star Alliance partner airline, like Lufthansa or Swiss.

Related: Best United Airlines credit cards

United now has two tiers of paid membership for entry to the Club.

This membership offers the primary member unlimited access to all 45-plus United Club locations. There are no discounts available for United Premier members. Individual members can pay to bring guests into the lounge on a one-off basis; a one-time pass costs $59 per guest and is subject to availability.

Individual members do not have access to Star Alliance partner lounges.

Annual fee: Varies depending on Premier status

All Access members can enjoy unlimited United Club access for the primary member and up to two adult guests, or one adult and any dependents under 18.

This membership also includes access to Star Alliance partner lounges and other select partner locations, subject to applicable access policies.

Lifetime United Club members have been converted to All Access memberships.

TPG values United MileagePlus miles at 1.2 cents each per our November 2026 valuations, so your best bet is to pay the annual membership fee with cash rather than miles.

Having an eligible cobranded United credit card can be the most cost-effective way to consistently enter the United Club.

You can get lounge access with the following cards (note that some cards only offer one-time passes):

*The information for the United Club Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Unlike a paid Individual membership, a United Club membership earned via a cobranded credit card offers a unique access policy that includes entry for primary cardmembers, one adult guest and any dependents under 18 years old.

Cardmembers can unlock an All Access membership, which increases the guest allowance and provides access to participating Star Alliance partner lounges, by earning Premier Gold status or higher, or by spending $50,000 on eligible purchases with their United Club Card or United Club Business Card in a calendar year.

Since the annual fee on both the United Club Card and the United Club Business Card is $695, having a credit card to enter the lounge remains a more attractive option than outright buying a membership.

Additionally, the United Club Card and the United Club Business Card offer four one-time passes on each account anniversary. A pass can be used by one person accompanying the primary cardholder or an authorized user into the lounge.

If you'd prefer to avoid the hefty annual fee, you can opt for the entry-level United Explorer Card or the United Business Card, both of which include two single-use United Club passes each year. Note that these day passes don't include guest access, nor can they be transferred to friends or family who aren't authorized users or accompanying a cardmember into the lounge.

Certain MileagePlus Premier and Star Alliance Gold members can access United Clubs when traveling on eligible flights.

United Premier Gold (and higher) members can access United Clubs when traveling internationally on United or another Star Alliance carrier, regardless of their class of service. They can also bring along one guest who's traveling on the same flight.

Travelers who earn Star Alliance Gold status through another member airline can access United Clubs when flying on any eligible Star Alliance flight, including domestic United flights. Again, guests must be traveling on the same flight as the elite member.

United's invite-only Global Services members can enjoy lounge access on all United-operated flights, including those operating exclusively within the U.S. Note that this new perk only covers the Global Services member — you'll only be able to bring a guest into the lounge with an All Access membership, eligible cobranded credit card or when flying internationally.

Travelers flying in certain premium cabins on United or its Star Alliance partners can also access United Clubs. However, eligibility and guest privileges vary by airline, route and cabin class, as outlined below.

If you don't travel enough to justify an annual membership, you can also purchase a one-time United Club pass for $59 per person at United Club locations or through the United mobile app. Just note that day passes don't guarantee entry when lounge is at capacity.

Travelers using a one-time pass can enter a United Club only up to three hours before their scheduled departure time. (This exclusively applies to departure flights, and there is no time limit for entry on connecting flights.) These one-time passes are not accepted at grab-and-go locations, United Polaris lounges, United Arrivals Lounges or partner lounges.

You can also earn complimentary one-time passes with select cobranded credit cards, including:

One-time passes issued through United cobranded credit cards must be redeemed by the primary cardholder, an authorized user or a guest accompanied by either. Each pass admits one person.

United's lounges are open to a few other travelers, including:

Some premium-class passengers also have access to United's Polaris lounges, which offer a more premium experience. You can expect modern furnishings, private spa-like shower suites and elevated culinary options.

Three types of passengers are eligible for Polaris lounge access:

In addition to United Clubs and Polaris Lounges, the carrier operates a grab-and-go lounge concept called United Club Fly.

The first such space opened at Denver International Airport (DEN) in November 2022, and a second one opened at George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in 2025. Eligible travelers can enter Club Fly by scanning their boarding pass at the self-service entry gate.

Once inside, you can head to the snack bar that's stocked with packaged and prepared foods. You can also order a coffee from the barista.

Given Club Fly's focus on efficiency, the access policies are a bit different. Eligible United Club members and travelers flying in international premium cabins are eligible to enter, but they cannot bring any guests.

The Chicago-based carrier operates more than 45 United Club lounge locations. Of course, you'll find a plethora of United Clubs in the carrier's main hubs, including:

Apart from DEN, all of the aforementioned airports also have Polaris lounges.

There are other United Club locations scattered across the U.S., including in airports such as Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW), Philadelphia International Airport (PHL), Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX), Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) and Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP), among others.

Check out United's website for a complete list of the airline's Club and Polaris lounge locations.

United offers a variety of ways to access its United Clubs, both for premium-cabin frequent flyers and for those with a membership.

If you frequently travel with United, it's worth analyzing which options offer the best bang for your buck to unlock a relaxing lounge experience.

#6183. Air India CEO Wants ‘More Widebody Aircraft’

Air India is looking to buy more widebody jets as it expands overseas and works to return to profitability.

“We want more widebody aircraft,” CEO Tewolde Gebremariam said Tuesday at the Aviation India and South Asia summit in New Delhi, according to Reuters. The carrier has held talks with both Airbus and Boeing. Gebremariam did not say how many aircraft Air India might buy.

The airline’s most recent Boeing order, announced in January, was for 30 narrowbodies: 20 737 MAX 8s and 10 MAX 10s.

The carrier is also updating the widebodies it already flies. In April, Air India took delivery of the first of 26 older Boeing 787-8s slated for cabin retrofits. The aircraft went from two cabins to three with the addition of premium economy.

Gebremariam, who previously led Ethiopian Airlines, described high operating costs as a “major concern” but said he expects Air India to return to profitability “very soon.”

Air India Group lost S$3.56 billion in the fiscal year ended March 31, according to financial disclosures from Singapore Airlines, which owns a 25% stake in the group. The loss came as the carrier dealt with disruption from the war in Iran and Pakistan’s closure of its airspace to Indian airlines.

#6182. Park Hyatt Riviera Maya Cancun, Brand’s First All-Inclusive, Opens Soon

Want to take advantage of Hyatt Privé benefits, including a room upgrade, complimentary breakfast, a hotel credit, and more, when booking a cash stay? Contact Ford ([email protected]) for more details. He may even be able to help if you already have a stay booked.

In late 2023, Hyatt and Parks Hospitality Holdings announced a collaboration that will expand Hyatt’s footprint in Mexico, with the development of four new properties. If you ask me, the most interesting of these is the new Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, which will also be the brand’s first all-inclusive property.

There’s now an update, as the hotel’s opening date has just been moved forward by a couple of months, and it’s now expected to open in the coming weeks.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, located in Cancun, Mexico, is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 3, 2026. The hotel was initially supposed to open in 2025, then it started accepting reservations for stays as of February 2027, and now it’s accepting reservations for stays as of late 2026.

Hopefully the current opening date sticks, but if you book in the first several months the hotel is open, don’t be surprised if we see an additional delay, or at least don’t be surprised if not everything is ready.

The 148-key property will have a first-ever concept for the Park Hyatt brand, as it will be all-inclusive. Admittedly this is pretty normal for the Cancun area, but still, it’s noteworthy for a brand like Park Hyatt.

Hyatt has been leaning heavily into the all-inclusive space in recent times, particularly through acquisitions. So while Hyatt has grown massively in terms of its number of all-inclusive brands, it’s surprising to see even a traditionally non all-inclusive brand get this kind of an experience.

I’m generally not a fan of all-inclusives, or at least historically haven’t chosen to vacation at them. However, after my recent Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection cruise, there is something I really enjoyed about not being nickel-and-dimed for everything, given how expensive luxury hospitality has become in so many places.

When it comes to the dining outlets, they’ll include Beach Grill IK’AL (the beachfront restaurant with seafood and Yucatecan flavors), Bruma (the steakhouse), Nutre Kitchen (the all-day dining restaurant), Pool Bar Brisa (the pool bar serving drinks & light snacks), Patisserie Market & Cafe (the coffee shop), Living Room (the lobby bar).

Accommodations will range in size from 559 square feet (52 square meters) to 2,303 square feet (214 square meters), so they’re generously sized, as you’d expect. The decor looks nice enough, but not like anything special.

As you’d expect, the resort will have amenities including several pools, a full-service spa, a gym, and more.

Once open, this adds to a growing number of luxury points hotels in the Cancun area. Just recently we saw the opening of the St. Regis Kanai and Waldorf Astoria Cancun, so it’s nice to see Hyatt’s most luxurious brand also expand to the Cancun area. As a matter of fact, the Park Hyatt will be immediately next to the Waldorf Astoria (which also recently became all-inclusive, as it wasn’t initially).

The Park Hyatt brand is really growing in Mexico right now. We’ve seen the recent opening of the Park Hyatt Los Cabos at Cabo Del Sol, while the Park Hyatt Mexico City is expected to open in early 2027. Beyond that, we also saw the recent opening of the Alila Mayakoba, another good luxury option in the Cancun area.

With the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya now bookable, what are rates like? If paying cash, rooms seem to generally start at around $1,500 per night, but that does include taxes & fees. So it’s obviously very expensive, but given Mexico’s high taxes & fees, it’s actually not quite as crazy as some may have expected.

Then again, I’m not necessarily expecting this to be typical Park Hyatt quality, given the extent to which this is outside the typical Park Hyatt wheelhouse. Oddly, at least as of now, rates seem to be the same whether one or two people are staying, which is unusual for an all-inclusive.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, a hotel credit, and more.

When redeeming points, the hotel follows World of Hyatt’s Category F all-inclusive award chart, which is the most expensive award pricing for all-inclusive properties.

Under Hyatt’s current award chart, the cost is typically 45,000 to 85,000 points per night, and that’s the same whether the room has single or double occupancy.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 2026. The hotel is expected to be an all-inclusive, making it the first Park Hyatt property in the world where that’s the case.

It’s awesome to see Hyatt’s luxury expansion in Mexico, as this will be the third Park Hyatt to open in a fairly short time period. However, the Park Hyatt brand is becoming increasingly inconsistent, and I find the all-inclusive pivot to be a bit strange, especially given how many all-inclusive brands Hyatt already has.

What do you make of plans for the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya?

Opening weeks also tend to be soft launches with a few kinks. FWIW Google Hotels is fun for keeping one eye on the price with Track Prices on while the first reviews trickle in. #6181. Air Canada Ordered 8 Airbus A350-1000s To Fly Nonstop Where Its Boeing 777-300ERs Cannot

Air Canada has gone all in on the extra-long widebody Airbus A350-1000, with an order for eight examples that will begin to arrive in 2030. The introduction of the A350-1000 marks a monumental shift for the airline, breaking a decades-long reliance on Boeing 777-300ERs for its long-haul operations. The A350 has a maximum range of 9,000 nautical miles (16,668 km), compared with 1,630 nautical miles for the 777-300ER.

This allows Air Canada to freely expand its destination list. Air Canada already flies to Delhi, Tokyo, Sydney and Brisbane, so its order for eight Airbus A350-1000s is not simply a ticket to new cities. While the 777-300ER has been highly successful as a twin-aisle aircraft, the A350-1000 offers significant performance advantages. On existing long routes like Vancouver to Delhi, the 777 often faces strict weight restrictions.

This forces the airline to leave behind passengers or cargo to carry enough fuel, but the new A350 removes that limitation. With the prolonged certification of the next-gen 777X still ongoing, the A350 offers a much faster path for fleet renewal. Powered by Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-97 engines and built with a 70% composite airframe, the A350 is dramatically more efficient than the 777.

It also has a lower 6,000-foot (1,828.8 m) altitude, 25% lower than legacy jets, and enhanced humidity controls to reduce jet lag on grueling 17+ hour flights. The A350 will become Air Canada's flagship, complementing the new A321XLRs now joining the fleet.

Among the numerous technical and economic reasons that make the A350 a powerful new platform for the Air Canada fleet, geopolitical considerations have also made long-haul flying even longer in recent years. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 Canada, the US, the UK, and the EU banned Russian aircraft from their skies.

In a reciprocal move, Russia barred NATO-aligned nations from its airspace, cutting off access to Siberian corridors. The shortest distance between North America and Asia or South Asia isn't a straight line across the Pacific, but a Great-Circle route that arcs upward through the Arctic and down through eastern Russia.

Losing this airspace complicated Air Canada’s flight paths and forced significant operational changes. According to ch aviation, Air Canada responded by adding a fuel stop in London to its Vancouver to Delhi service. That layover makes a 14-hour nonstop journey into two flights of about nine and eight hours with a stop of one to two hours.

Lester B. Pearson International Airport (YYZ)

Indira Gandhi Delhi International Airport (DEL)

Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (BOM)

Previously operated with a layover at Frankfurt Airport (FRA) or London Heathrow Airport (LHR), now axed.

Flights to India from Toronto and Montreal stayed nonstop, the same report said. For flights bound for East Asia, such as Vancouver to Hong Kong or Tokyo, Air Canada had to shift its paths drastically eastward. Planes are forced to fly over Alaska and trace a narrow international airway skirting just 30 miles outside Russian territory over the Bering Sea. These routes typically add 10% to a trip's distance.

This translates to multiple hours of extra time in the air each way. Carrying the extra fuel needed for a 1,000-mile detour significantly increases the plane's takeoff weight. Because aircraft have strict maximum takeoff weights, Air Canada frequently faces payload penalties. It also drastically increases crew labor costs and shortens engine maintenance cycles.

Ultra-long-haul routes operate on razor-thin margins, and detours decimate profitability. While Air Canada must absorb these costs and charge higher ticket prices for longer, less convenient flights, competitors unaffected by the bans continue to fly direct. An extra two hours of flight time burns thousands of additional gallons of fuel, which is an airline's single largest expense.

Increasing fares in response drives price-conscious passengers away, destroying the route's economic viability. When a flight path is stretched by 1,000 miles due to airspace bans, the plane must carry tons of additional fuel just to stay airborne for the extra two hours. Because the MTOW cannot change, every extra pound of fuel loaded into the tanks directly forces a pound of payload off the aircraft.

To save weight, the airline must implement severe weight-restriction caps. Air Canada is forced to block out seats, leaving them empty and unsold, and refuse lucrative belly commercial cargo. Carrying massive fuel loads makes the plane much heavier for the first half of the flight. The plane uses significantly more fuel just to carry the extra weight of its own fuel, all while generating less revenue from a half-empty cabin.

A 777 packed to its absolute weight limit with detour fuel cannot climb directly to its optimal fuel-efficient cruising altitude around 35,000 feet because the air is too thin for the extra weight. The plane is forced to spend the first several hours of the flight at lower altitudes, like 29,000 feet, where the air is denser, creating significantly more aerodynamic drag and increasing fuel burn and engine wear. The longer itinerary also requires paying the flight deck and cabin crew for extra block hours.

This often triggers mandatory crew rest rules that require putting up relief crews in expensive destination hotels. Additionally, adding two hours to every leg pushes an aircraft into heavy maintenance checks months ahead of schedule. For an older fleet of Boeing 777s already midway through their service lives, this relentless compounding of flight hours drastically shortens the calendar years they can remain in service.

The 777X is nearly ready for service, how will it fare against Airbus's A350?

The A350-1000 was designed long after the 777, specifically tailored for the realities of modern ultra-long-haul flying. Over 50% of the A350's airframe is built from lightweight carbon-fiber composites instead of traditional aluminum. This drastically lowers the empty weight of the aircraft; thus, it can carry extra fuel without being forced to cut passenger seats or cargo on almost any ultra-long-haul route.

The A350 provides Air Canada with the raw performance capability to restore axed routes like Toronto to Mumbai and protect the profitability of routes to Delhi and Hong Kong. The Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-97 engines operating on the A350-1000 are optimized for high-altitude efficiency. Combined with an advanced morphing wing design, the aircraft can climb quickly to optimal cruising altitudes even when heavily loaded, burning roughly 25% less fuel per seat than the 777. Beyond the balance sheet, the A350 delivers a superior premium passenger experience that protects its brand on grueling flights.

Traditional aluminum airframes limit how much a cabin can be pressurized and humidified without causing structural rust over time. The Airbus jet's composite fuselage does not corrode, allowing the cabin altitude to be set much lower with significantly higher ambient humidity. Passengers step off an 18-hour flight experiencing far less physical fatigue, headaches, and dehydration.

Air Canada has around 90 aircraft on order made up of Airbus, Boeing, and former Bombardier passenger jets.

While the A350-1000 is an incredibly efficient leap forward, replacing the Boeing 777-300ER isn't a flawless victory. Air Canada is making concrete trade-offs, and several distinct physical attributes, operational realities, and sensory experiences unique to the 'Triple Seven' will be lost.

The Boeing 777-300ER features an incredibly wide internal cross-section at 19 feet, three inches (5.87 m). The A350-1000 is physically narrower at 18 feet, five inches (5.61 m). Because of the 777's massive, boxy upper fuselage cross-section, its overhead pivot bins are structurally deeper and taller.

The 777 is also top of the class when it comes to revenue-generating belly cargo. It handles a standard underfloor capacity of up to 44 cargo containers. The A350-1000 maxes out closer to 40 containers. Given these traits, it begs the question: why didn't Air Canada order the 777X instead of the next-gen Airbus?

Air Canada's decision to pass on the 777-9 in favor of the A350 came down to a mix of persistent engineering delays and operational constraints. While the 777-9 was the expected successor within Air Canada's heavily Boeing-dominated system, its design did not align with the airline's immediate technical and operational requirements.

More importantly, timing was the critical driver because Air Canada’s current fleet of 19 Boeing 777s is rapidly aging, with an average age now over 16 years. The 777-9 is a super heavy twinjet, with an MTOW of 775,000 pounds. Its folding carbon-fiber wings make it highly efficient on normal routes.

However, its size works against it on Air Canada's longer routes through Russian airspace compared with the A350. Worse still, the 777X program has notoriously suffered from years of rolling setbacks and testing delays, pushing it to 2027 or later. Air Canada simply could not risk waiting on an unstable timeline after so many years.

Premium cards are not just about travel — they’re continuing to add lifestyle value you can use at home. The American Express Platinum Card® offers up to $75 per quarter (up to $300 per calendar year) in Lululemon statement credits.*

Whether you're looking for casual attire, travel essentials or workout gear, here are seven items we recommend buying with your quarterly $75 Lululemon statement credit.

*Enrollment is required, and outlets are excluded. Only applies to purchases at U.S. stores and online.

Although the Amex Platinum's $895 annual fee (see ) may seem very high, perks like the quarterly up to $75 Lululemon statement credit (up to $300 each calendar year) help offset the cost.

The up to $75 quarterly statement credit is valid for eligible purchases made at U.S. Lululemon stores (excluding outlets) and on lululemon.com (after enrollment).

Many TPGers are big fans of Lululemon and find its clothing to be an excellent choice for travel-day outfits. It's also comfortable for city travel and lightweight for exercise.

Related: How to maximize benefits with the Amex Platinum Card

I used my Amex Platinum's Q3 Lululemon statement credit for a black Steady State SuperLoft Crew shirt. Although it’s designed for men, this sweatshirt fits me exceptionally well.

Lululemon also offers a women's version of this, if you'd prefer a different fit. I currently plan to use my Q4 statement credit to buy another of these shirts in a different color.

TPG credit cards writer Stephanie Stevens is a huge fan of the clear version of the Everywhere Belt Bag.

She feels the bag is great for stadiums or events with clear-bag policies. Best of all, it is reasonably priced and makes a great gift.

Buying two bags for $76 would use your full $75 quarterly statement credit, leaving you with just $1 to pay (before applicable taxes). You could also buy one bag and put the remaining credit toward another eligible purchase.

Buy: Everywhere Belt Bag 1L Clear for $38

TPG's lead writer for loyalty programs, Katie Genter, recently used her statement credit on this hoodie. It comes in three different basic color options, making it easy to pair with a variety of outfits.

If you're someone who gets cold easily while traveling, this hoodie could be a great item to throw on during your flight, train ride or car ride. The Amex Platinum's up to $75 quarterly Lululemon statement credit brings the total cost down to just $23.

Katie also noted that she used a statement credit from a different quarter to purchase this long-sleeve shirt. This is a soft, casual shirt that can work for a relaxed day around the house, a long travel day or as a casual top for a day of sightseeing.

Keep in mind that this item is marked Final Sale, so you won't be able to return it online if it doesn't fit or otherwise meet your expectations. However, your Amex Platinum's shopping protections should be usable here if your item arrives damaged or not as described. Alternatively, you may be able to return it in-store for store credit.

Buy: All Yours Organic Cotton-Blend Long-Sleeve Shirt for $29

I used my up to $75 Lululemon statement credit for Q1 2026 on a pair of these joggers. They're incredibly soft and feel high-quality.

If you're looking for a comfortable pair of joggers to throw on after work or for a light workout, these pants are hard to beat. (This is a Final Sale item.)

Buy: Heavyweight Soft Jersey Relaxed Fit Jogger for $69

TPG senior analyst Jared Nord noted that, while he already has one of these hoodies, he may pick up another, given that the price is currently within the threshold for the Amex Platinum's up to $75 quarterly Lululemon statement credit.

This hoodie is available in a wide range of colors, making it easy to find a color you like. As with some other items mentioned, this is marked Final Sale.

Buy: Smooth Spacer Classic-Fit Pullover Hoodie for $69 in select colors; regular price $138

TPG's managing editor for credit cards, Giselle Gomez, bought this item earlier this quarter. She "found them to be super comfortable for traveling," and added she "might circle back and get them in another color."

The price for these pants varies, so make sure to pay close attention to the total amount when adding your color choice to your cart. Depending on the color you choose, your Amex Platinum's quarterly up-to-$75 Lululemon statement credit may not cover the entire purchase.

Buy: Groove Nulu High-Rise Flared Pant Regular $59 in select colors; regular price $118

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $75 in Lululemon statement credits each quarter. If you shop at the retailer only once and spend less than $75, you’ll forfeit any unused portion of the statement credit when the next quarter begins.

To maximize this benefit, first make sure you’re enrolled in the statement credit, then click through a shopping portal before making your purchase. While you’ll earn only 1 point per dollar spent with your Platinum Card, you may be able to pick up additional rewards through a shopping portal. (At the time of publication, Rakuten is not offering rewards on Lululemon purchases.)

Next, aim to use the full $75 statement credit each quarter. You don’t have to spend it all in a single transaction, and you can spread your purchases across multiple orders if needed. Since many popular Lululemon items — including jackets, pants and shirts — cost more than $75, using the entire statement credit shouldn’t be difficult.

If you buy an item you’re not happy with, consider exchanging it instead of returning it. A return could trigger a statement credit reversal, and you may not be able to use your statement credit again during that quarter.

You can also stretch your statement credit further by purchasing sale items. (Note that purchases made at Lululemon outlet locations don’t qualify.)

Finally, don’t wait until the last minute to use your quarterly statement credit. If your purchase doesn’t post before the end of the quarter, it could trigger the following quarter’s statement credit instead.

Related: Forgettable statement credits checklist: Perks and benefits not to be overlooked

The Lululemon statement credit on the Amex Platinum is a great benefit for those who enjoy the brand. Consider these TPG-recommended items, or, if you already have your own favorites, be sure to purchase them using your Amex Platinum next time.

Don't forget to use your Q4 Lululemon statement credit, since you don't want to leave that value on the table.
