#6154. Priceline Faces $1 Billion Fine After Hotel Guests Were Tricked Into Paying Up To 85% More For Rooms

You search for a hotel, click what looks like its reservation page, and book a room—only to discover you’ve gone through a middleman charging hundreds of dollars more per night. That’s the deception alleged against Guest Reservations, a Priceline partner whose advertised rate could be up to 85% higher than booking directly. Now Priceline’s parent has recorded a $1 billion accounting charge toward a possible Federal Trade Commission settlement involving the partner’s practices, with the potential penalties and consumer refunds still being negotiated. A refundable room at San Francisco’s Palace Hotel was $419 on Marriott’s website. Guest Reservations wanted $775 for a comparable room with the same cancellation deadline. And the city’s lawsuit says the booking site was designed to make travelers think they were dealing with the hotel directly. The company supplying the rooms was Priceline, and its parent Booking Holdings which also owns Booking.com, has taken a $1 billion accounting hit while negotiating a possible regulatory settlement for its involvement in intercept guests who had already chosen a hotel, making them think they’d reached the hotel’s own site, and charging them more – and making it difficult to undo the purchase when they discover what happened. San Francisco’s suit includes a Google search for “palace hotel sf” on an iPhone. The top sponsored result displayed palacesanfrancisco.guestreservations.com, above Marriott’s own hotel website. Clicking led to a page devoted to the Palace Hotel. The city says the small “An independent travel network” on the site was easy to miss and ambiguous. “Guest reservations” sounds like a department of the hotel you’re trying to book. Put the property’s name in front of it, add hotel photos, and a traveler can think they’ve arrived at the hotel’s guest reservations department. The city compared prices within minutes of each other on July 1 for a July 8 stay. These were Marriott’s public nonmember rates, including taxes: King Room Cancellation Terms Marriott Direct Guest Reservations Markup Refundable for one day after booking $381 $595 56% Refundable until July 5 $419 $775 85% A separate investigation found a two-night stay at the Westin Denver Airport cost $237 more through Guest Reservations than booking the same stay directly. Guest Reservations said it clearly identifies itself as an independent platform, complies with Google’s advertising rules, and discloses its taxes and service fees before purchase. Customers also describe trouble getting refunds after discovering the intermediary. And booking through a third party means giving up hotel points and elite benefits, along with the ability to deal directly with the property when plans change. Guest Reservations isn’t owned or operated by Priceline. Priceline Partner Solutions was reportedly its exclusive hotel inventory supplier. Their operation furnished the hotel information, booking technology and payment processing, and earned revenue from completed reservations. The city’s case also targets BookOnline.com. It alleges Booking knew how the sites were acquiring customers and continued helping them sell rooms. Booking responded that it takes consumer protection seriously and believes the lawsuit lacks merit. One example of Priceline’s involvement comes from Seth Kugel’s New York Times investigation. An 85-year-old woman searching for Bologna’s Grand Hotel Majestic reached Guest Reservations and requested an eight night standard room stay. She was charged $16,559 for a suite, including $4,276 in taxes and fees. When she disputed the charge with American Express, Priceline Partner Solutions was the merchant of record and successfully sought to have the charge reinstated. Guest Reservations later told the paper it had issued her a refund. Priceline told the Times that fewer than 0.09% of Guest Reservations transactions generated complaints, that partners must comply with laws and contractual obligations, and that it takes action when it identifies violations. A low complaint rate doesn’t tell us how many people were misled. Some never discover it. Others blame the hotel. Many may think they have no recourse. Most consumers do not complain when they’re unhappy (or complain to friends and family). The odds that a complaint reaches Priceline as supplier of the inventory seem low. And they’re saying they’re getting complaints… not what they did with those! In its latest quarterly filing, Booking recorded: A $900 million reduction in revenue. A separate $100 million loss in general and administrative expenses. Booking says the FTC could seek even more. A negotiated agreement would likely include payments to the agency, money back to U.S. consumers, and changes to Priceline’s practices. There are also civil penalties for qualifying rule violations, with a current ceiling of $53,088 per violation. The government has a straightforward argument about the alleged sales process: a reasonable customer gets misled by the appearance of an ad and booking page, while the booking site says guests should have read the disclaimer more carefully. The site apparently was literally designed to create the wrong impression among customers. The FTC’s business impersonation rule covers falsely posing as another company or misrepresenting an affiliation, including by implication. The government likely needs to show that Priceline knew about the deception and participated in it or had authority to control it. But there are several defenses: Charging more isn’t illegal. Travel agencies can charge service fees, and customers can buy expensive rooms. Guest Reservations says it discloses its role and charges. The actual booking screens and phone calls have to establish deception. It doesn’t appear that Guest Reservations websites offer any value add of any kind. The question is going to be whether they were in fact actively trying to generate bookings through deception. Supplying rooms alone doesn’t make Priceline responsible for every advertisement of them. It can argue that it provided ordinary distribution services and didn’t design or control the misleading sales pitch. The FTC declined to adopt a broad provision making suppliers liable for furnishing the tools of impersonation. So the FTC needs to demonstrate Priceline’s complicity. The FTC has to establish its authority to collect the money. The Supreme Court limited the agency’s general route to obtaining refunds in 2021. The amount of harm is unclear. Travelers could have gotten their rooms for less but generally did receive the stay they booked, at a price they were willing to pay. I wouldn’t make every wholesaler liable whenever a reseller behaves badly. It’s not yet clear exactly what Priceline knew and when they knew it. But I infer from taking a billion dollar accounting charge that the evidence against them is significant. Online travel agencies can earn their commissions by helping customers find the hotel they want, comparing options and searching for better prices (despite rate parity rules). I’ve written about the financial incentive to make comparison shopping harder. Here, it seems the traveler had already chosen the hotel, was looking for the hotel site to go ahead and book it, and the middlemen got paid by confusing them into thinking that’s what they were doing. #6153. What the FTC Wants to Know About How Airlines Set Fares

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Airline pricing has come under more scrutiny in recent years after Delta disclosed it was using AI to price some fares and a lawsuit was filed against JetBlue, alleging that the company uses personal data to price airfares. The airline industry has said it uses no personal data to determine pricing.

Airline pricing is once again under scrutiny. Last week, the Federal Trade Commission ordered Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and JetBlue to provide data on how they set fares, as part of a study of whether companies use personal information to set prices.

The agency wants details on the companies’ pricing methods. The companies have 45 days to respond.

“We intend to scrutinize the opaque methodology that some companies in these industries may be using to determine how much consumers pay or how much gig workers are paid for the same product or service,” FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said in a statement.

The FTC sent similar orders to Lyft, DoorDash, Uber, Instacart, Target and Walmart, seeking data on pricing and, for the gig companies, on worker pay.

The Federal Trade Commission has ordered Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and JetBlue to hand over data on how they set fares, part of a broader study into whether companies use personal information to price goods and services. The airlines have 45 days to respond. The same orders went to Lyft, DoorDash, Uber, Instacart, Target, and Walmart, with FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson saying the agency intends to scrutinize "opaque" pricing methodology. The inquiry lands as fares have risen sharply this year, largely because of surging jet fuel costs, and as airlines expand their use of AI in pricing. Delta, which told investors in 2024 it was working with the Israeli startup Fetcherr and said last year it was pricing about 3% of domestic routes with AI with a goal of up to 25% by the end of 2025, said it does not use personal data to set fares and has never used, tested, or planned individualized pricing. United referred questions to Airlines for America, which said it welcomes the study and that its carriers do not engage in personalized pricing. JetBlue faces a class action filed in April alleging it uses trackers to set prices dynamically. Roughly a dozen states have proposed laws this year limiting how companies collect and use customer search data, with California, Arizona, Hawaii, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and Vermont proposing outright bans on surveillance pricing.

#6152. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as âThe most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.â

âWhen you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,â Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to âblow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.â

âIf the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,â Trump said midway in his speech. âNow that doesnât happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesnât win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.â

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report âThe party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.â The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting âthat Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.â If a sweep happens in the toss up races, itâll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.Â

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6151. American Airlines Dropped Trump’s Name From West Palm Beach Departure Screens

Update: This change actually happened in August. Reminder: Palm Beach airport code changing from PBI to DJT On Aug. 18, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) airport code for President Donald J. Trump International Airport in Palm Beach, Florida, will change from PBI to DJT. This is the code used on most customer- and team member-facing systems. What you can expect: Airport applications, including QIK, ACE and Falcon, will transition to using the new airport code, DJT, on Aug. 18. Customer applications, such as the American app and AA.com will also use the DJT code. Transition period: Some tools and manuals may continue to reference this airport by its previous name and airport code during a transition period. If you are unable to use DJT in these systems, revert to using PBI. If you receive any questions from customers about the change, refer to these talking points: Why is American using the DJT airport code for President Donald J. Trump International Airport? American follows airport codes as determined by the International Air Transport Association and other bodies. After Florida passed a law earlier this year to rename the airport, IATA announced they would change the three-digit airport code. Why is American referring to this airport as President Donald J. Trump International Airport? Earlier this year, a law was passed in the State of Florida renaming this airport from Palm Beach International Airport to President Donald J. Trump International Airport. American follows all airport names and guidance as determined by international bodies as well as federal, state and local governments. Why does the screen behind you say, “West Palm Beach, FL”? Given that this transition is now complete and both the ICAO and IATA codes have changed, GIDS displays will once again say “West Palm Beach, FL.” American Airlines has dropped “Pres DJT” from the gate monitors of its West Palm Beach flights, going back to “West Palm Beach, FL,” as flagged by aviation watchdog JonNYC. It undoes the unusual decision to give the sitting president billing that other airport namesakes don’t get. JonNYC flagged the change Wednesday night, then added that he isn’t claiming a connection to the election results. It’s not clear exactly when American flipped the switch. so… has anyone noticed that AA has changed the gate monitors from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL” ? — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 4, 2026 Back in July, I wrote about American breaking its usual gate screen display pattern for Trump. They generally display the city, adding an airport name where it helps distinguish between airports serving the same destination. New York’s JFK versus LaGuardia makes sense. Little Rock doesn’t get billed as Clinton airport, and Grand Rapids doesn’t get Gerald Ford. West Palm Beach got “Pres DJT.” Here’s the screen from that July coverage: American even gave agents talking points to explain the change. Their internal memo pointed to Florida’s renaming law and the change in the airport’s three-letter code, saying: American follows all airport names and guidance as determined by international bodies as well as federal, state and local governments. That explained why the airport had a new name, but not putting the president’s name on the gate screen. And there’s no change made by the airport itself! Florida’s renaming of Palm Beach International as President Donald J. Trump International Airport took effect July 9. The passenger-facing airport code changed from PBI to DJT on August 18. American still very much needs this administration. The Department of Transportation and Federal Aviation Administration heavily regulate them. In September I wrote about Robert Isom’s praise for Trump and what American might want in return, including closer cooperation with Alaska Airlines. Just two days later, American and Alaska announced plans for Alaska to join American’s Atlantic and Pacific joint businesses. That needs DOT approval and antitrust immunity, and the administration’s help for approvals overseas. As I explained at the time, this would let them share revenue and coordinate fares and schedules with Alaska and their international partners. Reminder: Palm Beach airport code changing from PBI to DJT

On Aug. 18, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) airport code for President Donald J. Trump International Airport in Palm Beach, Florida, will change from PBI to DJT. This is the code used on most customer- and team member-facing systems.

Transition period: Some tools and manuals may continue to reference this airport by its previous name and airport code during a transition period.

If you receive any questions from customers about the change, refer to these talking points:

Why is American using the DJT airport code for President Donald J. Trump International Airport?

American follows airport codes as determined by the International Air Transport Association and other bodies. After Florida passed a law earlier this year to rename the airport, IATA announced they would change the three-digit airport code.

Why is American referring to this airport as President Donald J. Trump International Airport?

Earlier this year, a law was passed in the State of Florida renaming this airport from Palm Beach International Airport to President Donald J. Trump International Airport. American follows all airport names and guidance as determined by international bodies as well as federal, state and local governments.

Why does the screen behind you say, “West Palm Beach, FL”?

Given that this transition is now complete and both the ICAO and IATA codes have changed, GIDS displays will once again say “West Palm Beach, FL.”

American Airlines has dropped “Pres DJT” from the gate monitors of its West Palm Beach flights, going back to “West Palm Beach, FL,” as flagged by aviation watchdog JonNYC. It undoes the unusual decision to give the sitting president billing that other airport namesakes don’t get.

JonNYC flagged the change Wednesday night, then added that he isn’t claiming a connection to the election results. It’s not clear exactly when American flipped the switch.

so… has anyone noticed that AA has changed the gate monitors from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL” ?

Back in July, I wrote about American breaking its usual gate screen display pattern for Trump. They generally display the city, adding an airport name where it helps distinguish between airports serving the same destination. New York’s JFK versus LaGuardia makes sense. Little Rock doesn’t get billed as Clinton airport, and Grand Rapids doesn’t get Gerald Ford.

West Palm Beach got “Pres DJT.” Here’s the screen from that July coverage:

American even gave agents talking points to explain the change. Their internal memo pointed to Florida’s renaming law and the change in the airport’s three-letter code, saying:

American follows all airport names and guidance as determined by international bodies as well as federal, state and local governments.

That explained why the airport had a new name, but not putting the president’s name on the gate screen. And there’s no change made by the airport itself! Florida’s renaming of Palm Beach International as President Donald J. Trump International Airport took effect July 9. The passenger-facing airport code changed from PBI to DJT on August 18.

American still very much needs this administration. The Department of Transportation and Federal Aviation Administration heavily regulate them. In September I wrote about Robert Isom’s praise for Trump and what American might want in return, including closer cooperation with Alaska Airlines.

Just two days later, American and Alaska announced plans for Alaska to join American’s Atlantic and Pacific joint businesses. That needs DOT approval and antitrust immunity, and the administration’s help for approvals overseas. As I explained at the time, this would let them share revenue and coordinate fares and schedules with Alaska and their international partners.

#6150. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trumpâs trusted lawyerÂ and cable newsâs favorite nutcase.

Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Boratâs ultimate get in 2006âs âBorat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,â the pranking of Americaâs mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: hisÂ corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

All it took for the producers of âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ to succeed in theirÂ mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohenâs exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie.Â By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

Performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout âSubsequent Movefilmâ for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment weâre introduced to Bakalovaâs Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

Tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on parÂ with the sinking of the Titanic.Â Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, âthe happiest wife in the world,â emboldening her to join Boratâs latest trip as a stowaway.

Similarly life, and Boratâs government, have not been kind to him since âCultural Learningsâ conquered America with great success â high five! â 14 years ago.

America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

When Kazakhstanâs current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, heâs hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form â ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all â and given a new mission to smooth glorious leaderâs entry into the worldâs strongman club. How? By presenting toâVice Premier Mikhail Penceâ valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, âKazakhstanâs Minister of Culture and No.1Â porno star.â

This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the filmâs release fails to ruin âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas, Â plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the filmâs full title: âBorat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstanâ merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

In the main, the humor driving âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series âWho Is America?â â which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American â enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit heâd pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. âTheyâre fun!â

Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, âSubsequent Moviefilmâ makes Tutarâs empowerment the centerpiece of the movieâs second half. Â Baron Cohenâs signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Wolinerâs past TV work (which includesÂ series such as âNathan for Youâ) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

Either way, the fact that âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

Thereâs the practical matter that the character ofÂ Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that âthe problem with success, although itâs fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I âgetâ with Borat again, so itâs a kind of self-defeating form, really.â

What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today.Â However, heâs right about the problem of Boratâs fame. âSubsequent Moviefilmâ confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

Nonetheless, Boratâs relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant â except for when he revealshis subjectsâ prejudices.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original âBoratâ donât involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Boratâs stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Fewer of those sight gags exist in âSubsequent Moviefilm.â Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctorâs office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohenâs infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama âwith the Wuhan flu.â

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business donât tell us anything we donât already know. Instead, itâs what the context implies about Americaâs psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isnât merely in the pastorâs misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutarâs stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutarâs father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?)

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesnât disturb the status quo.

Thereâs the Texas baker who uses icing toÂ pipe the wordsÂ âJews Will Not Replace Usâ on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. Thereâs theÂ shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the âno means yesâ dress section. Thereâs the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, âWhat color is best for racist family?â says without pause or reaction, âI wouldnât go any darker than a six or a seven.â

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; sheâs also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first âBoratâ and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, sheâs a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of âSubsequent Moviefilmâ relative to the first âBoratâ sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has arenât deadly, although itâs plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the filmâs ending in ways that donât feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the âBoratâ of 2006 and the 2020 âSubsequent Moviefilmâ is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trumpâs election in 2016, to say nothing of howÂ decline and fall of basic critical thoughtÂ has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

At the same time, thereâs simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If thereâs a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called âlesserâ nations.

Now it doesnât allow the audience to be so sure of itself,Â implying in the final sceneÂ that we arenât merely ugly Americans. Weâre a once glorious nationÂ being led by goons who areÂ sliding us backwardÂ into diminishment, and dangerously so. ThatÂ is nothing to laugh about.Â

âBorat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstanâ is currently streaming on Amazon.

If you have yet to take a solo trip, there are many reasons why you really should. Solo travel helps you build confidence and new skills. It also provides time to reflect, recharge and reconnect with yourself — so you can return home the best version of yourself for the people who rely on you day-to-day.

I know it can be daunting to embark on your first big trip alone. But never fear, intrepid soloist. I've rounded up the top solo travel mistakes so that you can avoid them to ensure your trip goes smoothly.

Related: Travel mistakes that could ruin your next trip

One of the perks of solo travel is that you get to decide where to stay and what to do, so put some thought into it. This will ensure you have the best trip possible.

A good starting point is to check the State Department travel advisory for your destination, which will help you understand any safety concerns and identify neighborhoods you may want to avoid. It's also a good idea to enroll your trip in STEP, so you'll be alerted to things like natural disasters and security threats.

Safety isn't the only thing to consider. Are you looking for a quiet, relaxing getaway or a bustling neighborhood with endless things to do? Would you rather stay close to the action or save money by staying in a less popular area? Choose your accommodations accordingly.

Don't make the mistake I made on my first solo trip and not plan any activities. Spontaneity sounded fun, but I found making decisions on my own much harder than expected. You don't need to have your entire itinerary planned out to the minute, but doing some planning before you travel will reduce your stress during the trip.

Plus, many popular tourist attractions and trendy restaurants fill up quickly — and waiting in long lines is even less fun with no one to talk to. Do your research, and if needed, make a reservation or book a timed-entry ticket ahead of time.

Sometimes, the difference between traveling solo and with others really shines through in the little things...like using an airport bathroom.

You can't simply ask a companion to hold your luggage while you run to the restroom or figure out how to operate a metro ticket machine; you must keep track of it at all times. So think twice about packing that extra-large checked bag or hauling a not-so-ergonomic shoulder duffel on an international trip, as you will have to take it with you literally everywhere.

I personally prefer a backpack and small rolling carryon, which I can easily maneuver through crowded airports and over cobblestoned streets — without reaching my destination with a backache. Plus, it's big enough to accommodate sufficient clothing for a week (or more). My carryon is expandable, so if I buy too many souvenirs, I can unzip the extender and check it on the way home.

Related: How to pack your carryon right and avoid checking a bag

Connecting with new people is one of the many joys of solo travel, but that doesn't mean you should completely let your guard down. You may run into pickpockets, con artists and worse on your journey, and as a solo traveler, you're more likely to be targeted.

One simple step to reduce your risk is by not broadcasting your solo status. Err on the side of caution when chatting with new friends — and if they start getting nosy, tell them you're meeting up with friends later.

One way to prevent hotel staff from knowing your single status is opting for mobile check-in so that you can bypass the front desk completely. Or, you can ask the concierge for an extra key and allude that someone will be joining you shortly. And when catching a ride to or from your accommodation, it's a good idea to be picked up or dropped off down the street from your hotel.

Related: Solo travel safety tips every traveler should know

You only want to be incognito to the locals.

Let your actual friends and family know your travel plans: flight numbers, where you'll be staying on which dates, contact info for your tour operator, etc. You'll be glad you did if you hit a snag and need help rebooking on the fly. You can go a step further by sending them a copy of your passport or ID, in case you lose your documents while traveling.

You'll probably want to stay in contact with loved ones through text messages, phone calls or social media posts every so often. But you can also share your location continuously with apps like Find My, which can help ease their minds as well as give you an added layer of security. That way, both you and your loved ones can enjoy your trip stress-free.

Some things are must-haves no matter how many people you're traveling with, but they become even more critical when you're on your own — because if you forget something, you can't just reach into a companion's suitcase.

For instance, do you have a backup plan in case your phone dies while you're navigating a new city or road-tripping through an unfamiliar country? You can't simply borrow someone else's phone, so a charged power bank or old-fashioned map can come in clutch.

The same goes if you wind up at a store that doesn't accept your credit card. Always pack a couple of backup cards (preferably ones that don't charge foreign transaction fees) and keep some cash on hand.

Similarly, if you catch a cold on your flight or get food poisoning during a solo trip, there's no one else to run to a drugstore. And if you hurt yourself while out hiking alone, it may take a while for help to arrive. Prepare yourself for anything with a travel-ready first-aid kit.

Related: Travel essentials that can save your trip when things go wrong

One of the downsides of solo travel is that it can start to feel lonely, especially on longer trips. Making new friends is a great way to combat loneliness, as well as learn more about local culture and/or meet likeminded travelers.

If striking up a conversation with a stranger sounds more stressful than fun, you're not alone. Thankfully, there are plenty of ways for even the shyest travelers to make connections, including cruises and small-group tours designed specifically for solo travelers.

Female Travel Buddies is one of many Facebook groups ideal for those flying solo: Members post open invitations for fellow travelers in the same area to join you for brunch, sightseeing or a show. If this type of thing interests you, consider joining a handful of groups a few months ahead of your trip to get familiar with the members and learn how they work.

Related: 6 tips for meeting people when traveling solo

Just because you're traveling alone doesn't mean you can't take photos along the way — but capturing memories can be trickier by yourself.

The good news is you don't have to be limited by the length of your arm. Be sure to pack a selfie stick, mini tripod with remote shutter or selfie monitor screen. You'll find it well worth the investment, as having the right tools will make it far easier to snap the perfect selfie. (Just remember: safety first, especially when hiking, taking selfies near cliff edges, etc.!)

If, like me, you feel a little awkward or uncomfortable taking selfies alone, the best advice I can give you is to do it anyway. The more you do it, the more comfortable you'll get and the better your photos will turn out.

Solo travel doesn't have to be daunting. Follow these tips to embark on your first solo trip with confidence and ensure it goes smoothly, and before you know it, you'll be a seasoned solo traveler.

Ready to start planning? Check out these guides for more inspiration:

#6143. Trip.com Group Builds a Bigger Travel Business Around Concerts

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Taylor Swift The Eras Tour Wikimedia Commons / Paolo Villanueva

The concert might be the reason to travel, but Trip.com Group wants to make sure it's not the only thing fans spend money on. Tickets and hotel rooms are just the opening act.

Trip.com Group wants to turn concert trips into longer and more lucrative travel bookings. It is eyeing a move beyond tickets and hotel stays to offer fans everything from local attractions to ground transportation and dining experiences.

The company is betting that fans traveling to see their favorite artists are an opportunity to capture more of their overall travel spending, and particularly as major concerts often draw audiences across borders.

“Most concertgoers ideally wanted to spend an average of four days at the destination,” said Edison Chen, vice president of destination marketing and strategic alliances at Trip.com Group, at a media briefing in Singapore on Wednesday.

A fan flying in for a show can likely also be persuaded to spend a few extra days exploring the destination, said Chen. That creates opportunities for the company to sell attractions, transport and other experiences.

Trip.com Group is building live entertainment into a travel demand channel, moving beyond concert tickets and hotel stays to sell attractions, ground transport, and dining around shows. Edison Chen, vice president of destination marketing and strategic alliances, said most concertgoers ideally wanted to spend an average of four days at the destination, and described them as "artist-first" rather than "destination-first" travelers who pick hotels by proximity to the venue and will pay up for better seats and rooms. The company said bookings for concert travel packages rose 64% year over year in the first half of 2026, with music-related package trips up 80% in the second quarter alone. Trip.com entered live-entertainment travel in Asia about a year ago through a partnership with Live Nation, and in November 2025 began selling concert, sports, and theater tickets directly through an agreement with Dublin-based ticketing firm Coras, giving it primary inventory across European football, U.S. sports, Broadway, and the London West End. After an exclusive presale for BTS concerts in Bangkok, flight bookings from Hong Kong to Bangkok roughly tripled and bookings from Singapore rose about 200%, according to Jesse Yang, head of corporate branding and global events partnership. A new Trip Events section on the homepage lists shows even where Trip.com has no ticketing relationship, while Live Nation Asia expands its venue footprint in Bangkok, Singapore, and Hong Kong.

#6142. The GOP’s midterm plan: Make America hate Muslims again

With less than a week to go before the midterms, the Republicans’ desperation is becoming obvious. Donald Trump is stumping in Mississippi, where Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is locked in a tight race, and half the Cabinet is running around giving speeches to people who don’t know who they are. But the biggest sign of the GOP’s anxiety is the resurrection of a tried-and-true tactic: racism.

Only months ago, the party went all-in on red-baiting, accusing mainstream Democrats of being communist sympathizers, a reaction to the 2025 victory of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the primary wins of a few democratic socialist candidates. This came alongside the now perennial attacks on transgender Americans, led by the president who continues to insist that elementary schools are performing gender-affirming surgeries in the nurse’s office without parental consent.

We knew they would rely on xenophobia, which has  been the central organizing principle of Trump’s decade of political dominance. He may not have kept most of his promises, such as “no new wars” and “bringing prices down on day one,” but he has delivered magnificently on his pledge to incarcerate and deport as many immigrants, undocumented and otherwise, as humanly possible. In fact, he’s even exceeded expectations.

Since they make up the largest share of immigrants, Latinos have been hit the hardest by this cruel policy, and Trump has long asserted that they are all violent criminals. But as we were warned in the 2024 presidential campaign, Haitians have also been among the top immigrant groups targeted by MAGA leaders, with Vice President JD Vance homing in on the racist right-wing id by declaring that these Black immigrants were eating the household pets of their Real American white neighbors.

For a moment, there seemed to be a new target when a social media post by Bo French, the GOP’s nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, went viral, exposing a growing conservative antipathy to Indian Americans. This was somewhat surprising since Vance, one of the party’s leading race-baiters, is married to the daughter of Indian immigrants, and Vivek Ramaswamy, another child of Indian immigrants, is Ohio’s Republican nominee for governor.

But none of these attacks and lies has gotten the traction they were hoping for, so the party has gone back to the deep well to draw up a big bucket of Islamophobia.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

In the wake of 9/11, some in the GOP became infected by a strain of anti-Arab bigotry that, to his credit, George W. Bush attempted to fight. It waxed and waned as the attacks grew more distant. Then came Trump, whose demonization of Muslims goes back to the 2016 campaign. At that time, the U.S. was in the midst of an outbreak of “lone-wolf” terrorist attacks, and his violent rhetoric really got the crowds going.

Trump famously said he wanted to take up waterboarding “and worse,” and told lurid stories about dipping bullets in pigs blood to scare terrorists. Declaring that he would ban all Muslims from coming to America “until we can figure out what the hell is going on,” he executed his infamous “Muslim ban” days after taking office in 2017, an order that became the focus of legal challenges and, after some re-tooling by the administration, was ultimately upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has long been a particular focus of Trump’s ire. As a progressive, she has been a fierce critic of the administration, but no more than most other Democrats. But she’s a Black woman, an immigrant and a Muslim who wears a hijab. Omar, who fled Somalia with her family at eight and lived for years in a Kenyan refugee camp, represents Minnesota, which became one of Trump’s bete noirs after Kamala Harris chose the state’s governor, Tim Walz, as her running mate. Trump began attacking Minnesota’s community of Somali Americans with some of the most bigoted comments in American history, and that’s saying something.

Somalia, he said, is “garbage, a “sh*thouse country” that “stinks.” He has even claimed that 98% of Somali immigrants don’t work and that they are all criminals driving around in Mercedes-Benz and BMWs. Reprising his role as inciter-in-chief, the president called for (white) Minnesotans to “fight back” against the state’s Somali population, writing that they “view you as weak and stupid people.”

Another target of MAGA’s anti-Muslim bigotry is Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan-born Democratic nominee for the Senate. Earlier this week, Vance referred to him as “very, very evil,” a “psychopath” who pushes “anti-white racial hatred.” This charge of reverse racism is one of the favorite tropes of the modern right, guaranteed to draw cheers at a MAGA rally. Trump called El-Sayed a violent jihadist, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. expanded the attacks, saying that the one billion Muslims worldwide contribute nothing to society, having never won the Nobel Prize or any other prestigious awards, an easily disprovable lie.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people. The famous quote from the notorious GOP strategist Lee Atwater, who recommended referring to “welfare” and “busing” to stand in for overtly racist language, held true for years.

Republicans stuck with that tactic for decades, starting with Richard Nixon, who used the term Trump thinks he invented, “law and order,” as a code word for cracking down on Black protests in inner cities. Ronald Reagan famously talked about “welfare queens” during his 1976 primary bid for president, and four years later he opened his presidential campaign by declaring his belief in states’ rights — another dog whistle — in Mississippi, near the spot where white civil rights workers were killed. Three decades later, Trump turned even more creative with his “birther” campaign against President Barack Obama, combining the party’s burgeoning Islamophobia with classic All-American racism. To this day, Trump refers to Obama using his full name — Barack Hussein Obama — with a childish glee.

I don’t think claiming that a whole African country is a “sh*thouse” or saying that Black immigrants are barbecuing their neighbors’ cats for dinner is the kind of subtlety Atwater was talking about. In fact, I will not be surprised to see Trump, who has lost virtually all rhetorical restraint, drop the ugliest epithets of all someday soon. It’s just a matter of time. And if he does, I’m sure JD Vance and all the rest of MAGA’s staunchest loyalists will find a way to rationalize it as something the other side is responsible for.

#6141. ENDING SOON: 100,000 Points Plus A Companion Award—Why Alaska’s Best Credit Card Beats Those From Bigger Airlines

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card is probably the best airline cobrand credit card, and it has a limited-time offer – 100,000 bonus points. Get 100,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award with this offer. To qualify, spend $6,000 or more on purchases within the first 90 days of opening your account. The annual fee is $395.

The offer gives you two different things. The 100,000 bonus points and the 25,000 point Global Companion Award that reduces the points needed for a second passenger’s award ticket.

I think the strongest reasons to consider it are the annual companion award and earning 3 points per dollar on eligible foreign purchases. Alaska has also put a substantial reward at $60,000 in annual spending.

Each account anniversary brings another 25,000-point Global Companion Award, with no annual spending requirement. Spending $60,000 in your card anniversary year earns a separate 100,000 point Global Companion Award. You can earn both. These work on eligible Alaska, Hawaiian and partner awards available through Alaska’s website, in any cabin. Suppose an award costs 35,000 points per passenger. Two tickets would normally require 70,000 points. Applying a 25,000-point certificate brings that down to 45,000 points, plus applicable taxes and fees. If each ticket costs 100,000 points apiece, the larger certificate brings the combined price down from 200,000 to 100,000 points, plus taxes and fees. Things to know: Book both travelers together on the same itinerary. The certificate applies to a new booking, not an existing reservation. You can use it for one-way or roundtrip travel. Multi-city and open-jaw itineraries are excluded. If the companion’s ticket costs more than the certificate covers, pay the difference in points. If it costs less, you lose the unused value. Book within one year of issuance. Travel can take place later, but changes after certificate expiration forfeit the discount. Partially used tickets can’t be changed. Only one certificate can be applied per reservation, and it can’t be combined with another discount. Pay taxes, fees and surcharges with the Summit card. The cardholder doesn’t need to travel – you can book for any two travelers. You still need award space for two. Using all 25,000 points of the anniversary certificate would cover the $395 fee if those saved points are worth 1.58 cents each to you. At 1.5 cents, it’s $375. That’s close enough that using another benefit can put you ahead. But don’t give the certificate full value if you’d otherwise let it expire or use it to save only 10,000 points. Foreign Purchases Are The Standout Earning Category The card earns: 3 points per dollar on eligible dining, foreign transactions, and Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases. 1 point per dollar on other purchases. A 10% relationship bonus on purchase points when you have a qualifying Bank of America or Merrill account. That makes the rates 3.3 and 1.1 points per dollar. Dining and airline bonuses are something offered by numerous cards. Getting a bonus on eligible shopping and other purchases abroad that wouldn’t ordinarily fall into a bonus category is much more interesting. (Generally Chase buys points at a discount from its cobrand partners on foreign transactions, effectively subsidized by the program, making it uneconomic to offer something like this.) The relationship bonus triggers with qualifying checking accounts, consumer savings and certificates of deposit, as well as Merrill investment accounts. A new account can take up to 60 days to trigger the bonus. The Card Can Save Money On American Award Tickets Atmos charges a $20 partner award booking fee per person, each way. Summit waives it when you redeem points from the primary cardholder’s account and pay the award’s taxes and fees with that card. The primary cardholder doesn’t have to be traveling. That saves $80 on a roundtrip partner award for two. Five such bookings would save $400, more than the annual fee, without assigning any value to the companion award or lounge passes. This is a fee Alaska imposes and then lets its premium cardholders avoid. I’d prefer they didn’t charge it in the first place. But if you’re booking these awards anyway, the savings are great. Free points sharing helps, too. The primary cardholder can establish a network with up to ten other Atmos members and move redeemable points between linked accounts without a transfer fee. Each member can belong to only one network, and the primary cardholder can change each linked account only once every 12 months. Status points can’t be transferred. Being able to combine balances is useful when several family members have points but no one has enough for the award you want. Lounge Access, Bags And Travel Benefits The card’s travel benefits include: Eight Alaska Lounge passes annually, issued two per calendar quarter. They expire at the end of that quarter. Each covers one adult and up to two accompanying children under 21, with access to Alaska Lounges for the travel day. You need an eligible same-day boarding pass, and access is subject to capacity. These don’t admit you to Hawaiian’s lounges or partner lounges. Eight Alaska Wi-Fi passes annually, also two per quarter. Each is for one flight, and unused passes expire at quarter-end. A first checked bag free and preferred boarding for the cardholder and up to six guests on the same reservation on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian flights, when airfare is purchased with the card. Include the primary cardholder’s Atmos number. 20% back on eligible onboard purchases. This is for Alaska food, beverages and Wi-Fi, and Hawaiian food and beverages, when paid with the card. Up to $120 for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fees every four years when charged to the card. Complimentary upgrade waitlist priority for eligible elite members. A same-day confirmed change fee waiver. Alaska’s benefits page includes eligible Alaska and Hawaiian flights. Saver fares are excluded, and routing and same day travel restrictions apply. For a family of two adults and two children under 21, two lounge passes can cover everyone for a travel day. There’s also a $50 delay voucher. For an eligible Alaska booking purchased directly with the Summit card, a departure delay of at least two hours or a cancellation within 24 hours of departure can qualify. It’s for the primary cardholder, limited to one per calendar day, and expires 48 hours after issuance. Activation instructions arrive by email, and eligible spending is reimbursed as a statement credit. There’s also trip and baggage delay coverage, trip cancellation and interruption protection, and lost luggage reimbursement. along with primary rental car collision coverage. The $60,000 Spend Strategy Summit earns one status point per $2 in purchases, plus 10,000 status points each account anniversary beginning with your first anniversary. Atmos Gold requires 40,000 status points and comes with oneworld Sapphire. So $60,000 of spending produces 30,000 status points. An anniversary deposit of 10,000 in the same qualification year gets you to Gold which is oneworld sapphire. Status qualification runs by calendar year. The $60,000 companion award threshold runs by card anniversary year. Spending split between two calendar years can earn the certificate without producing Gold in either year. And a new cardholder doesn’t receive the anniversary status points immediately upon opening the account. Suppose you put $60,000 of purchases that earn the base rate on Summit. With the relationship bonus, you’d earn 66,000 redeemable points and the 100,000-point companion certificate. A card earning 2 points per dollar would generate 120,000 points on that same spending. You’re giving up 54,000 points in the alternative program in exchange for the certificate and the status credit. That can definitely be worth it even aside from the status. This card is too much value. I have too many points and certificates to the point that I can barely use them all. I haven’t paid for a flight in a year. Please stop signing up for this card so I can find more Saver J awards

I love this card. Easily worth the annual fee – after the SUB.

There’s one other benefit for high status AS flyers. Having the Summit card is a tiebreaker for upgrade priority. AS still has (for now) a higher number of seats available for upgrade than say Delta, so it can matter.

I avoided going for airline status in the past; the Summit card changed the calculus for me, because the opportunity cost (3x Dining and Foreign purchases) of earnings is so much lower, and because of the consumer friendliness of the Atmos program (distance-based earnings, status points earnings on award flights). Now I’m an Atmos Platinum and I’m looking forward to visiting some First Class lounges in the near future.

Also echo EasyMoney, it’s been too easy for me to find opportunities to use my points in the past 18 months; including a Starlux J flight and booking AA Flagship Suites for my brother and sister-in-law (not the best use of the 100K companion cert, but it was their first time ever flying J so it was worth it). Hope AS doesn’t start nerfing those opportunities anytime soon.

Great card, use VFTW links, but most importantly, welcome to late October, may the increased year-end SUBs descend upon all of us.

@Peter — Move over Toyotathon, it’s a SUB-Festivus for the rest of us! Time for the Airing of Grievances against C1—torching all 3 bureaus for a single rejection is the Feat of Strength nobody asked for. May the Q4 approval odds be in your favor!

primary auto rental collision damage waiver coverage WITHOUT excluding New York residents as Chase does.

I made the mistake last year with Capitol 1 Venture/Venture X… and I paid the price of not reading the fine print/asking enough questions.

@Jack. I would not count on a product change to get you a signup bonus. You can have both the Ascent and Summit at the same time. I have 2 grandfathered Ascents and the Summit so I know it’s possible.

@LK — I don’t get why there’s still confusion with this. In NY, if you don’t have a primary auto insurance policy, because, let’s say, you don’t have a car (many people in NYC don’t), then Chase Sapphire Reserve (and Preferred) are effectively primary, if you decline CDW, etc. (follow all their other rules.)
